description: Skeletal muscle fibre differentiation is the route by which unspecialised myogenic precursors become contractile muscle: myoblasts exit the cycle, fuse into multinucleate myotubes, switch on sarcomeric and structural genes, and mature into fibres that generate force. Failure at these steps underlies congenital myopathies and muscular dystrophies. Several of the genes here build or decorate the glycan on alpha-dystroglycan that links the fibre to laminin in its basement membrane, so that loss of the glycosyltransferases and their partners produces dystroglycanopathy with weakness and, in severe forms, brain and eye malformation; a collagen VI chain contributes the matrix side of the same connection. Others act earlier or inside the fibre: transcriptional and RNA-binding regulators drive the myogenic programme and stabilise muscle transcripts, retinoic acid catabolism shapes patterning cues, and a kelch-family sarcomeric protein is needed for thin-filament assembly and normal fibre strength.

Proteins only work where they are delivered, and this pathway covers the control layer over that delivery dash how strongly, how fast and in which direction proteins are moved between compartments inside a cell. It governs whether a transcription factor reaches the nucleus, whether a newly made secretory protein leaves the ER, and whether a misfolded one is pulled back to the cytosol for destruction, so its failure shows up as mislocalised signalling proteins, ER stress and aggregate accumulation. Several arms are visible: COPII coat assembly and cargo selection at ER exit sites through SAR1 GTPases, SEC13/SEC31 and the SEC24 cargo adaptors; nuclear import and export via RAN, its GAP, importins and exportins with nucleoporins; ER-associated degradation using lectin-like recognition, derlins and dedicated ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes; and kinases, phosphatases, 14-3-3 proteins and centrosomal scaffolds that time and target these movements.

Cells commit to duplicating their genome only once per cycle, and the RB1:E2F axis is the switch that licenses that commitment. E2F1 with its DP partners drives transcription of the machinery S phase requires — origin recognition complex subunits, the MCM8 helicase, and the DNA polymerase alpha/primase heterotetramer that lays down initiating RNA-DNA primers — while RB1 binds E2F and holds those genes silent until cyclin-dependent kinase phosphorylation releases it. Beyond transcription, E2F1 acts directly at replication initiation, and the pathway is tuned by protein phosphatase 2A holoenzymes and by mitotic CDK1-cyclin B activity, linking origin firing to cell cycle position. Loss of RB1 control uncouples proliferation from growth signals and is one of the most common events in human cancer, whereas intact signalling also couples replication to DNA damage responses and to exit from the cycle during differentiation.

Mature neurons are post-mitotic, and this pathway describes how loss of control over CDK5 forces them back toward cell cycle activity and death, a sequence implicated in Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegeneration. Amyloid-beta, excitotoxicity, ischemia and oxidative stress raise intracellular calcium and activate calpains, which cleave the CDK5 activator p35 into the longer-lived, unanchored p25; the resulting CDK5:p25 complex is constitutively active and mislocalized to cytoplasm and nucleus, where it reaches substrates the kinase normally never sees. Among these are the CDC25 phosphatases, whose phosphorylation both boosts their activity and frees them from 14-3-3 sequestration, allowing inappropriate activation of mitotic and G1 CDKs. Downstream consequences include FOXO3-driven expression of pro-apoptotic BIM and FasL, altered antioxidant enzymes, and breakdown of nuclear lamina and Golgi architecture, culminating in neuronal apoptosis.

Triglyceride metabolism is how the body stores surplus fatty acids as neutral lipid and releases them again when fuel is needed, and it links dietary fat absorption, adipose storage, hepatic lipid handling and plasma lipoprotein transport into one continuous economy. Synthesis proceeds through glycerol-3-phosphate acylation by GPAT and AGPAT enzymes, dephosphorylation of phosphatidate by lipins, and final esterification by DGAT1 and DGAT2; monoacylglycerol acyltransferases provide the intestinal re-esterification route after pancreatic lipases digest dietary fat. Mobilisation runs the other way through ATGL (PNPLA2) with its activator ABHD5, hormone-sensitive lipase and monoacylglycerol lipase acting on perilipin-coated droplets under protein kinase A control. Circulating triglyceride is delivered by apoB-containing particles and hydrolysed by lipoprotein lipase with its APOC2 activator and GPIHBP1 anchor, while SREBF1, INSIG and liver X receptors set transcriptional tone. Defects cause hypertriglyceridaemia, lipodystrophy, hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance.

Tissues need brakes on cell division as much as accelerators, and this collection of growth-suppressing activities is what stops, slows or limits expansion of a cell population. It underlies organ size control, wound resolution, terminal differentiation and immune self-restraint; when it fails, hyperplasia and cancer follow. The machinery is broad: cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors and the retinoblastoma-p53 axis impose cell cycle arrest, tumour suppressors such as PTEN, NF1, NF2, VHL, STK11 and the Hippo kinases restrain growth-factor and mTOR signalling, and secreted cues including TGF-beta family ligands, BMPs, Wnt antagonists such as the SFRPs, and somatostatin acting through its receptors deliver antiproliferative signals from outside. Antiproliferative RNA-binding and BTG/TOB proteins and many microRNAs damp growth transcripts, while inhibitory immune receptors like CTLA4, PD-L1 and PTPN6 curb lymphocyte clonal expansion.

Interleukin-2 acting through STAT5 is the main growth and survival signal for antigen-activated T cells, and this transcriptional programme is what that signal produces. It sustains clonal expansion after antigen encounter and maintains regulatory T cells, so its loss causes severe immunodeficiency while its unchecked activity drives lymphoproliferation; it is also the axis targeted by IL-2 based immunotherapy and by JAK inhibitors. Ligand binding to the IL2RA/IL2RB receptor chains activates JAK-STAT5, which induces its own brakes in CISH, SOCS1 and SOCS2, together with cell-cycle and anti-apoptotic effectors such as CCND2, CCND3, MYC, PIM1, BCL2 and BCL2L1. Much of the output defines activated and regulatory T cell identity: CTLA4, ICOS, TNFRSF4, TNFRSF18, IKZF2 and IRF4, alongside cytokines, chemokine receptors, adhesion molecules and nutrient transporters that support the metabolic demands of proliferation.

Circulating low-density lipoprotein does not by itself trigger platelets, but at normal plasma concentrations it lowers their threshold for activation, so that thrombin, collagen or ADP produce a larger aggregation response. This sensitization links dyslipidaemia to the prothrombotic tendency seen in atherosclerosis. The apolipoprotein B component of LDL is recognised by ApoER2 (LRP8), a splice variant of the apolipoprotein E receptor family, whose engagement recruits the Src-family kinase Fgr and leads to phosphorylation of p38 MAP kinase on its activation loop. Active p38 phosphorylates cytosolic phospholipase A2, releasing arachidonate for thromboxane production and amplifying granule release and aggregation. The signal is self-limiting: LDL also promotes PECAM-1 signalling, which recruits the phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2 together with protein phosphatase 2A holoenzymes to dephosphorylate p38 and terminate the primed state.

Neural crest cells arise at the border between neural plate and epidermis, and this pathway covers the step at which a cell is locked into that fate rather than remaining neural or epidermal. The commitment matters because crest derivatives build much of the face and skull, peripheral neurons and glia, melanocytes and cardiac outflow structures, and failures produce craniofacial and cardiac malformations of the kind seen in neurocristopathies. Wnt ligands and secreted frizzled-related antagonists set the dose of signalling at the neural plate border, while endothelin 1 acting through its receptor EDNRA patterns the branchial arch crest and drives the homeobox factor GSC in pharyngeal skeletal precursors. SOX9 then commits crest-derived cells toward chondrogenic and skeletal programmes. The pathway thus links inductive signalling at the ectodermal border to lineage-defining transcription downstream.

Organs acquire their shape through iterative branching, budding, folding and condensation of epithelium against mesenchyme, and this set covers the factors that tune how far, how fast and in what pattern that shaping proceeds. It matters because the same tuning determines nephron number in the kidney, branch density in lung, salivary gland and mammary tissue, tooth and hair placode spacing, and skeletal and craniofacial form; its disturbance underlies renal hypodysplasia, cleft and tooth agenesis syndromes, and polycystic kidney disease. Secreted cues dominate — BMPs with their antagonists noggin and gremlin, FGF7 and FGF10 signalling to FGFR1 through FRS2 with Sprouty feedback, hedgehog acting via smoothened, GDNF driving ureteric bud outgrowth, and WNT ligands read out through beta-catenin or planar cell polarity via VANGL2. Transcription factors including WT1, PAX8, SIX1/SIX2, SOX9 and GATA3 convert these gradients into progenitor fate and epithelial morphogenetic behaviour.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 4 transmits signals from FGF ligands into RAS-ERK activation, and the feedback circuits that shut this output down are what keep the response transient and dose-appropriate. Negative regulation of FGFR4 signaling matters because sustained receptor output drives proliferative and metabolic programmes; FGFR4 in particular, paired with the co-receptor beta-Klotho, mediates FGF19 and FGF23 signalling that controls bile acid synthesis and phosphate handling, and its deregulation is implicated in liver cancer. Restraint is imposed at several levels: the E3 ligase CBL ubiquitinates the activated receptor and routes it for endocytic degradation, ERK-mediated phosphorylation of the adaptor FRS2 blunts further recruitment of GRB2 and PTPN11, Sprouty proteins interfere with signal propagation to BRAF, and protein phosphatase 2A subunits reverse activating phosphorylation. Several inhibitors are themselves induced by the pathway, forming delayed negative feedback.

Iron is indispensable for heme, iron-sulfur clusters and oxygen transport, yet free iron drives Fenton chemistry and oxidative damage, so cells hold it within a narrow range. This homeostatic programme couples uptake, storage, use and export: transferrin and its receptors deliver iron to acidified endosomes, ferrireductases and divalent metal transporters move it into the cytosol, ferritin heavy and light chains sequester it, and ferroportin provides the sole cellular exit. Sensing runs through the iron-regulatory proteins ACO1 and IREB2 acting on mRNA iron-responsive elements, with FBXL5-directed degradation tuning that switch, while NCOA4 delivers ferritin to lysosomes for ferritinophagy. At the organismal level, BMP6-SMAD signalling through hemojuvelin and HFE sets hepcidin output, which internalises ferroportin. Failure produces hemochromatosis, anaemias, and iron-dependent cell death, and links this chemistry to hypoxia signalling and heme catabolism.

When misfolded protein accumulates in the endoplasmic reticulum, cells mount the unfolded protein response, a stress programme that restores folding capacity or, failing that, commits the cell to death. It matters most in professional secretory cells — plasma cells, pancreatic beta cells, chondrocytes, hepatocytes — whose normal differentiation depends on it, and its failure underlies diabetes, neurodegeneration and skeletal dysplasias. Three sensors act in parallel: IRE1 (ERN1) dimerizes and splices XBP1 mRNA unconventionally to yield an active transcription factor; membrane-tethered ATF6 and related CREB3 factors travel to the Golgi for cleavage by site-1 and site-2 proteases, releasing their cytosolic transcriptional domains; and PERK (EIF2AK3) phosphorylates eIF2α to throttle translation while inducing ATF4 and CHOP (DDIT3). Outputs include ER chaperones such as BiP (HSPA5), GRP94 and calreticulin, disulfide isomerases, ERAD components including SYVN1 and EDEM1, and expanded secretory and mRNA-decay machinery.

Moving solutes from the cytosol into the endoplasmic reticulum lumen against a gradient requires dedicated ATP-driven pumps, and this pathway covers that directed import. Two of its jobs are physiologically distinct. The sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPases ATP2A2 and ATP2A3 pump cytosolic Ca2+ back into the ER and sarcoplasmic reticulum, terminating calcium signals, refilling the store that supports muscle relaxation and secretory signalling, and maintaining the high-calcium environment that ER chaperones need; loss of ATP2A2 function causes Darier disease and its depletion triggers ER stress. The transporters TAP1 and TAP2 form a heterodimeric ABC pump that translocates proteasome-generated peptides into the ER for loading onto MHC class I, so cytotoxic T cell surveillance of virus-infected and tumour cells depends on it. Together these activities link store loading, ER homeostasis and antigen presentation to import across the ER membrane.

Genomes are continuously damaged by radiation, chemical mutagens, endogenous oxidants and alkylating agents, and by errors made during replication; DNA repair is the collective response that restores the original sequence and keeps cells viable and non-mutagenic. Its failure produces cancer predisposition and progeria-like and immunodeficiency syndromes, as seen with mutations in BRCA1/BRCA2, the Fanconi anaemia genes, mismatch repair genes such as MLH1 and MSH2, and the nucleotide excision repair factors XPA and XPC. Distinct routes are represented: direct reversal by alkyltransferases and dioxygenases, base excision initiated by DNA glycosylases and APEX1, nucleotide excision coupled to transcription, mismatch correction, translesion synthesis by Y-family polymerases, and double-strand break repair by homologous recombination or end joining. Sensing and signalling through ATM, ATR and checkpoint kinases coordinate arrest with repair, while chromatin remodellers, ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases control access to damaged DNA.

How much fat a cell esterifies into triglyceride is set by the controls gathered here, which tune the rate and extent of triglyceride biosynthesis rather than carrying out its core acyltransferase steps. The output matters for whether the liver stores or exports lipid, whether adipose tissue expands appropriately, and whether excess flux produces steatosis and insulin resistance. Transcriptional input dominates: SREBF1 drives lipogenic gene expression, the liver X receptors NR1H2 and NR1H3 induce it in response to sterol load, and SIRT1 and KAT5 impose acetylation-dependent restraint, with several microRNAs trimming transcripts of lipogenic enzymes. Other members act on flux and substrate supply — fatty acid uptake through SLC27A1 and lipoprotein receptors, phosphatidate phosphatase regulation by CTDNEP1 with its partner CNEP1R1, terminal acylation by DGAT2, and droplet-surface PLIN5 governing whether stored triglyceride is retained or mobilised.

Mitosis ends only when the proteins that sustained it are destroyed, and this is the step that destroys them. Once mitotic kinases phosphorylate the anaphase-promoting complex, the activator Cdc20 docks onto the core to form APC/C:Cdc20, a multisubunit ubiquitin ligase that, with E2 enzymes such as UBE2C and UBE2S, polyubiquitinates cyclin A, cyclin B and securin for proteasomal destruction. Loss of securin frees separase to cleave cohesin so sister chromatids can part, while cyclin B loss inactivates CDK1 and permits mitotic exit and cytokinesis. The ligase is held in check until chromosomes are correctly attached: BUB1B, BUB3 and MAD2L1 sequester Cdc20 as part of spindle checkpoint surveillance. Mistiming here yields premature separation, aneuploidy and chromosomal instability of the kind seen in tumours, placing this irreversible proteolytic switch at the heart of cell cycle control.

HIV-1 Nef strips immune receptors from the surface of an infected cell by linking them to the clathrin adaptor machinery, and this rerouting is a large part of why Nef is needed for full viral virulence and progression to disease. CD4, CD8, CD28 and MHC class I are pulled into AP-1 and AP-2 dependent endosomal and lysosomal itineraries rather than recycling to the plasma membrane, with ARF1, the vacuolar ATPase subunit ATP6V1H and the sorting connector PACS1 contributing to adaptor recruitment and trafficking. Loss of surface MHC class I, presented with beta-2-microglobulin, hides the infected cell from cytotoxic T lymphocytes, while removal of CD4 and the costimulatory receptor CD28 weakens contacts with antigen-presenting cells and limits superinfection. LCK signalling from the T cell receptor complex is disrupted in parallel, so viral immune evasion here is achieved entirely by subverting normal receptor endocytosis and sorting.

Mating behavior covers the coordinated courtship, partner recognition, copulatory and pair-bonding interactions through which animals achieve fertilization, and it sits at the intersection of neuroendocrine signalling and reproductive physiology. The genes here span the neuropeptide axis that shapes sexual and affiliative behaviour — oxytocin and vasopressin with their receptors, substance P and its receptor — alongside the monoamine systems that supply motivation and reward, including tyrosine hydroxylase for catecholamine synthesis, dopamine D1 and D5 receptors, the serotonin transporter and the striatal signalling proteins DARPP-32 and spinophilin. Hormonal context is set by thyroid hormone receptors and a nuclear receptor coactivator, while melatonin receptor signalling ties behaviour to photoperiod. A separate arm acts in the reproductive tract and semen, where semenogelin and protease inhibitors govern coagulation and liquefaction. Disruption impairs courtship, erectile and ejaculatory function, and social bonding.

Cells navigate by reading chemical gradients, and this pathway covers the inputs that tune how strongly and in which direction they move. It governs leukocyte recruitment to infected or injured tissue, endothelial sprouting during angiogenesis, and axon pathfinding in the developing nervous system, so its dysregulation contributes to chronic inflammation, fibrosis, tumour invasion and defective wiring. The bulk of the machinery is ligand-receptor: CC and CXC chemokines acting through receptors such as CCR2, CCR7, CXCR2 and CX3CR1, complement fragments signalling via C5AR1 and C3AR1, and growth factor systems including VEGF-KDR, PDGF, CSF1-CSF1R and HGF-MET. Guidance cues of the slit-robo, semaphorin-plexin and netrin-related families set repulsion and attraction in neurons and vessels alike. Downstream, Rac GTPases, focal adhesion kinases, ERK signalling and actin regulators convert receptor occupancy into polarised protrusion, while phosphatases, DUSP1 and several microRNAs damp the response.

Blood glucose must be used, stored, or made as conditions demand, and this pathway covers the controls that set the rate of glucose metabolism rather than the catabolic steps themselves. It links hormonal signals to hepatic, muscle and adipose fuel choice: insulin and glucagon, insulin receptor signalling through IRS1/IRS2 and AKT to FOXO1, adipokines such as leptin and adiponectin acting via their receptors, and glucocorticoid and PPAR-family transcriptional programmes. Glucokinase sets hepatic glucose sensing, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase gates gluconeogenesis, pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases shunt pyruvate away from oxidation, and protein phosphatase 1 glycogen-targeting subunits together with phosphorylase kinase components determine glycogen storage. AMPK subunits, sirtuins, PPARGC1A and circadian factors including CRY1 and RORA impose energy-status and time-of-day control. Failure of this regulation underlies insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and glycogen storage disorders.

Short-lived transcripts encoding cytokines, growth factors and cell cycle regulators carry AU-rich elements in their 3' untranslated regions, and KSRP is one of the proteins that reads those elements and condemns the message to rapid decay. This route sets how long an inflammatory or proliferative signal persists after transcription stops; losing it leaves transcripts such as cytokine mRNAs abnormally stable, a route to chronic inflammation and unrestrained growth signalling. Bound KSRP recruits the deadenylase PARN to shorten the poly(A) tail, the decapping enzyme DCP2 to strip the 5' cap, and the multisubunit exosome with its DIS3 ribonuclease to degrade the body of the message 3' to 5'. Kinases set the switch: Akt phosphorylation at serine 193 creates a 14-3-3zeta binding site that sequesters KSRP in the nucleus and blocks decay, while p38 MAPK signalling likewise tempers its destabilizing activity.

HIV-1 depends on a single viral protein to convert a stalled polymerase at its promoter into a processive one, and this step — assembly of the Tat-containing elongation complex — is what allows full-length viral transcripts to be made rather than short abortive ones. Without it the provirus stays latent, which is why this transition is central both to viral replication and to latency-reversal strategies. Tat binds the TAR stem-loop in the nascent transcript and recruits P-TEFb, the cyclin T1–CDK9 kinase, which phosphorylates the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain together with the pausing factors DSIF (SUPT4H1/SUPT5H) and NELF, releasing the paused enzyme. The complex also carries general factors TFIIF and TFIIH, elongin and ELL elongation activities, TFIIS, the FACT histone chaperone, and cap-binding proteins, mirroring normal host promoter-proximal pause release hijacked for viral gene expression.

Phagocytosis is how macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells and microglia swallow microbes, dying cells and debris and route them to the lysosome for destruction. It underlies innate defence against bacteria and fungi, the silent clearance of apoptotic cells that prevents autoimmunity, surfactant and lipid turnover in the lung, and synaptic pruning in the brain. Recognition comes from opsonins and their receptors complement components with integrin partners, IgG-binding Fc receptors, collectins and pentraxins and from direct sensors of exposed phosphatidylserine such as MERTK, TIMD4 and MFGE8, while CD47 SIRPA signals self and spares healthy cells. Receptor engagement activates Src-family and SYK kinases, PLCG2, and Rho-family GTPase exchange through VAV and DOCK ELMO modules to drive actin remodelling and cup closure. Phosphoinositide turnover and a RAB cascade then mature the phagosome, coupling it to NADPH oxidase assembly, antigen presentation and cytokine output.

Solute carriers are the membrane transporters that move sugars, amino acids, ions, metals, nucleosides, vitamins and organic anions across plasma and organelle membranes, and this collection gathers those in which loss-of-function mutations cause recognisable human disease. The clinical range shows how much depends on them: glucose transporter defects cause epileptic encephalopathy and renal glycosuria, thiazide- and loop-sensitive salt transporters underlie Gitelman and Bartter syndromes, divalent metal and ferroportin transporters cause iron overload or anaemia, amino acid carriers cause cystinuria and lysinuric protein intolerance, nucleotide-sugar transporters cause congenital glycosylation disorders, and thyroid iodide uptake failure causes hypothyroidism. Alongside the carriers themselves are accessory subunits and the nuclear pore complex, whose nucleocytoplasmic transport channel represents a distinct route of macromolecular movement with its own nephrotic and neurological disease phenotypes. Together they frame epithelial absorption, reabsorption in the kidney and intestine, and neurotransmitter clearance as transporter-dependent physiology.

Sphingolipids are built on a long-chain amino alcohol backbone rather than glycerol, and their synthesis supplies membranes with ceramide, sphingomyelin, and the glycosphingolipids and gangliosides that define lipid rafts, myelin, and the skin permeability barrier. The route begins at the endoplasmic reticulum with serine palmitoyltransferase, whose activity is restrained by ORMDL proteins to keep sphingoid base supply matched to demand; ceramide synthases acylate the base with fatty acids of defined chain length, and desaturase and reductase steps finish the ceramide. Transfer proteins carry ceramide to the Golgi, where sphingomyelin synthases and glucosylceramide synthase branch the pathway, and successive galactosyl-, N-acetylgalactosaminyl- and sialyltransferases elaborate the ganglioside series. Kinases and a transporter generate and export sphingosine-1-phosphate, a signal for lymphocyte trafficking and vascular integrity, while ceramidases and sphingomyelinases feed catabolic balance. Defects cause lysosomal storage disease, ichthyosis, and neurodegeneration.

Otolith development builds the calcium carbonate stones of the inner ear that give vertebrates a sense of gravity and linear acceleration. These biomineral structures sit on the maculae of the utricle and saccule, and their absence or malformation causes vestibular dysfunction "imbalance, abnormal righting reflexes, and in humans a contribution to benign paroxysmal positional vertigo when crystals detach. The process depends on an organic matrix scaffold secreted into the endolymph, with otoconin-90 and otolin-1 forming the protein framework onto which mineral is deposited. An NADPH oxidase restricted to the vestibular epithelium supplies reactive oxygen species needed for matrix assembly, while a proton channel regulates the pH and calcium handling of the surrounding fluid. Autophagy components and vesicle-trafficking machinery contribute to matrix secretion and crystal seeding, linking otolith formation to broader control of protein delivery and epithelial mineralization.

Carnitine is the carrier that lets long-chain fatty acids cross into the mitochondrial matrix for beta-oxidation, so cells that burn fat for energy depend on an adequate supply, and shortfalls present as metabolic disease with impaired fasting tolerance. Most carnitine comes from the diet, but it can also be made de novo in four steps from trimethyllysine, itself released when proteins bearing S-adenosylmethionine-methylated lysines are degraded. A mitochondrial hydroxylase acts first on trimethyllysine, an aldolase step releases the aldehyde, a dehydrogenase oxidises it to gamma-butyrobetaine, and a final dioxygenase hydroxylates that intermediate to carnitine. Only liver and kidney carry out this last step appreciably, so muscle and other high-demand tissues rely on export and plasma-membrane uptake transporters. Loss of the first enzyme is associated with a disorder of carnitine biosynthesis linked to neurodevelopmental phenotypes.

Cell cycle checkpoints are the surveillance systems that hold division in check until the previous step has been completed correctly, and they are the reason somatic cells maintain a stable genome while tumour cells generally do not. Damage sensors and the apical kinases ATM and ATR, with CHEK1 and CHEK2 downstream, delay CDK activation at the G1/S and G2/M transitions, acting through TP53 and CDKN1A, through degradation of CDC25A phosphatases, and through inhibitory phosphorylation by WEE1 and PKMYT1, with 14-3-3 proteins sequestering mitotic regulators. At mitosis, unattached kinetochores built on the centromere and NDC80/MIS12 networks generate a MAD2/BUB-dependent signal that restrains CDC20 and the anaphase-promoting complex until every chromosome is bioriented. Ubiquitin ligases and the proteasome execute the resulting decisions. Loss of these controls produces aneuploidy, replication stress and the mutational tolerance that underlies cancer predisposition.

Platelets must switch from a quiescent circulating state to an adhesive, aggregating one within seconds of vessel injury, and this arm of platelet activation covers the tyrosine-kinase route that does it. Collagen exposed in damaged subendothelium engages the glycoprotein VI receptor, whose signal passes through the immune receptor gamma chain FCER1G, the Src-family kinase LYN and the spleen tyrosine kinase SYK, then through the adaptor LCP2 and the exchange factor VAV1 to phospholipase C-gamma2 and PI3K. The resulting inositol phosphate and calcium signals, reinforced by Gq-family alpha subunits GNAQ and GNA15 acting downstream of thrombin and thromboxane receptors, drive granule secretion, integrin activation and shape change. Loss of PLCG2 or SYK function causes bleeding, while overactivity of the same route contributes to arterial thrombosis, making these kinases antiplatelet drug targets.

Genomes are damaged continuously by radiation, chemicals, replication errors and oxidative metabolism, and the DNA damage response is the cell's coordinated reaction to that damage: detect the lesion, halt the cell cycle, repair it, or kill the cell if repair fails. Loss of this surveillance produces the mutator phenotypes behind cancer predisposition, immunodeficiency and premature ageing syndromes. Sensor kinases ATM, ATR and DNA-PK are activated at breaks and stalled forks and signal through CHEK1, CHEK2 and TP53 to induce CDKN1A-mediated arrest or apoptosis via BAX and PMAIP1. Downstream lie every major repair route — base and nucleotide excision, mismatch correction, non-homologous end joining, homologous recombination with BRCA1/BRCA2 and RAD51, Fanconi anaemia crosslink repair and translesion polymerases — supported by chromatin remodellers, ubiquitin and PARP signalling at damage sites, and by replication fork protection and telomere maintenance.

Fibroblast growth factors binding FGFR2 do more than drive proliferation: through the phosphoinositide 3-kinase arm of the receptor's output they keep cells alive, and this survival signalling is what allows growth factors to protect tissues from apoptosis. Ligand-bound, dimerised FGFR2 phosphorylates the docking protein FRS2, which recruits GRB2 and the phosphatase SHP2 to assemble a complex with GAB1; GAB1 then brings in the p85 regulatory and p110alpha catalytic subunits of PI3K. The resulting PIP3 recruits PDK1 and AKT, and active AKT suppresses pro-apoptotic effectors and inhibits GSK-3beta, adding further anti-apoptotic tone. The same axis contributes to migration, metabolism and growth. Because FGFR2 is used in limb, skeletal and craniofacial development and in epithelial maintenance, mutations that alter its signalling cause craniosynostosis syndromes, while amplification sustains survival signalling in gastric and breast cancers.

Hereditary fructose intolerance is what happens when the liver cannot process the fructose it takes up. Dietary fructose is phosphorylated to fructose 1-phosphate, and aldolase B, encoded by ALDOB, is the enzyme that cleaves this intermediate to dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde so the carbons can enter glycolysis and gluconeogenesis. When aldolase B activity is lost through recessive mutation, fructose 1-phosphate accumulates and sequesters phosphate and adenine nucleotides, inhibiting gluconeogenesis and glycogen breakdown. Affected infants develop hypoglycaemia, vomiting, lactic acidosis, liver and kidney injury after fructose or sucrose exposure, and the illness can be fatal, though it is controlled simply by lifelong exclusion of fructose and sorbitol from the diet. The condition illustrates how a single step of hepatic carbohydrate metabolism governs tolerance of a common dietary sugar.

ERBB2 is the receptor tyrosine kinase that no ligand binds directly; it works instead as the preferred partner for EGFR, ERBB3 and ERBB4 once those receptors are engaged by EGF-family ligands or neuregulins, and the resulting heterodimers drive epithelial proliferation, survival and differentiation. Because a dimerization-ready receptor needs no ligand of its own, amplification of ERBB2 forces constitutive signalling and defines an aggressive subtype of breast and gastric cancer that is the target of receptor-directed antibodies and kinase inhibitors. Inactive receptor is held by HSP90 with CDC37, while ERBIN confines it to basolateral membrane in polarized epithelium. After dimerization, trans-autophosphorylated C-tail tyrosines recruit GRB2, SHC1, GAB1 and PI3K, feeding the RAS-RAF-MAP kinase cascade, AKT signalling and phospholipase C gamma. Ubiquitin ligases including RNF41 and STUB1, deubiquitination by USP8, and phosphatases such as PTPN12 and PTPN18 set signal duration and receptor turnover.

Glycerophospholipid metabolism builds, remodels and breaks down the phospholipids that make every cellular membrane, and it also generates most of the lipid second messengers cells use to signal. Its outputs set membrane curvature, fluidity and surface charge, supply lung surfactant and lipoprotein lipids, anchor proteins to the cell surface through GPI attachment, and mark organelle identity. Synthesis proceeds from glycerol-3-phosphate through acyltransferases and cytidine-nucleotide steps to phosphatidylcholine, ethanolamine, serine, inositol and cardiolipin, while phospholipases, lysophospholipid acyltransferases and serine hydrolases remodel acyl chains and release arachidonate. A large kinase and phosphatase network writes and erases phosphoinositide codes that recruit trafficking and autophagy machinery, with PTEN and phosphoinositide 3-kinases governing growth signalling. Defects cause surfactant deficiency, myotubular and demyelinating neuropathies, GPI-anchor deficiencies, and cardiolipin-linked cardiomyopathy.

Erythrocyte development covers the maturation of a committed progenitor into the enucleated, haemoglobin-filled red cell that carries oxygen, and it is the process that sets circulating red cell mass and, when disturbed, produces anaemias and haemoglobinopathies. Erythropoietin drives survival and expansion of progenitors, while GATA1, TAL1, KLF2 and ZBTB7A form the transcriptional core that switches on globin genes; the full globin repertoire here, from embryonic and fetal chains to adult HBB and HBD, reflects the developmental switching that determines oxygen affinity at each life stage. Terminal maturation demands iron and haem handling through transporters such as SLC11A2, ABCB10 and FLVCR1, assembly of the deformable membrane skeleton by band 3, protein 4.2, dematin and tropomodulin, and cytoskeletal remodelling via Rac GTPases and DIAPH3 for enucleation. G6PD and BPGM equip the mature cell for oxidative defence and oxygen release.

L-serine catabolism disposes of surplus serine and links it to one-carbon and sulfur metabolism, so that amino acid supply from diet and gluconeogenic precursors is balanced against demand. Serine dehydratase, expressed mainly in liver, deaminates serine to pyruvate and ammonia, feeding carbon into gluconeogenesis and the citric acid cycle; a related dehydratase-like protein accompanies it. Cytosolic serine hydroxymethyltransferase transfers the side-chain carbon of serine to tetrahydrofolate, yielding glycine and 5,10-methylene-THF, the entry point for nucleotide synthesis and methylation. Cystathionine beta-synthase instead condenses serine with homocysteine in the transsulfuration route toward cysteine and glutathione, and its loss causes homocystinuria with thrombosis and skeletal and ocular disease. Flux through these steps is sensitive to hormonal and dietary protein status, tying serine disposal to hepatic nitrogen handling.

Many bacterial diseases are caused not by the bacterium itself but by secreted toxins that enter host cells and sabotage them, and the uptake and actions of bacterial toxins covers that shared route of intoxication. Each toxin is bipartite: one moiety binds a surface receptor and delivers the second, catalytic moiety into the cytosol. The host proteins here are the doors and the targets. Anthrax toxin uses the receptors ANTXR1 and ANTXR2, is activated by the protease furin, and its lethal factor cleaves MAP kinase kinases to shut down MAPK signalling; diphtheria toxin enters via HBEGF and ADP-ribosylates elongation factor EEF2 to halt translation; botulinum and tetanus neurotoxins bind synaptic vesicle proteins and synaptotagmins, then cleave SNAP25, syntaxins and VAMPs to block neurotransmitter release; heat-stable enterotoxin activates GUCY2C to drive secretory diarrhoea. The outcomes are paralysis, tissue necrosis, arrested protein synthesis and fluid loss.

Camera-type eye development does not finish at birth: after the eye's basic form is laid down, tissues continue to be sculpted, vascularised and refined into the mature optical organ, and this post-embryonic phase is what these genes serve. Programmed cell death shapes the outcome, with the pro-apoptotic effectors BAX and BAK1 clearing surplus cells from retinal and lens-associated tissues; loss of this pruning leaves hyperplastic, disorganised structures. Vascular remodelling is the other arm, with VEGFA acting through its receptor KDR to pattern the ocular vessels on which the retina depends for oxygen, a balance whose disturbance underlies proliferative retinopathy. Transcriptional regulators including BCL11B and KLF4, together with the Wnt receptor FZD5 and the chromatin protein HMGN1, control cell fate and layer organisation, linking this biology to eye malformation and postnatal visual impairment.

Whenever DNA is replicated, transcribed, repaired or packaged, its double helix must be bent, unwound, or have its supercoiling and linking number reset, and this collection of activities carries out those changes in DNA conformation. Without them, torsional stress accumulates ahead of polymerases, strands become catenated or knotted, and replication forks stall and break. Type I and type II topoisomerases, including a mitochondrial-specific enzyme and TOP3A acting with the BLM helicase, cut and religate the backbone to relieve supercoiling and resolve tangled intermediates; HMGB proteins bend and distort the helix to make it accessible to other factors; WRN and DNA2 process aberrant structures at forks and resected ends. The topology of DNA thus sits upstream of transcription, chromosome segregation and genome stability, and defects in these helicases cause premature ageing and cancer predisposition syndromes. Topoisomerase II is the target of widely used chemotherapeutics.

This grouping centres on stress-activated transcriptional signalling and its supporting membrane and metabolic machinery. Its recognisable core is the kinase TAK1 (MAP3K7) acting upstream of the CREB/ATF family factors ATF1 and ATF2, a route by which cytokine, TGF-beta and stress inputs are converted into changes in gene expression governing inflammation, survival and differentiation; loss of TAK1 signalling causes inflammatory and developmental failure. Around this sit components of vesicular and secretory biology, including the early endosome tether EEA1 that organises incoming cargo on Rab5-positive membranes, the P4-ATPase ATP11C that flips phosphatidylserine to maintain plasma membrane asymmetry and is required for B lymphopoiesis and erythrocyte integrity, and the calcium-binding ER protein RCN2. Post-transcriptional and metabolic contributors include the splicing regulator MBNL2, the zinc-finger factors IKZF5 and ZBTB41, and glycogen debranching enzyme AGL, whose deficiency causes glycogen storage disease type III.

Otoliths are the dense biomineral bodies of the inner ear vestibular organs, and their generation and shaping determines whether an animal can sense gravity and linear acceleration. Defective otolith morphogenesis produces balance and postural deficits without necessarily affecting hearing, the classic signature being head-tilt and vestibular ataxia phenotypes. The process requires seeding and growth of calcium carbonate crystals on a proteinaceous matrix within the endolymph, and depends on precise control of endolymph ion and pH composition as well as on tethering of the otoconial mass to the sensory macula. OTOP1 acts in the endolymphatic epithelium as a proton-conducting channel that regulates local pH and calcium handling during mineral deposition, while LRIG1 and LRIG3, leucine-rich repeat membrane proteins that dampen receptor tyrosine kinase signalling, contribute to patterning of the surrounding otic tissue. A membrane trafficking component also participates, linking vesicular delivery to matrix secretion.

Calcium entering a dendritic spine through the NMDA receptor is the trigger that converts brief synaptic activity into lasting change, and the events downstream of NMDA receptor activation are how that calcium signal is decoded. They underlie long-term potentiation, and with it learning and memory; disturbance of these steps contributes to intellectual disability, epilepsy and neurodegeneration. Calmodulin-dependent kinases, adenylate cyclases with cAMP-dependent protein kinase, and the Ras-ERK route each converge on phosphorylation of CREB1 at serine 133, switching on transcription of genes that consolidate the synapse. In parallel, scaffolding proteins of the PSD-95 family anchor the receptor to signalling enzymes, AMPA receptor subunits are inserted and modified to strengthen transmission, and Rac1 with its regulators remodels the actin and microtubule cytoskeleton so the spine changes shape. Neuregulin-ERBB4 signalling tunes the process.

The early neural tube is subdivided along its head-to-tail axis into forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain and spinal cord territories, and rostrocaudal patterning is the process that assigns those identities before any neurons are born. It sets where the midbrain-hindbrain boundary forms, and hence where dopaminergic and cerebellar precursors arise; disturbance produces gross malformations of the brainstem and cerebellum. Signals from organizing centres, notably FGF8 and WNT1 at the isthmus, maintain reciprocal expression of the transcription factors EN1 and GBX2, while PAX6 marks more rostral forebrain territory and HES1 keeps progenitors undifferentiated so patterning can precede differentiation. Polycomb components including BMI1 and the H3K36 demethylase KDM2B supply chromatin-level repression that stabilizes regional gene expression once established. The pathway therefore links secreted morphogen gradients to heritable positional identity in the developing central nervous system.

The p53 tumour suppressor decides whether a damaged cell arrests, repairs itself, senesces or dies, and regulation of TP53 activity is how that decision is set. In unstressed cells p53 is kept scarce: the ubiquitin ligase MDM2, with MDM4 and other ligases, marks it for proteasomal destruction, while deubiquitinases such as USP7 oppose this. DNA damage sensing through ATM, ATR with its partner ATRIP, the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex, the RAD9-HUS1-RAD1 clamp and TOPBP1 activates CHEK1 and CHEK2, and phosphorylation at the amino terminus blocks MDM2 binding and stabilises the protein. Further marks tune output rather than amount: acetylation by EP300 and KAT5 favours transcription, methylation by SMYD2, EHMT2 or KMT5A can silence it, HIPK2 phosphorylation biases towards apoptotic targets, and PIN1 isomerisation licenses cofactor binding. Loss of this control underlies much of human cancer.

Kidney formation depends on a pool of metanephric mesenchyme that must first be specified and maintained before it can be converted into nephrons, and this programme describes how those unspecialized cells acquire mesenchymal identity during renal development. Its output determines nephron endowment: too little progenitor maintenance or premature differentiation yields hypoplastic kidneys with too few nephrons, while failure of specification underlies renal agenesis and congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract. SIX2 keeps cap mesenchyme progenitors self-renewing, PAX2 and OSR1 establish intermediate mesoderm and nephric lineage identity, TCF21 contributes to stromal and podocyte-lineage mesenchyme, and WNT4 acts in the mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition that generates renal vesicles. Regulation of Wnt signalling, including by AMER1, ties the balance between progenitor renewal and differentiation to patterning of the developing kidney.

Hedgehog ligands are secreted morphogens that pattern the embryo, and their biogenesis is the set of processing and release steps that turn a precursor protein into an active signal. The three mammalian ligands direct limb, notochord and neural tube organization (SHH), bone and cartilage growth (IHH), and germ cell and peripheral nerve sheath development (DHH); loss of processing causes holoprosencephaly and skeletal malformation. The precursor cleaves itself, and the N-terminal fragment is modified with cholesterol and, via the acyltransferase HHAT, with palmitate. These lipids tether the ligand in membrane rafts, so long-range spread requires untethering by the transmembrane protein DISP2 with secreted SCUBE2, by shedding, or by packaging into lipoprotein particles and vesicles. Quality control is part of the picture: misfolded precursor is retrotranslocated through the SEL1L–SYVN1 machinery with VCP and degraded by the proteasome, and secreted NOTUM and glypicans tune ligand availability.

FLT3 is a class III receptor tyrosine kinase carried by hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and by dendritic cell precursors, and its signalling tells those cells to survive, divide and differentiate. Loss of the pathway depletes dendritic cells and early lymphoid progenitors; constitutive activation by internal tandem duplication is one of the commonest lesions in acute myeloid leukaemia and the reason FLT3 kinase inhibitors exist. Binding of FLT3 ligand dimerises the receptor and triggers autophosphorylation, creating docking sites for GRB2, GAB2 and the PI3K regulatory subunit, which drive RAS-MAPK and AKT signalling, while STAT5A/B are phosphorylated directly. The output is suppression of the pro-apoptotic protein BIM and of FOXO3 and p27, favouring cycle entry. Counter-regulation is prominent here: CBL-mediated ubiquitination, the phosphatases PTPN11 and PTPRJ, SOCS proteins and adaptors such as SH2B3 and SLA restrain the receptor, and their failure sustains leukaemic growth.

Grouped here are gene products that increase the ability of other factors to engage DNA, a layer of control that sits above transcription itself and determines whether a promoter is read at all. Because a transcription factor is only as active as its access to chromatin, these positive regulators of DNA binding set the gain on developmental and stress-responsive gene programmes. The mechanisms represented are varied: HMGB1 bends and distorts DNA to help partner factors load, thioredoxin keeps redox-sensitive cysteines in DNA-binding domains reduced, general factor GTF2B stabilises polymerase II preinitiation assembly, and SUMO and coactivator-like proteins modify or bridge factors to change their affinity. Lineage regulators such as GATA3, FOXC1 and the POU4F factors, together with RB1 and HES1, connect this control to immune cell specification, eye and neuronal development, and proliferative restraint, so loss of it distorts differentiation rather than any single metabolic step.

Dendrite development covers the whole life history of a neuron's receptive arbor, from the first outgrowth of a nascent branch to a stable, appropriately sized and oriented tree bearing spines. Because dendritic geometry sets how many inputs a neuron can receive and where, this programme determines cortical layering, circuit wiring and synaptic capacity; its disruption underlies intellectual disability, autism and the dendritic simplification seen in Rett syndrome and fragile X. Extracellular cues acting through Reelin receptors, ephrin receptors, semaphorins, netrin and Wnt signalling are converted by Rho-family GTPases such as RAC1 and CDC42, their regulators and WAVE-complex and actin effectors including CFL1 and drebrin into local cytoskeletal remodelling, while MAP2 and other microtubule-associated proteins build the shaft. Calcium- and activity-dependent kinases, MEF2 transcription factors, MECP2 and local mRNA-binding proteins such as FMR1 tune branching to experience.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 transmits growth and differentiation cues, most conspicuously as a brake on chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate, and its output must be switched off promptly; the negative regulation of FGFR3 signaling is the set of feedback devices that does this. Ligand-bound receptor recruits the FRS2 adaptor with GRB2 and the phosphatase PTPN11 to drive BRAF and the ERK kinases MAPK1/MAPK3, and the same cascade then turns on its own inhibitors. The ubiquitin ligase CBL, working with ubiquitin and ubiquitin-ribosomal fusion precursors, tags the receptor for internalisation and degradation, SPRY2 intercepts signalling at the adaptor level, ERK-dependent phosphorylation of FRS2 dampens further recruitment, and PP2A subunits reverse activating phosphorylations. Loss of this restraint underlies achondroplasia and related skeletal dysplasias, and activating FGFR3 lesions recur in bladder carcinoma and myeloma.

Many hormones, neurotransmitters and chemokines act through G protein-coupled receptors that raise intracellular calcium, and this pathway covers the relay from receptor-activated heterotrimeric G proteins to calcium-dependent enzymes. It is how a brief extracellular signal becomes secretion, contraction, gene transcription or synaptic change, and its components are drug targets across cardiovascular, neurological and inflammatory medicine. Gq-class subunits such as GNAQ and the hematopoietic GNA15 activate phospholipase C beta, which cleaves PIP2 to generate inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol and releases calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores; released calcium binds calmodulin, which in turn activates kinases including CAMK4 to drive nuclear transcriptional responses. Gi-class subunits and a Gγ subunit couple the same receptors to adenylate cyclase and thereby to cAMP and protein kinase A, so the two second-messenger arms are integrated rather than separate. Dysregulated Gq signalling underlies several cancers and cardiac hypertrophy.

When a damaged or mismatched base is excised by a DNA glycosylase, the DNA is left with an abasic site whose sugar-phosphate remnant must be cleared before the gap can be filled; this is the short-patch, single-nucleotide replacement arm of base excision repair. Without it, abasic sites and their 5'-deoxyribose phosphate residues persist as blocking, mutagenic lesions that stall replication and drive base substitutions, which is why this chemistry underlies genome stability against oxidative and alkylation damage. APEX1 displaces the glycosylase from its product and incises the backbone on the 5' side of the base-free deoxyribose, creating a nick with a 3'-hydroxyl. DNA polymerase beta is then recruited to the resulting gap and uses its lyase activity to release the 5'dRP group, leaving a clean single-nucleotide gap for fill-in synthesis and ligation.

Membrane proteins marked for destruction are sorted into the interior of late endosomes and delivered onward to the lytic compartment, the vacuole in yeast and the lysosome in human cells. This route terminates signalling by receptors such as EGFR and the leptin receptor, whose trafficking depends on LEPROT, and it determines how long a cell responds to a growth factor or cytokine. The genes here are the ESCRT machinery: ubiquitin-binding recognition by HGS and STAM, sequential ESCRT-I, -II and -III assemblies built from TSG101, VPS37, VPS25 and CHMP subunits, deubiquitination by PTPN23-associated steps, and membrane scission followed by disassembly through the VPS4 ATPases with VTA1. The same components pinch off other necks, including those used in viral budding and cytokinesis, and BECN1 with PIK3R4 links the pathway to autophagosome maturation and phosphoinositide-marked endosomal identity.

The liver is unusual among adult organs in being able to regrow after injury or partial resection, and this grouping covers the signals that drive hepatocytes back into the cell cycle. Positive regulation of hepatocyte proliferation matters for regeneration after toxic damage, viral hepatitis or surgery, and when it runs unchecked it contributes to hepatocellular carcinoma. Inflammatory input is prominent: TNF acts as an early mitogenic cue, while TNFAIP3 and CFLAR restrain the death arm of the same receptor so that surviving hepatocytes can divide rather than apoptose. Secreted growth factors such as midkine and pleiotrophin and WNT3A-driven beta-catenin signalling supply proliferative and patterning cues, MED1 couples nuclear receptors to transcription, and XBP1 links secretory and lipid demands of the unfolded protein response to hepatocyte expansion.

Skeletal muscle is built from mononucleated myoblasts that exit the cell cycle, switch on a contractile programme and fuse into multinucleated myotubes; this differentiation programme underlies muscle growth during development and its reactivation by satellite cells underlies regeneration after injury, with failure producing myopathy and impaired repair. Myogenic transcription factors such as MYOD1, MYF5, MYOG, MYF6 and MEF2C drive the commitment step, while class II histone deacetylases and muscle-restricted microRNAs including miR-1 and miR-206 gate when that programme is allowed to run. Fusion itself requires dedicated membrane machinery, notably myomaker and myomerger, together with tetraspanins, integrin-linked adhesion and Rac-activating DOCK proteins. Downstream, sarcomeric and excitation-contraction components such as ACTA1, RYR1, CACNA1S and STAC3 appear, alongside glycosyltransferases that mature dystroglycan and a large ribosomal protein contingent supporting the biosynthetic demand of hypertrophic growth.

Epithelia and endothelia only work as barriers and coherent sheets because their cells are physically linked to one another and to the basement membrane, and cell junction organization is the assembly, remodelling and turnover of those links. Tight junctions built from claudins and JAM-A seal the paracellular space and set ion selectivity; classical cadherins with alpha- and beta-catenin, p120 and plakoglobin form adherens junctions; nectins and nectin-like adhesion molecules nucleate contacts; and integrin alpha6beta4 with collagen XVII, plectin, laminin-332 and keratins 5/14 anchors basal keratinocytes through type I hemidesmosomes, loss of which causes blistering skin disease. Integrin-linked kinase, kindlin, parvin, paxillin, vinculin and talin-associated adaptors couple adhesion to actin and to Rho-family GTPases, while Crumbs and Par polarity complexes position junctions apicobasally. Transcriptional repressors such as SNAI1/2, ZEB1/2 and TWIST dismantle this programme during epithelial-mesenchymal transition and tumour invasion.

Free heme is a potent oxidant, and the stress-inducible heme oxygenase HMOX1 protects cells by degrading it into biliverdin, carbon monoxide and ferrous iron, each of which carries its own protective signal. Loss of this response leaves tissues vulnerable to oxidative and inflammatory injury, particularly in lung, vasculature and liver, while its induction limits apoptosis, inflammasome activity and immune cell expansion. HMOX1 transcription is driven by NFE2L2 with small Maf partners and repressed by BACH1, a heme-sensing switch that couples enzyme levels to heme load. Biliverdin reductases convert the product to bilirubin, a radical scavenger that also engages PPARA with RXRA and associated coactivator and corepressor complexes to alter gene expression. Carbon monoxide binds ferrous hemoproteins, notably cytochrome c oxidase subunits, damping mitochondrial respiration and reactive oxygen production, while HMOX1 additionally restrains NLRP3 and STAT3-dependent inflammatory programmes.

Oocytes halve their chromosome number through two specialized divisions, and female meiotic nuclear division covers the nuclear events that make this possible: homologue pairing and crossover formation in prophase I, the long arrest that follows, and the asymmetric spindle-driven segregation at maturation. Errors here are the dominant source of human aneuploidy, underlying miscarriage, trisomic pregnancy and age-related infertility. Recombination machinery such as MEIOB, HSF2BP and the MLH1-MLH3 resolvase pair ensures each bivalent receives a crossover, while cohesion regulators and TRIP13 govern how long chiasmata hold. Meiotic resumption depends on kinase-phosphatase balance, with WEE2, MASTL and PP2A subunits setting CDK1-cyclin B activity, and AURKA, PLK1, TTK and the NDC80-SKA kinetochore components executing chromosome capture. Actin nucleators FMN2 and the spire proteins drive the off-centre spindle positioning that produces a polar body and conserves ooplasm for the embryo.

Neutral amino acids taken in with food are absorbed across the brush border of the small intestine and reclaimed from the glomerular filtrate in the proximal tubule, and B(0)AT1, encoded by SLC6A19, is the sodium-coupled transporter that performs both jobs. Loss-of-function mutations abolish this uptake and cause Hartnup disorder, in which tryptophan and other neutral amino acids are lost in urine and stool; because tryptophan is the precursor for niacin and serotonin, affected individuals can show pellagra-like photosensitive rash, cerebellar ataxia and psychiatric disturbance, typically episodic and provoked by poor diet or intercurrent illness. Certain variants instead contribute to the milder aminoaciduria phenotypes iminoglycinuria and hyperglycinuria. Transport depends on the inward sodium gradient and on accessory proteins including ACE2 and collectrin for correct apical membrane delivery, placing this pathway within epithelial nutrient absorption and renal solute reabsorption.

This grouping marks cells engaged in presenting peptides to CD4 T cells via MHC class II. The core of it is the class II locus itself — DR, DP and DQ alpha and beta chains together with CD74, the invariant chain that chaperones nascent class II molecules, blocks premature peptide loading and directs them to endosomal compartments where its degradation frees the groove. Expression of these products defines dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells and sets the threshold for helper T cell activation, autoimmunity and transplant rejection; loss of class II expression produces severe combined immunodeficiency of the bare lymphocyte type. Accompanying genes point to the activated myeloid state in which presentation occurs: heme oxygenase and cyclooxygenase-2 shape the inflammatory and oxidative milieu, the urokinase receptor supports migration, and lipid-handling enzymes reflect the metabolic reprogramming of maturing antigen-presenting cells.

S phase is the interval in which a cell copies its genome, producing two sister chromatids from every chromosome and committing itself to division. Origins licensed in G1 by the origin recognition complex, CDC6 and CDT1 are fired once cyclin E- and cyclin A-CDK2 activity rises, converting loaded MCM2-7 hexamers into active CMG helicases with the GINS proteins and CDC45; RPA coats unwound DNA while polymerases alpha, delta and epsilon, primase, PCNA, the clamp loader, FEN1 and ligase I synthesise and join nascent strands. Cohesin rings with SMC1A, SMC3, RAD21 and the ESCO acetyltransferases hold the new copies together for later segregation. Timing is enforced by E2F-RB transcription, the DREAM complex, CDK inhibitors p21 and p27, WEE1, CDC25 phosphatases, and ubiquitin-proteasome destruction of cyclin E, geminin and licensing factors, which prevents re-replication. Loss of this control produces replication stress, genome instability and cancer.

Phosphate esters are the common currency of metabolism, and this catabolic branch covers their degradation: the breakdown of sugar phosphates, nucleotides, cyclic nucleotides, phospholipids and phosphoanhydrides back to simpler products. It supplies ATP and carbon skeletons, terminates second-messenger signals, and clears damaged or non-canonical building blocks before they poison the genome. The largest contingent is glycolytic — hexokinases, phosphofructokinases, enolases, pyruvate kinase and their PFKFB regulators — feeding glucose carbon toward pyruvate under insulin, HIF1A and mTOR/AMPK control. Nucleotide turnover is handled by 5'-nucleotidases, ecto-nucleotidases and NUDT hydrolases together with purine and pyrimidine salvage enzymes, while phosphodiesterases degrade cAMP and cGMP and phospholipases and sphingomyelinases release lipid-derived messengers. Loss of individual steps produces haemolytic anaemia, glycogen and lysosomal storage disease, immune dysregulation from nucleotide accumulation, and inherited neurodegeneration.

In unstressed cells p53 is held at low levels by ubiquitin ligases that mark it for destruction, and COP1 is one of them; this route describes how COP1 itself is eliminated so that p53 can accumulate after genotoxic stress. The switch matters because it converts DNA damage sensing into a stable p53 response that drives cell cycle arrest, senescence or apoptosis, and its loss permits damaged cells to keep dividing. The damage-activated kinase ATM phosphorylates COP1 on Ser387, which triggers COP1 autoubiquitination; polyubiquitin supplied by the ubiquitin precursor genes is then read by the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of 20S core and 19S regulatory subunits carries out degradation. Removing the ligase abrogates p53 ubiquitination, making this a self-limiting brake within tumour suppressor control and a point at which COP1 overexpression can blunt p53 in cancer.

Oxidative attack on DNA constantly creates damaged bases such as 8-oxoguanine and ring-opened pyrimidines, and base excision repair removes them by cutting the damaged base out and restoring the correct one. Defects in the DNA glycosylases that initiate this repair define an inherited cancer predisposition: biallelic loss of MUTYH, which excises adenine mispaired opposite 8-oxoguanine, causes adenomatous polyposis and colorectal cancer, while NTHL1 deficiency produces a multi-tumour syndrome, and OGG1, the glycosylase for 8-oxoguanine itself, and the NEIL enzymes that clear oxidised pyrimidines and hydantoin lesions carry variants linked to tumour risk and to other oxidative stress-related disease. Because the lesions they remove are mutagenic rather than blocking, failure of this repair route shows up as characteristic G:C to T:A transversion signatures in tumour genomes, placing these diseases at the junction of genome maintenance and redox stress.

Most cytoplasmic mRNAs are retired by deadenylation-dependent decay, the default route that ends a transcript's working life after rounds of translation and thereby sets mRNA half-life, message abundance and the speed with which a cell can change its expression programme. Shortening of the poly(A) tail begins with the PAN2-PAN3 pair and is completed by the multisubunit CCR4-NOT complex, whose CNOT6/6L and CNOT7/8 nuclease modules, or by PARN, stripping the platform that poly(A)-binding protein and initiation factors use to keep the message stable and translatable. The trimmed body is then destroyed from either end: the Lsm1-7 ring and decapping factors DCP1-DCP2 with DDX6, EDC3 and EDC4 expose the 5' end to XRN1, or the exosome with its helicase-containing cofactors degrades 3' to 5', leaving a cap fragment cleared by DCPS. Much of this occurs in cytoplasmic granules, and its regulation underlies developmental and immune transcript turnover.

HIV-1 cannot make full-length viral RNA on its own: polymerases that initiate at the proviral promoter stall soon after and release short abortive transcripts, so the virus depends on its Tat transactivator to convert them into processive elongation complexes. This step sets the switch between latency and productive replication, and blocking it is the rationale behind CDK9-directed antiviral strategies. Tat binds the TAR stem-loop in the nascent leader RNA and tethers the P-TEFb kinase, cyclin T1 with CDK9, to the paused polymerase. CDK9 hyperphosphorylates the RNA polymerase II carboxy-terminal domain and also modifies the SPT5 subunit of DSIF and the RD subunit of NELF, relieving their negative effect on elongation. The remaining machinery here is the host's own: the general initiation and TFIIH kinase components, elongation factors such as ELL and the elongin complex, FACT histone chaperones, and the nuclear cap-binding proteins.

Most proteins are made in the cytosol but must end up somewhere else, and this pathway covers the targeting and delivery steps that put them there: import into the nucleus, mitochondria and peroxisomes, insertion into the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, and sorting onward to lysosomes and endosomes. Each route has its own recognition machinery — signal recognition particle subunits and the Sec61 translocon with signal peptidase for the secretory pathway, importins, nucleoporins and the Ran system for nucleocytoplasmic transport, TOM and TIM complexes with matrix processing peptidases for mitochondria, and peroxins with the PEX5 receptor for peroxisomal matrix enzymes. Mannose-6-phosphate tagging and receptors such as M6PR and IGF2R route hydrolases to lysosomes, while ESCRT components and Rab GTPases handle cargo in multivesicular bodies. Because compartment identity depends on correct delivery, mistargeting underlies peroxisome biogenesis disorders, lysosomal storage disease, mitochondrial dysfunction and protein aggregation.

Neurotrophins such as NGF and BDNF act on their receptors at the cell surface, but the lasting consequences — neuronal differentiation, survival, dendritic growth and the synaptic changes underlying learning — require the signal to reach the nucleus and rewrite gene expression. That step is what nuclear events downstream of neurotrophin signalling accomplish: ERK and p38 family kinases, together with the ribosomal S6 kinase family, phosphorylate transcription factors including CREB1, ELK1 in partnership with SRF, ATF1/ATF2 and MEF2 proteins, recruiting the p300 acetyltransferase to activate transcription. The immediate result is induction of immediate-early genes — FOS, FOSB, JUNB, the EGR family, ARC and VGF — many themselves transcription factors that drive a second, delayed-early wave. Phosphatases of the DUSP family and PP2A subunits restrain the cascade, while CDK5 with its neuronal activators and the repressor REST tune the neuronal output. Disruption affects neuronal plasticity and survival.

These genes mark a perivascular stromal and endothelial compartment, the interface where capillaries meet connective tissue matrix. Secreted matrix components such as EFEMP1 (fibulin-3) and ECM2 organise the basement membrane and elastic fibre environment that keeps vessels and surrounding tissue mechanically coherent, while IL33 acts both as a nuclear factor in endothelium and, when released from damaged cells, as an alarmin that recruits type 2 immune responses. Several adhesion G protein-coupled receptors are represented, including ELTD1/ADGRL4, which is endothelial and shapes angiogenic sprouting, and GPR116/ADGRF5, required for alveolar surfactant homeostasis; GNG12 supplies a G protein gamma subunit for such signalling, and MPDZ scaffolds junctional complexes. Together the set describes matrix deposition, junction organisation and vascular-stromal crosstalk, processes underlying tissue remodelling, fibrosis and vessel integrity.

Neurons cannot excrete cholesterol directly, so they convert it to 24-hydroxycholesterol, which crosses the blood-brain barrier and is degraded to bile acids in the liver. This route contributes only a small fraction of the total bile acid pool but provides the main outlet for surplus brain cholesterol, and its impairment is linked to cholesterol accumulation and neurodegenerative change. CYP46A1 performs the brain-specific 24-hydroxylation; in hepatocytes CYP39A1 adds the 7alpha-hydroxyl, HSD3B7 isomerises and oxidises the A ring, and AKR1D1 with the AKR1C reductases reduce it, before CYP27A1 initiates side-chain oxidation. Activation to a coenzyme A thioester, peroxisomal beta-oxidation involving AMACR and the transporter ABCD3, and conjugation to glycine or taurine yield cholate and chenodeoxycholate. The chemistry spans cytosol, mitochondria and peroxisomes, tying sterol disposal to bile formation and intestinal lipid absorption.

Myofibroblasts are the contractile, matrix-secreting cells that close wounds, and their persistence after repair drives fibrosis of lung, liver, heart and kidney. This pathway covers the brakes on that conversion: signals that stop fibroblasts, pericytes or epithelial-derived cells from acquiring smooth muscle actin and a profibrotic secretory programme, or that limit how many do so. Several microRNAs act here by repressing transcripts downstream of TGF-beta, the dominant differentiation cue, while PDCD4 restrains translation and TP53INP1 links stress and p53 signalling to a less activated state. RB1 ties the decision to cell cycle control, and TSKU, a secreted small leucine-rich protein, modulates matrix and growth factor signalling outside the cell. Loss of these restraints favours scarring over regeneration, making them of interest as antifibrotic targets.

Kidney mesenchyme development covers the maturation of the loose mesenchymal tissue of the embryonic kidney from its first specification through to its mature derivatives, and it determines how many nephrons a person is born with. The metanephric mesenchyme is the source of nephron epithelium, and a separate stromal compartment marked by FOXD1 gives rise to interstitium, pericytes and renin-producing cells. Progenitor identity and self-renewal depend on the SIX1/SIX2 and PAX2 transcription factors together with OSR1 and WT1, while BMP7, SHH and WNT4 provide the inductive signalling that converts progenitors into tubular epithelium; SMAD4 transduces the BMP arm. Premature exhaustion of this progenitor pool leaves a hypoplastic kidney with reduced nephron number and later hypertension, and failure of the progenitors to differentiate is the origin of Wilms tumour, the common paediatric kidney cancer.

This grouping covers the control layer that sets how readily proteins engage DNA, tuning transcription factor occupancy rather than carrying out transcription itself. Because a factor's affinity for chromatin determines which genes are heard, this regulation shapes lineage decisions, proliferation control and stress responses, and its loss contributes to developmental malformation and cancer. Several routes are represented: redox and cofactor modulation of factor binding, as by thioredoxin acting on AP-1 components such as JUN; architectural and chromatin proteins including HMGB1, HMGA2, linker histone H1-0 and the remodelling subunit RSF1 that alter DNA accessibility; histone methyltransferases DOT1L and NSD1 that mark the template; and inhibitory partners such as RB1, which restrains E2F1, and the co-repressor SKI. Also present are lineage factors GATA3, LEF1, SOX11, FOXC1 and POU4F1/2 whose own binding is subject to this control, together with the general initiation factor GTF2B.

This grouping centres on inflammatory cytokine output from activated lymphocytes and the signalling that licenses it. Tumour necrosis factor, the IL-6-family members LIF and oncostatin M, and the p19 subunit of IL-23 are secreted effectors that drive acute inflammation, acute-phase and stromal responses, and the expansion and stabilisation of Th17-type responses; excess of these mediators underlies chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease, and TNF and IL-23 are themselves targets of biologic therapy. Upstream, calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase IV and protein kinase C alpha couple antigen-receptor and calcium signals to the transcription of these genes, while CRTAM mediates cell-cell contact that sustains cytotoxic and helper effector differentiation. Also represented are modulators of the surrounding tissue response: urokinase plasminogen activator in pericellular proteolysis, a TGF-beta co-receptor that sequesters ligand, and the Hedgehog receptor Patched.

KIT is a receptor tyrosine kinase for stem cell factor, and activating mutations in it drive gastrointestinal stromal tumours, mastocytosis and some acute leukaemias. Such tumours are usually treated first with imatinib, and sunitinib is given second line when resistance emerges; this pathway captures the subset of KIT alleles that resist sunitinib as well. Resistance arises because substitutions in the kinase domain, particularly in the activation loop, reshape the pocket so the drug can no longer hold the receptor in the inactive conformation it requires, leaving the kinase constitutively autophosphorylated and signalling to proliferation and survival effectors without ligand. Clinically this defines the point at which second-line therapy fails and later-generation inhibitors with different conformational preferences are needed.

Moving away from a chemical cue is as directed a behaviour as moving toward one, and this pathway controls how strongly and how often a cell or growth cone turns down a gradient. It is the logic behind axon repulsion in the developing nervous system: Slit ligands secreted by the midline are read by Robo receptors on crossing axons, and plexin signalling reads semaphorin cues, together steering commissural projections, setting whether an axon crosses the midline once and never again, and shaping longitudinal tract position. Tuning this repulsive output determines the precision of wiring rather than whether growth occurs at all. Loss of Robo3 function in humans causes horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis, a direct consequence of commissural axons failing to cross. The same repulsive guidance is reused outside neurons in branching morphogenesis and in the migration of leukocytes and other motile cells.

In humans, alkaloid metabolism covers two linked activities: the handling of plant-derived nitrogenous compounds taken in as drugs or dietary constituents, and the turnover of nicotinamide, the pyridine alkaloid backbone of NAD. Hepatic oxidases such as CYP1A2, CYP2D6 and CYP3A4/5 together with the esterases BCHE and CES2 oxidise and hydrolyse caffeine, nicotine, morphine-type and other alkaloids, setting their clearance rate and accounting for much of the person-to-person variation in drug response and toxicity. In parallel, NAMPT and the nicotinamide riboside kinases NMRK1/2 salvage nicotinamide into NAD, NNMT methylates it for disposal, and NAD-consuming enzymes including CD38 and several PARP family members release nicotinamide again, while a mitochondrial carrier moves NAD across the inner membrane. The pathway therefore connects xenobiotic detoxification to cellular redox and signalling cofactor supply.

Vesicle-mediated transport is the system by which cells move proteins, lipids and extracellular cargo between compartments inside membrane-bounded carriers, and it underlies secretion, receptor uptake, lysosomal delivery and the maintenance of organelle identity. Its failure blocks hormone and antibody secretion, leaves receptors such as LDLR, TFRC and EGFR uncleared from the surface, and causes storage and pigmentation disorders. The genes here cover the full itinerary: COPII components with SAR1B and the SEC23/24 subunits bud carriers from the ER, COPI and the Golgi-associated conserved oligomeric Golgi and TRAPP complexes handle intra-Golgi and retrograde steps, clathrin with AP-1 and AP-2 adaptors, dynamins and endophilins drive endocytosis, and ESCRT subunits with TSG101 and VPS4 sort ubiquitinated cargo into multivesicular bodies. Rab GTPases with their GEFs and TBC-domain GAPs specify identity, SNAREs and NSF execute fusion, and kinesin, dynein and myosin motors carry vesicles along cytoskeletal tracks.

PD-L1 is the ligand that shuts down T cells through the PD-1 receptor, dampening T cell receptor and costimulatory signalling to keep immune responses self-limiting and prevent autoimmunity; tumours exploit the same brake to escape cytotoxic T cells, which is why antibodies against this axis became mainstream cancer therapy. How much PD-L1 reaches the cell surface is set at every layer, and those layers are what this regulation comprises. Interferon-driven JAK1-STAT1 signalling, NF-kB, HIF1A and EPAS1 under hypoxia, MYC, AP-1 factors, Wnt-beta-catenin with TCF/LEF, and YAP/TAZ-TEAD all act on the CD274 promoter, while Polycomb (EZH2, SUZ12, EED) and MLL-WDR5 complexes with core histones supply the epigenetic setting. Several microRNAs, including miR-34 and miR-200 family members acting through Argonaute complexes, restrain the transcript. Post-translationally, N-glycosylation by the oligosaccharyltransferase complex, CSNK2 and GSK3B phosphorylation, ERAD components, and SPOP-CUL3 and SCF ubiquitin ligases feeding the proteasome determine PD-L1 stability.

Platelets only aggregate, change shape, secrete their granules and expose procoagulant phosphatidylserine when cytosolic Ca2+ rises, so the control of that rise and its reversal sets the threshold for haemostasis and thrombosis. In the resting state, calcium is kept low by pumps: plasma membrane Ca2+-ATPases extrude it, SERCA isoforms sequester it into the dense tubular system, and sodium-calcium exchangers of the SLC8 family provide an additional exit route. On agonist stimulation, phospholipase C-derived IP3 opens IP3 receptor channels on that store; store depletion is sensed by STIM1, which gates Orai channels in the plasma membrane to sustain store-operated entry. Receptor-operated entry through the ATP-gated P2X1 channel and TRPC channels adds further influx, and calmodulin and sorcin tune the response. Loss of STIM1 or Orai1 function blunts platelet activation and confers bleeding, while excessive signalling favours thrombus formation.

Glycogen is the body's rapidly mobilizable glucose store, and its regulated synthesis and breakdown keeps blood glucose stable during fasting and supplies fuel to muscle and brain during exercise and stress. Inherited defects in the enzymes that build, branch, or release glycogen cause the glycogen storage diseases, whose presentations range from fasting hypoglycaemia and hepatomegaly to myopathy, cardiomyopathy and neutropenia. Loss of the liver or muscle glycogen synthases blocks storage outright; deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase or its endoplasmic reticulum glucose-6-phosphate transporter traps glucose inside hepatocytes, while loss of lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase leaves undegraded glycogen in lysosomes. Defects in the branching enzyme or in glycogenin, the self-glucosylating protein that primes new chains, yield structurally abnormal or absent glycogen.
