Failure of the laforin-malin pair, a phosphatase and a ubiquitin ligase acting with ubiquitin on overphosphorylated glycogen, produces insoluble polyglucosan and progressive myoclonic epilepsy.

The nucleolus is a membraneless compartment assembled around ribosomal DNA, and proteins must be actively delivered to it and retained there for ribosome subunit production, telomerase maturation and nucleolar stress signalling to work. Targeting depends on nucleolar localization signals read against RNA polymerase I transcription and on chaperone-like hubs: nucleophosmin shuttles between nucleolus and nucleoplasm and escorts partners in, while the ARF tumour suppressor encoded at the CDKN2A locus is sequestered there and, when released, stabilises p53. Other members act in pre-rRNA processing and large subunit assembly and export, including the AAA-ATPase NVL, the NMD3 adaptor, and RRS1/RPF2, with RAN providing the nucleocytoplasmic gradient. Mislocalisation of these factors underlies ribosomopathies, drives the nucleolar stress response after ribosome biogenesis is blocked, and disturbs telomere maintenance through TERT and PINX1.

FGFR3b is the epithelial splice variant of fibroblast growth factor receptor 3, and this step describes which fibroblast growth factors actually engage it and switch it on. The choice of ligand matters because FGFR3 signalling restrains chondrocyte proliferation in growth plates and supports epithelial and skeletal patterning; gain-of-function receptor mutations cause achondroplasia and related dwarfing skeletal dysplasias, while activating lesions in epithelia contribute to bladder carcinoma and multiple myeloma. Binding of FGF1, FGF8, FGF9, FGF17, FGF18 or FGF20, with heparan sulfate as a co-factor, dimerises the receptor and juxtaposes its kinase domains for trans-autophosphorylation, creating docking sites that feed into the RAS-MAPK, PI3K and PLC-gamma routes. The affinities of these ligands differ widely, so the isoform's response is set by which factors a tissue secretes rather than by the receptor alone.

Immune responses depend on the ability of white blood cells to expand clonally once they detect antigen or inflammatory cues, and leukocyte proliferation is that expansion by cell division. It sets the size of a lymphocyte clone, the output of myeloid progenitors, and therefore the strength of an immune response; too little produces immunodeficiency and poor vaccine responses, too much drives autoimmunity, lymphoproliferative disease and leukaemia. Antigen receptors and their proximal kinases such as ZAP70, SYK, LYN and BTK, with adaptors CARD11 and RASGRP1, couple recognition to calcium, MAPK and NF-kB signalling and to cyclin and MYC-driven cell cycle entry. Growth is licensed by cytokines including IL2, IL7, IL15, IL21, CSF1, CSF2 and FLT3LG acting through shared receptor chains and STAT5, and by costimulation via CD28 and CD40. Counterweights are equally represented: CTLA4, PD-L1, PTPN22, CBLB, TNFAIP3 and FOXP3-dependent regulatory restraint impose tolerance and limit expansion.

M phase is the part of the cell cycle in which a cell divides its duplicated chromosomes and then splits in two, proceeding through prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase before cytokinesis. Getting it right is what keeps chromosome number constant; errors produce aneuploidy, micronuclei and the genomic instability typical of tumours. The genes here cover the machinery that does the work: CDK1-cyclin B and Aurora B/INCENP kinase activity, centrosome and gamma-tubulin ring assembly of the spindle, kinetochore and outer-plate complexes such as NDC80 and MIS12, condensin and cohesin with separase cleaving cohesin at anaphase, and the spindle assembly checkpoint (MAD1/MAD2, BUB1, BUB3) restraining the anaphase-promoting complex and its proteasomal destruction of securin and cyclin B. Also included are nuclear envelope and pore disassembly and reformation, Golgi partitioning, and ESCRT-dependent abscission of the midbody.

Once a T cell has recognised antigen and committed to an effector response, it acquires the tools to kill target cells and to inflame tissue, and this arm of T cell signalling captures that activated state. Cytotoxic output is represented by granzyme B and perforin, which together breach a target cell membrane and trigger apoptosis, alongside Fas ligand for receptor-mediated killing; interferon gamma and TNF provide the inflammatory and macrophage-activating output. Sustained expansion depends on high-affinity interleukin-2 receptor subunits, while the costimulatory TNF receptor family members OX40, 4-1BB and GITR reinforce survival and proliferation after the initial activation signal, with AP-1 component FOSL1 among the transcriptional responders. This programme drives antiviral and antitumour immunity, is the effector limb manipulated by checkpoint and agonist immunotherapies, and when poorly restrained contributes to autoimmune tissue damage and cytokine-driven pathology.

Natural killer cells decide whether to kill a target by reading its surface HLA class I, and the killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptor cluster provides the receptors that make that judgement. These genes sit together in a highly polymorphic, variably haplotyped region on chromosome 19 and are expressed in a clonally variegated pattern across NK cells and some effector T cells, so each cell carries its own combination. Long-tailed forms such as KIR2DL1, KIR2DL3 and KIR3DL1 carry inhibitory cytoplasmic motifs that recruit phosphatases and veto cytotoxicity when self HLA is intact; short-tailed forms signal activation instead. Loss of class I on virus-infected or transformed cells removes the inhibitory signal and licenses killing, the basis of missing-self recognition. Inherited receptor and HLA combinations shape susceptibility to viral infection, autoimmunity, pregnancy complications, and outcomes after stem cell transplantation.

PD-1 co-inhibition is the brake that T cells apply to their own activation, limiting autoimmunity and tissue damage but also enforcing the exhausted, unresponsive state of tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes that checkpoint-blockade antibodies are designed to release. Engagement of PD-1 by PD-L1 or PD-L2 presented alongside peptide-MHC class II recruits the tyrosine phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2 to the synapse, where they dephosphorylate CD3 chains and LCK-dependent intermediates and dampen PI3K-AKT output, cutting IL-2 production, survival signalling and effector differentiation. Much of the biology here concerns how the ligand itself is controlled: PD-L1 abundance is set by transcription factors including HIF1A, MYC, NF-κB, STAT1/3 and IRF1, by YAP/TAZ-TEAD and Wnt-β-catenin inputs, by chromatin regulators such as the PRC2 and MLL-WDR5 complexes, by numerous microRNAs acting through Argonaute complexes, and post-translationally by N-glycosylation, casein kinase 2 and GSK3β phosphorylation, and ubiquitin-proteasome and ER-associated degradation.

This is a monocyte-enriched expression module: a small group of transcripts whose abundance marks cells of the monocyte/macrophage lineage and distinguishes them from lymphocytes and granulocytes in blood. Such signatures are used to infer myeloid content in tissue and blood profiling and to track monocyte activation in inflammation. The genes fit that identity: the Src-family kinases HCK and FES transduce signals from Fc and growth factor receptors toward phagocytosis, adhesion and myeloid differentiation; the galectins LGALS1 and LGALS3 are abundant secreted lectins that modulate cell adhesion and immune cell activation; TNFSF13 (APRIL) is a monocyte-derived TNF-family ligand supporting plasma cell survival and antibody production; and a copper transporter and cytoskeletal or membrane-skeleton components round out the phenotype. Together they reflect the phagocytic, antigen-presenting and cytokine-secreting functions on which innate immune defence and tissue remodelling depend.

Sister chromatids must stay physically linked from replication until the spindle is ready to pull them apart, and this regulatory layer sets how long and how tightly that linkage is held. Premature loss of cohesion produces unequal chromosome segregation, lagging chromosomes and aneuploidy; excessive retention blocks anaphase. Control operates at several levels: the kinase BUB1 phosphorylates centromeric histone H2A to recruit the shugoshin-based protection system that shields centromeric cohesin from cleavage, while chromatin factors such as ATRX and the histone variant macroH2A shape the centromeric and heterochromatic environment in which cohesion is established. A SUMO ligase branch built around SMC5 with NSMCE2 and its SLF1/SLF2 recruitment partners links cohesion maintenance to replication-fork repair and resolution of joint molecules, and tankyrase activity contributes to telomeric sister separation. The pathway sits within mitotic chromosome segregation and genome stability.

Humans cannot make pyridoxal 5'-phosphate de novo, so all of it comes from dietary pyridoxine, pyridoxal and pyridoxamine, and vitamin B6 activation to pyridoxal phosphate is the salvage route that converts these vitamers into the usable cofactor. PLP is the working group of transaminases and of decarboxylases that make GABA, serotonin and dopamine, and of enzymes in heme synthesis, glycine cleavage and transsulfuration, so the supply of active cofactor sets the capacity for amino acid and neurotransmitter metabolism. Only two committed steps are needed: pyridoxal kinase phosphorylates the free vitamers, and pyridoxine 5'-phosphate oxidase oxidizes the pyridoxine and pyridoxamine phosphates to PLP; an aldehyde oxidase also handles pyridoxal turnover. Loss of the oxidase step causes neonatal epileptic encephalopathy that responds to PLP rather than pyridoxine, showing how directly brain excitability depends on this conversion.

Complement activation is the humoral arm of innate immunity that tags microbes and damaged cells for lysis and phagocytic clearance while amplifying inflammation. The genes here span both the triggering proteases and the brakes: C1R and C1S form the catalytic subunits of the C1 complex that initiates the classical route on antibody-coated surfaces, factor B (CFB) drives the alternative amplification loop, and C3 is the shared hub whose cleavage deposits opsonin on target membranes and releases chemotactic fragments. C7 contributes to the membrane attack complex that punches pores in target cells. Regulation is equally represented, with factor H and factor I restraining C3 convertase activity and clusterin inhibiting terminal complex assembly, alongside vitamin K-dependent protein S linking this chemistry to coagulation and apoptotic cell clearance. Loss of such restraint underlies atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and age-related macular degeneration, while IL33 ties the response to tissue-damage alarm signalling.

Peptide hormones are made as inactive precursors and only become signals after regulated cutting, modification, packaging and, eventually, destruction; this metabolism sets how much active hormone reaches a target tissue. Precursors such as proinsulin, proopiomelanocortin, proglucagon, progastrin-releasing peptide and proghrelin enter the secretory pathway, are cleaved by the granule endoproteases PCSK1 and PCSK2 with carboxypeptidase E trimming, and are stored in granules whose zinc supply and exocyst-, kinesin-, Rab27/myosin-Va- and syntaxin/VAMP-dependent transport deliver them to the surface. Ghrelin additionally requires octanoylation by MBOAT4 and is deacylated in blood by butyrylcholinesterase. Extracellular peptidases then shape activity: renin and ACE generate angiotensin II to drive vasoconstriction, sodium retention and aldosterone release, ACE2 and neprilysin produce alternative fragments, and DPP4 inactivates the incretins GLP-1 and GIP. Glycoprotein hormone subunits and lineage factors such as PAX6 and ISL1 link this biology to endocrine cell identity, diabetes and blood pressure control.

HIV-1 encodes Nef, a small myristoylated accessory protein made early in infection that is not required for virus assembly but largely determines how aggressively the virus replicates and how fast disease progresses — Nef-deleted SIV and HIV are strikingly attenuated. Its contribution to replication and pathogenesis works through host trafficking and signalling machinery: by engaging clathrin adaptor complexes AP-1 and AP-2 together with ARF1 and PACS1, Nef redirects CD4 and MHC class I molecules such as HLA-A and its β2-microglobulin partner away from the cell surface, blunting CD4 helper function and shielding infected cells from cytotoxic T lymphocytes. In parallel Nef binds Src-family kinases including LCK, FYN and HCK and activates a PAK2–RAC1 module with the DOCK2/ELMO1 exchange complex, perturbing T cell receptor and CD28 signalling, actin remodelling and cell motility while raising virion infectivity.

Base-excision repair handles the most common kind of everyday DNA damage: single bases that have been oxidised, deaminated, alkylated or mismatched, such as the 8-oxoguanine left by reactive oxygen species or the uracil left by cytosine deamination. Without it, these lesions become point mutations at every round of replication, and inherited defects in the glycosylases MUTYH and NTHL1 predispose to colorectal cancer. A damage-specific glycosylase (OGG1, UNG, TDG, MPG, SMUG1, MBD4, the NEIL enzymes) excises the base; the AP endonuclease APEX1 cuts the abasic sugar-phosphate backbone; polymerase beta fills the single-nucleotide gap, or FEN1 with PCNA and replicative polymerases performs longer-patch synthesis; and LIG3 with its scaffold XRCC1 seals the nick. PARP1 and PARP2 sense the strand break and recruit repair factors, which is why PARP inhibition is exploited therapeutically in tumours already deficient in other repair routes.

Cells and tissues must sense and dispose of chemicals they did not make — drugs, plant toxins, pollutants, industrial compounds — and the response to xenobiotic stimulus covers the whole reaction, from ligand sensing through enzymatic conversion, export and downstream changes in gene expression and physiology. This determines how drugs are cleared and dosed, why some individuals are sensitive to carcinogens, and how reactive intermediates cause liver injury. Ligand-activated transcription factors such as the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and the pregnane X receptor induce oxidative phase I cytochromes P450, followed by conjugation through glutathione transferases, UDP-glucuronosyltransferases, sulfotransferases and N-acetyltransferases, with ABC and SLC transporters handling uptake and efflux into bile and urine. Oxidative by-products engage antioxidant defences under NFE2L2 control, while DNA damage sensing, p53 signalling, apoptotic and inflammatory responses are recruited when detoxification is overwhelmed.

Oncogenic KRAS activation not only drives proliferative programmes but also silences a broad swathe of differentiation-associated genes, and this collection captures that repressed arm. The genes lost are largely markers of terminal, tissue-specific identity rather than growth: epidermal keratins and cornified-envelope components such as KRT1, KRT5, SPRR3 and TGM1; striated and cardiac muscle contractile proteins including CKM, MYH7, TNNI3 and the ryanodine receptors; ion channels and solute carriers that define specialized transporting epithelia and neurons; and lineage transcription factors such as SOX10, PAX3, PAX4, HNF1A and ZBTB16. Immune effector and antigen-presentation genes, including IFNG, IL12B, CD80 and CD40LG, are likewise among the down-regulated set, consistent with the immune-cold phenotype of KRAS-mutant tumours. Loss of these programmes underlies the de-differentiation, epithelial plasticity and immune evasion characteristic of RAS-driven pancreatic, colorectal and lung cancers, and re-expression accompanies response to RAS or MEK inhibition.

Abasic sites arise constantly in DNA, both spontaneously and as intermediates left behind by glycosylases that excise damaged bases, and they must be cleaned up before replication turns them into mutations or strand breaks. This branch of base excision repair resolves them without the usual AP endonuclease step: NEIL1 and NEIL2, bifunctional glycosylases with beta/delta lyase activity, incise the strand and leave a 3' phosphate and a 5' deoxyribose phosphate. DNA polymerase beta trims the 5'dRP but is blocked by the 3' phosphate, so the phosphatase activity of PNKP must restore a 3'-hydroxyl before a single replacement nucleotide can be inserted and the nick sealed by the XRCC1-scaffolded LIG3 complex. The route matters for handling oxidative lesions, including those generated by OGG1, and for limiting mutagenesis in transcribed and replicating DNA.

Purine nucleoside phosphorylase carries out a step in purine salvage and degradation, converting inosine and guanosine to hypoxanthine and guanine so that ribose is recovered and the bases are either reused or oxidised onward to uric acid. Loss of this activity is the archetypal nucleotide catabolism defect: deoxyguanosine and its nucleotides accumulate and are especially toxic to developing lymphocytes, producing a severe combined immunodeficiency with profound T cell depletion and, in many patients, neurological impairment and autoimmunity. The biochemistry illustrates why purine turnover must be kept in balance -- blocked degradation distorts the deoxynucleotide pool and stalls DNA replication in proliferating cells. Because the same chemistry limits nucleoside-analogue drugs, the enzyme is also a pharmacological target, linking inherited metabolic failure to immune development and purine homeostasis.

This is the aggregate of activating inputs into intracellular signalling: processes and molecules that switch on, amplify or prolong the relay of information from receptors to the cytoplasmic and nuclear machinery that changes cell behaviour. It spans growth factor and cytokine receptor tyrosine kinases with their adaptors and exchange factors, feeding RAS-RAF-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and mTOR complexes together with their amino-acid-sensing Rag and lysosomal scaffolds; innate immune receptors signalling through MyD88, IRAKs and TRAFs to NF-kB; inflammasome and death-receptor modules; TGF-beta/BMP, WNT, Hippo and G-protein-coupled receptor arms; and stress-, DNA-damage- and unfolded-protein-response kinases. Positive control is exerted by kinases, ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases, small GTPases, scaffolds and secreted ligands. The output is decisions about proliferation, survival, differentiation, metabolism and inflammation, which is why persistent overactivation of these steps underlies cancer, autoinflammatory and fibrotic disease.

Cells acquire the branched-chain amino acid leucine from the extracellular space by carrier-mediated uptake, and this import step does more than feed protein synthesis: cytosolic leucine is the amino acid that mTORC1 senses, so the transporters here set how strongly growth signalling, translation and autophagy suppression respond to nutrient supply. Two systems carry the traffic. The heterodimeric system L exchangers pair the light chains SLC7A5 or SLC7A8 with the heavy chain SLC3A2 for obligatory antiport, trading intracellular glutamine or other neutral amino acids for leucine and related large neutral substrates including aromatic amino acids and thyroid hormones. SLC43A1 and SLC43A2 instead move leucine by facilitated, sodium-independent diffusion. Because tumours upregulate SLC7A5 to sustain anabolic demand, and because these carriers deliver amino acids across the blood-brain barrier and placenta, leucine import links systemic nutrient distribution to cellular growth control.

Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors sitting at or near nerve terminals act as a volume control on transmitter release, letting cholinergic input tune the output of glutamatergic, noradrenergic and dopaminergic synapses rather than carrying the signal itself. This presynaptic modulation underlies the reinforcing effects of nicotine, and receptors built from alpha4 and beta2 subunits, or containing alpha6 and beta3, are the ones through which nicotine drives dopamine release in reward circuits; variation at the alpha5-alpha3-beta4 cluster is tied to smoking behaviour and dependence. All the subunits here are ligand-gated cation channels that assemble as pentamers, and their cation selectivity sets the mechanism: direct calcium entry can suffice for release, while sodium-dominated flux depolarises the terminal and recruits voltage-gated calcium channels. Homomeric alpha7 channels instead seed calcium-induced calcium release from internal stores via ryanodine and IP3 receptors, amplifying a small influx into a release-competent local signal.

Oxidative and electrophilic stress is met by a transcriptional programme that rebuilds the cell's antioxidant and detoxification capacity, and the nuclear phase of NFE2L2 action is where that programme is written. Once freed from KEAP1-directed ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover, NFE2L2 enters the nucleus, dimerises with small MAF proteins such as MAFG and MAFK, and occupies antioxidant response elements together with coactivators CREBBP and EP300. The genes switched on cover glutathione synthesis (GCLC, GCLM), thioredoxin and peroxiredoxin recycling, NQO1 and heme oxygenase, cystine uptake via SLC7A11, NADPH supply through the pentose phosphate enzymes G6PD and PGD, drug efflux transporters, and subunits of the proteasome itself. BACH1 competes for the same elements as a repressor, while GSK3B and beta-TrCP provide a second route to NFE2L2 degradation. Constitutive activation, often through KEAP1 loss, gives tumours chemoresistance and a metabolic advantage.

When an FGF ligand dimerizes and activates FGFR2, autophosphorylation of the receptor's cytoplasmic tail converts ligand binding into intracellular instructions for growth, movement and differentiation; this is the downstream signaling of activated FGFR2. The output governs limb bud outgrowth, branching morphogenesis of lung and salivary gland, keratinocyte behaviour and cranial suture and palate development, which is why FGFR2 mutations cause craniosynostosis syndromes such as Apert and Crouzon, and why activating lesions recur in gastric, endometrial and breast tumours. Mechanistically, the long juxtamembrane region binds the FRS2/FRS3 adaptors, which recruit GRB2 with the phosphatase PTPN11 and the exchange factor SOS1 to load the RAS proteins and drive MAP kinase signalling, while GAB1 brings in PI3K for AKT-dependent survival. SHC1 provides a parallel route to RAS, and PLCG1 binds the receptor directly to generate diacylglycerol and mobilize calcium.

Blood and lymphatic vessels form where VEGF ligands meet their receptor tyrosine kinases, and the pairing rules between them determine which kind of vessel grows. VEGF-A acting on VEGFR-2 drives endothelial proliferation, migration and permeability in angiogenesis, while VEGF-C and VEGF-D signalling through VEGFR-3 specifies and expands lymphatic endothelium; placental growth factor and VEGF-B bind only VEGFR-1, which also acts as a decoy that limits how much VEGF-A reaches VEGFR-2. Each active ligand is a homodimer, and alternative splicing and proteolytic processing tune receptor preference and matrix binding, with neuropilin co-receptors raising affinity without signalling themselves. This ligand-receptor layer sets the level of the signal that follows, and it underlies wound healing, tumour vascularisation, diabetic retinopathy and macular degeneration, making these proteins the targets of anti-angiogenic drugs.

Estrogen acting through its nuclear receptor rewires gene expression within minutes to hours, and the early response arm of that programme is the first wave of direct transcriptional targets. It drives proliferation and secretory differentiation in hormone-responsive tissues such as breast, endometrium and prostate epithelium, and its persistent activation underlies the growth of estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, which is why these transcripts serve as readouts of receptor activity and of resistance to antihormonal therapy. Classic direct targets appear here, including the progesterone receptor, GREB1, trefoil factors, cyclin D1 and MYC, together with growth factor and receptor tyrosine kinase components such as AREG, IGF1R and RET that convert hormonal input into mitogenic signalling. Also represented are lipogenic enzymes, nutrient and amino acid transporters, keratins and junctional proteins, coregulators such as NRIP1 and NCOR2, and the chaperone-associated FKBP4/FKBP5 pair.

At the border between neural plate and surface ectoderm, a strip of cells is set aside as the neural crest, the source of the migratory population that later builds craniofacial bone and cartilage, peripheral neurons and glia, melanocytes and parts of the heart outflow tract. Specification of this territory depends on graded WNT input, with a WNT ligand and the LRP6 co-receptor promoting border fate while a secreted frizzled-related decoy restrains it, and on SOX9 to confer crest identity. Ribosome biogenesis and RNA polymerase I function, via treacle and nucleolar partners, are unusually limiting here, as are cullin-RING adaptors that ubiquitinate the nucleolar machinery; failure causes the ribosomopathy-type craniofacial malformation seen in Treacher Collins syndrome. Endothelin signalling through its receptor patterns the pharyngeal arch derivatives that arise from these cells.

Androgen receptor signaling drives male sexual differentiation, spermatogenesis, muscle and bone anabolism, and the growth of prostate epithelium; tuning its output is what these genes do, and their failure underlies androgen insensitivity at one extreme and castration-resistant prostate cancer at the other. Most act as coregulators recruited to the receptor at hormone-responsive promoters: acetyltransferase and deacetylase activities such as EP300, HDAC1 and SIRT1, the demethylases KDM1A and KDM4C, corepressor scaffolds NCOR1 and NCOR2, and the chromatin remodeller SMARCA4 set whether a target gene is switched on or held silent. Others modulate receptor abundance, stability or localisation through ubiquitin ligases and SUMO pathways, or through kinase input. Growth factor and Wnt-related components add crosstalk, so hormone sensitivity is set jointly by endocrine and local signals rather than by ligand concentration alone.

Leukocytes must be captured from flowing blood and moved across the vessel lining to reach inflamed or injured tissue, and the cell surface interactions at the vascular wall described here are what make that possible. Selectins and their glycoprotein ligands, notably SELE, SELP, SELL and SELPLG, mediate reversible tethering and rolling, after which integrins such as ITGAL/ITGB2 and ITGAM convert rolling into firm adhesion on endothelium or on platelets already deposited at a site of injury. Junctional and immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion molecules including PECAM1, F11R, JAM2/JAM3, CD99 and ESAM control endothelial cell contacts and guide transendothelial migration, while Src-family kinases, phosphatases and PI3K/Ras adaptors relay adhesion into intracellular signalling. Related interactions cover thrombin- and protein C-dependent endothelial anticoagulant control, angiopoietin-TEK signalling, SIRPA-CD47 recognition, and amino acid transporter heterodimers at the plasma membrane. Dysregulation contributes to atherosclerosis, thrombosis and chronic inflammatory injury.

Female meiosis I is the reductional division in the oocyte that separates homologous chromosomes, and it is the step at which human eggs most often go wrong: errors here produce aneuploid eggs, miscarriage and trisomic pregnancy, and the risk rises steeply with maternal age. The genes involved span the two things this division must get right. Homologue pairing and crossover formation depend on meiotic recombination factors such as MEIOB, HSF2BP and BRME1, with MLH3 resolving crossovers so that homologues stay physically linked until anaphase. The other arm is cell cycle control and chromosome segregation: cyclin B2 with CDC25B drives maturation-promoting factor activity, FBXO5 restrains the anaphase-promoting complex during prolonged prophase arrest, and NDC80 with TRIP13 governs kinetochore attachment and spindle checkpoint silencing on the acentrosomal oocyte spindle.

A co-expression grouping that marks lymphocytes as a population rather than any single signalling route, mixing B cell and T cell identity genes and so tracking the abundance of infiltrating or circulating lymphocytes in a tissue sample. Its B cell side includes the surface antigen receptor coreceptor CD19, the adaptor BANK1 and the transcription factor MEF2C, which supports B cell proliferation and survival; its T cell side includes CD2 and the costimulatory receptor CD28, required alongside antigen recognition for full activation, together with the T cell-restricted adaptor SH2D2A and the scaffold GAB1 that couples receptor engagement to downstream kinase cascades. PRKCZ contributes to lymphocyte polarity and activation signalling. Signatures of this kind are read as immune-cell content in tumour, blood and inflamed-tissue expression data, where high scores indicate lymphocytic infiltration.

The permanent adult kidney arises from metanephric mesenchyme, and the specification of these mesenchymal cells is what allows nephron progenitors to be established and later converted into the epithelia of the nephron. Without it there is no functional nephron endowment: the mesenchyme fails to respond to ureteric bud signals, and renal agenesis or hypodysplasia follows. Transcriptional regulators set the identity of the progenitor field, with OSR1 marking and maintaining the intermediate mesoderm-derived nephron progenitor pool and PAX2 acting in the competence of the mesenchyme to undergo induction; TCF21 contributes to stromal and mesenchymal cell fate decisions within the developing kidney. WNT4 provides the autocrine signal that drives induced mesenchyme through mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition into pretubular aggregates and renal vesicles. The pathway therefore sits at the interface of progenitor maintenance, inductive signalling and organ size determination during kidney development.

This is a blood transcriptional module whose expression marks monocytes, the circulating phagocytes that traffic into tissue and become macrophages or dendritic cells. Its members define the monocyte's readiness to sense inflammatory cues and move: a chemokine receptor for MIP-1alpha and RANTES that guides recruitment to inflamed sites, a receptor for hydroxycarboxylic acid ligands typical of myeloid cells, and a metalloproteinase inhibitor shaping the matrix the cell migrates through. The transcriptional component is the myeloid-biased CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein beta together with a MiT-family factor and BCL6, balancing differentiation against inflammatory gene output. Immediate-early and stress-response genes such as FOS and IER3 and the ERK-directed phosphatase DUSP6 mark how rapidly these cells respond to stimulation. Changes in this signature track monocyte abundance and activation state in infection, sepsis and chronic inflammatory disease.

Fibroblast growth factors bind FGFR3 at the cell surface and dimerize it, switching on the receptor's tyrosine kinase activity; unusually among growth factor receptors, the output restrains rather than promotes growth, acting as a brake on chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plates of long bones. Ligand binding and activation of FGFR3 therefore sets skeletal proportion: constitutively activating mutations shorten bones, producing achondroplasia and the milder hypochondroplasia, while the same lesions acquired somatically drive multiple myeloma and bladder and cervical carcinoma. Selectivity comes from which FGFs an FGFR3 splice variant can engage, with heparan sulfate needed for stable complex formation. FGF23 stands apart as an endocrine, bone-derived phosphate-regulating hormone whose secretion depends on O-glycosylation by GALNT3, linking this receptor family to renal phosphate handling as well as to local skeletal growth control.

Whether a T cell lives or dies by apoptosis is decided repeatedly: during thymic selection, at the peak of an immune response, and whenever tolerance to self must be enforced. Controlling the rate of T cell apoptotic death shapes the repertoire, terminates expansion once antigen is cleared, and prevents both autoimmunity and lymphopenia. The genes here act on both sides of that balance. Survival inputs include IL7R signalling through JAK3 and costimulation via CD27, while death is promoted by the FADD adaptor, the BH3-only protein PUMA encoded by BBC3, and p53-dependent transcription. Environmental and immunosuppressive cues feed in too: PD-L1 engagement, tryptophan depletion by IDO1, arginine consumption by ARG2, galectin binding to surface glycans, TGF-beta, and glucocorticoid-induced TSC22D3. Defects cause immunodeficiency, as with ADA or DOCK8 loss, or failure of peripheral tolerance.

Abasic sites arise constantly, both spontaneously and as the intermediate left behind when a DNA glycosylase excises a damaged base, and they must be converted back to intact duplex DNA before replication turns them into mutations or strand breaks. Short-patch base excision repair, in which a single nucleotide is replaced, handles the majority of these lesions. The AP endonuclease APEX1 incises the backbone 5' to the abasic deoxyribose, DNA polymerase beta removes the remaining sugar-phosphate through its lyase activity and inserts the correct replacement nucleotide, and the XRCC1 scaffold delivers DNA ligase III to seal the nick before the complex dissociates. Loss of this route leaves persistent single-strand interruptions, driving genomic instability, sensitivity to alkylating and oxidising agents, and the neurodegeneration seen when XRCC1-dependent repair fails.

Neurofibrillary tangles are intraneuronal aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau, and this pathway covers the influences that promote or restrain their formation, a process central to Alzheimer's disease and other tauopathies where tangle burden tracks with neuronal loss and cognitive decline. Control operates largely through tau phosphorylation balance: the kinases DYRK1A and MARK2 phosphorylate tau at sites that reduce microtubule binding and favour aggregation, while a catalytic subunit of protein phosphatase 2A reverses such marks. Post-transcriptional limits on tau production are set by microRNA regulation. Lipid and trafficking factors act from the other side, with APOE isoforms, clusterin and the sorting receptor SORL1 shaping amyloid handling, endosomal trafficking and glial responses that feed back onto tau pathology. Together these determine how quickly tau shifts from a microtubule-stabilising protein to a filamentous deposit.

Leukocytes kill infected and transformed cells, phagocytose pathogens, and release granule contents, and this pathway covers the controls that set how strongly and how often they do so. Tuning matters in both directions: too little and tumours and intracellular infections go unchecked, too much and cytotoxic and inflammatory damage causes autoimmunity or cytokine-driven tissue injury. The genes here span activating and inhibitory receptor pairs on natural killer and T cells, including NKG2D with its stress-induced ULBP and MIC ligands, checkpoint receptors such as PDCD1, LAG3, TIGIT and HAVCR2 opposed by costimulation through CD28 and CD40, and MHC class I and CD1 molecules that present ligands for recognition. Downstream, Syk- and Src-family kinases, VAV1, WAS and RAC2 relay signals, the SH2D1A/SLAM axis and the phosphatase PTPN6 damp them, and UNC13D with syntaxins and VAMPs executes granule exocytosis. Complement regulators, Toll-like receptors and cytokines including IL12, IL18, IL10 and TGFB1 adjust the threshold further.

Humans cannot make the B vitamins or vitamin C, so dietary forms must be absorbed, carried into cells and converted into the coenzymes that intermediary metabolism runs on. This pathway covers that conversion: thiamine to thiamine pyrophosphate for decarboxylases, riboflavin to FMN and FAD, nicotinamide and niacin to NAD through salvage and de novo routes, pantothenate to coenzyme A, pyridoxine to pyridoxal phosphate, folate to its polyglutamylated one-carbon carriers, cobalamin to the cofactors used by methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, and sulfuration of the molybdenum cofactor. Dedicated transporters and binding proteins handle uptake, including intrinsic factor with cubilin and amnionless in the ileum and specific carriers for folate, riboflavin, thiamine and ascorbate. Defects produce recognisable disease: thiamine-responsive anaemia, megaloblastic anaemia with homocystinuria, methylmalonic acidaemia, biotinidase deficiency and neurodegeneration from disrupted coenzyme A synthesis. Biotin-dependent carboxylases and NAD-consuming enzymes act as the downstream consumers.

Excitable and non-excitable cells alike must limit how far and how often their membrane potential shifts toward positive values, and this pathway groups activities that oppose membrane depolarization, keeping resting potential stable and restraining excitability. Suppressing depolarization matters in two distinct settings: at the plasma membrane of muscle and neurons, where unchecked depolarization drives arrhythmia, hyperexcitability and calcium overload, and at the mitochondrial inner membrane, where loss of potential commits a cell to apoptosis. Members reflect both: BCL2 and its relative BOK act at mitochondria to control permeabilization and the collapse of the membrane potential, while caveolin-3 organizes the sarcolemmal membrane domains in which ion channels sit, and its mutation causes rippling muscle disease and cardiomyopathy. SRC-family signalling and a Frizzled receptor link surface receptor input to this restraint, placing the process at the junction of ion homeostasis and survival decisions.

Skeletal muscle cell differentiation is the route by which mesodermal progenitors and satellite cells become committed myoblasts and then fuse into multinucleated, contractile muscle fibres, the tissue that supports posture, locomotion and whole-body metabolism. Its failure or derangement underlies muscular dystrophies, congenital myopathies and the arrested differentiation seen in rhabdomyosarcoma, and its reactivation from PAX7-marked satellite cells drives repair after injury. A core transcriptional hierarchy runs the programme: SIX1/SIX4 and PAX7 upstream, MYF5 and MYOD1 specifying commitment, and MYOG with MEF2C and MYF6 driving expression of sarcomeric and contractile genes. Notch and Wnt inputs, myostatin-mediated restraint, retinoid clearance and chromatin modifiers tune the balance between proliferation and terminal differentiation, while glycosyltransferases that mature dystroglycan and sarcomere-assembly factors such as KLHL40/41 and SMYD1 finish the fibre.

G2 phase is the gap between the end of DNA replication and entry into mitosis, the interval in which a cell grows, synthesises protein, and stockpiles the cytoplasmic material that two daughter cells will need. It is also when replication is verified before chromosome segregation is allowed, so its regulation determines whether damaged or incompletely replicated DNA is carried into mitosis. The genes here represent the cyclin-dependent kinase activity that carries cells through this window: A-type cyclins partnering CDK2 after the S-phase transition, with E2F transcription factors driving the periodic expression of replication and cell cycle genes that underlies the switch. Loss of control over this interval, through deregulated E2F activity or cyclin A overexpression, shortens the delay before mitosis and contributes to the genome instability characteristic of tumour cells.

The hippocampus is built over development from a patterned region of dorsomedial telencephalon into the layered dentate gyrus and cornu ammonis fields that support spatial navigation and the encoding of episodic memory; disrupted formation underlies epilepsy, intellectual disability and lissencephaly-type malformations. The genes here span the sequence of events: transcriptional regionalisation and progenitor identity through EMX2, LHX5, ZIC factors, GLI3 and Wnt/Hedgehog signalling; dentate granule cell specification via PROX1 and NEUROD1; and radial migration governed by Reelin acting through its receptor LRP8 and the DAB1 adaptor, with CDK5 and its activators, LIS1 and tubulin providing the cytoskeletal machinery. Later steps include axon guidance by ephrin and semaphorin receptors, synaptic target selection by KIRREL3, glycosylation-dependent dystroglycan function, and mTOR restraint by PTEN and TSC1 that sets neuronal size and connectivity.

SUMO proteins are made as precursors that cannot be attached to anything until their C-terminal extensions are trimmed, and this maturation and charging step is what makes the entire sumoylation system available to the cell. Protein modification by SUMO governs nuclear transport, transcriptional repression, DNA repair, chromosome segregation and the integrity of nuclear bodies, so a block at this first step disables all of it. SUMO-specific proteases cleave the propeptides to expose the diglycine terminus, with individual enzymes preferring particular SUMO paralogues and occupying distinct nuclear compartments cleoplasm for SENP1 and SENP2, nucleolus for SENP5. Mature SUMO is then adenylated and bound as a thioester by the heterodimeric E1 activating enzyme formed by SAE1 and UBA2, and passed to the single E2 conjugating enzyme UBE2I, whose activity RWDD3 enhances before transfer to substrates.

NPAS4 is an activity-dependent transcription factor whose induction couples neuronal firing to changes in synaptic wiring, and the control of its expression is how calcium entry becomes a lasting change in circuit behaviour. Transcription rises within minutes of calcium influx through NMDA receptors and L-type channels, driven by factors including SRF and the calcium-sensitive repressor KCNIP3/DREAM, and is held down by REST in non-neuronal contexts; glucocorticoid signalling through NR3C1 links chronic stress to reduced hippocampal levels. Argonaute proteins with their TNRC6 scaffolds and the RNA helicase MOV10 place the transcript under microRNA-mediated post-transcriptional control as well. The output matters for excitatory-inhibitory balance, plasticity and contextual memory formation, and NPAS4 loss accompanies neurodegeneration and age-related memory impairment. The same calcium-driven regulation operates in pancreatic beta cells.

Lateral mesoderm morphogenesis is the shaping of the mesodermal territory that lies furthest from the midline, the source of the heart and blood vessels, the body wall and limb connective tissue, and the splanchnic layers that surround the gut. Getting its cells to the right place and organising them into these structures determines whether a heart tube forms and whether the ventral body wall closes; failure produces cardiac malformation and defects of the gut mesenchyme. The genes here span the signals and transcriptional responses that pattern this tissue: bone morphogenetic protein and fibroblast growth factor receptors receive the inductive cues, while forkhead and T-box factors act in the splanchnic and cardiogenic domains respectively, and a shared transcription initiation subunit supports their output. The pathway therefore links early germ-layer patterning to organ primordium formation.

Oxidative attack on DNA leaves ring-opened formamidopyrimidines, thymine glycol and deaminated bases that mispair or stall replication, and base excision repair is the route by which these lesions are excised. NEIL1 is one of the glycosylases that initiates that route, recognising oxidised purines and pyrimidines and cutting them out while its associated beta/delta lyase activity nicks the backbone so downstream repair can finish the job. When NEIL1 is defective this initiating step fails and oxidative lesions persist, producing genomic instability. Naturally occurring low-frequency variants illustrate the consequences: a glycine-to-aspartate substitution with crippled catalytic activity is linked to primary sclerosing cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma, an in-frame deletion found in gastric cancer cannot process thymine glycol, and a truncation removing the nuclear localisation signal strands the protein in the cytosol away from its substrate. Loss of expression, including by promoter hypermethylation, accompanies several cancers, and murine deficiency also produces a metabolic-syndrome phenotype.

Testosterone and dihydrotestosterone act largely through a single intracellular receptor, and androgen receptor signalling is the route by which that hormonal cue becomes a change in gene transcription. It builds and maintains male reproductive tissues and secondary sex characteristics, drives prostate epithelial identity through targets such as NKX3-1, and is the therapeutic axis in prostate cancer, where receptor reactivation underlies castration resistance; loss-of-function causes androgen insensitivity. Ligand binding releases the receptor from chaperone control, with the immunophilin FKBP4 assisting maturation, and allows nuclear translocation and binding at hormone response elements. Output is then set by coregulators: the acetyltransferase EP300 and the remodeller SMARCA4 favour activation, NCOR1/NCOR2 with HDAC1 and SIRT1 repress, and lysine demethylases including KDM1A and KDM3A tune chromatin, while ubiquitin ligases, SUMO and palmitoylation enzymes control receptor stability and localisation.

This grouping collects the activators that raise the rate or extent of DNA transactions — replication, recombination, repair, telomere maintenance and chromatin-templated access to the genome. Its output is a genome that can be copied on schedule and mended after damage; loss of these stimulatory inputs produces replication stress, unrepaired breaks, telomere attrition and the mutability that underlies cancer and premature ageing syndromes. Much of the work is chromatin remodelling and histone modification that opens damaged or replicating DNA: SWI/SNF subunits such as SMARCA4 and ARID1A, the INO80 and TIP60/EP400 complexes with their RUVBL1/RUVBL2 ATPases, and acetyltransferase KAT5. Damage sensing and signalling run through ATM, ATR and PRKDC with the MRE11–RAD50–NBN complex, RNF8/RNF168 ubiquitin marks and 53BP1–shieldin control of end resection. Replication licensing and clamp loading factors, shelterin components including POT1 and TERF2, and growth-factor and cytokine signals that drive cells into S phase also feed in.

Peroxisomes are small oxidative organelles that handle lipid chemistry the mitochondria cannot: beta-oxidation of very-long-chain and branched fatty acids, ether phospholipid (plasmalogen) synthesis, bile acid intermediate processing, and disposal of the hydrogen peroxide these reactions generate. The organelle's identity rests on import machinery — PEX5 recognises targeting signals and docks at the PEX13/PEX14 membrane complex, with PEX2 and PEX6 completing receptor recycling, while PEX11 proteins control proliferation and division. ABCD transporters deliver fatty acyl substrates across the membrane for ACOX1, the bifunctional enzyme HSD17B4 and thiolase ACAA1, and catalase with peroxiredoxins detoxifies the peroxide produced. Loss of import causes Zellweger spectrum disease; defects in single steps cause X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy and related leukodystrophies. Associated retinoid, sterol and lipid-handling enzymes tie this compartment to whole-cell lipid and redox homeostasis.

ERK1 and ERK2 drive proliferation, differentiation, inflammatory gene expression and cytoskeletal remodelling, and they can be switched on without the RAS-to-RAF route that textbooks emphasise. This RAF-independent activation of MAPK1/3 matters because cytokine receptors, immune receptors and stress signals reach the same terminal kinases through other MAP3 kinases, so tumours and inflammatory states can sustain ERK output while RAF is bypassed. Here interleukin-6 acting through its receptor and the shared IL6ST subunit engages JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2 with the phosphatase adaptor PTPN11, converging on MEK1 and MEK2 and then on ERK1/2. Output is shaped as much by termination as initiation: a large family of dual-specificity phosphatases dephosphorylates the activation loop, PEA15 sequesters ERK in the cytoplasm, and CDK1 links activity to cell cycle timing. Active ERK enters the nucleus to phosphorylate Ets-family factors such as ELK1 and reprogramme transcription.

When misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, cells mount the unfolded protein response, a transcriptional and translational programme that either restores folding capacity or commits the cell to death. It matters for any cell with a heavy secretory load — plasma cells, pancreatic beta cells, hepatocytes — and its failure underlies diabetes, neurodegeneration and the stress tolerance that lets tumours survive hypoxia and nutrient shortage. Three sensors branch from the ER membrane: IRE1 (ERN1) splices XBP1 mRNA, PERK (EIF2AK3) phosphorylates eIF2alpha to throttle translation while permitting ATF4 synthesis, and ATF6 is cleaved to a transcription factor. Their targets expand ER chaperones and redox enzymes such as BiP (HSPA5), HSP90B1, PDIA6 and ERO1A, boost ER-associated degradation via EDEM1 and HERPUD1, and reprogramme amino acid transport and biosynthesis through ASNS, PSAT1 and SLC7A5. Ribosome biogenesis, mRNA decay and signal peptide processing factors accompany the adjustment of protein flux.

SARS-CoV-1 alters programmed cell death in host cells, connecting antiviral defense to tissue injury and inflammation. Eliminating infected cells can restrict viral replication, but excessive inflammatory cell death releases cellular contents and cytokines, contributing to severe lung disease. Apoptosis of lymphocytes may also contribute to the lymphopenia observed in severe infection. The viral 3a protein promotes RIPK3 oligomerization and inflammatory cell death, while RIPK1 and RIPK3 participate in the host machinery governing necroptosis. Viral E and 7a proteins interact with the anti-apoptotic protein BCL2L1, weakening survival control and favoring apoptosis. These effects alter the balance between contained, caspase-mediated cell dismantling and membrane-disruptive death, linking viral protein activity to immune-cell depletion and amplified inflammatory responses.

Phosphatases need controlling as much as kinases do, and this pathway covers the processes that set how fast and where phosphate groups are removed from proteins and lipids. Because dephosphorylation terminates or reverses signalling, its regulation determines the duration of kinase output, the recycling of signalling intermediates, and the timing of events such as mRNA surveillance and cytoskeletal remodelling. The members act through several routes: regulatory and inhibitory subunits that gate protein phosphatase 1 and 2A holoenzymes, including IGBP1 and PPP1R17; myotubularin-family and inositol polyphosphate phosphatases that act on phosphoinositides rather than proteins, with MTMR2 loss causing demyelinating Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy; the SMG5-SMG6-SMG7 module that directs dephosphorylation of UPF1 during nonsense-mediated decay; and receptors such as DRD2 and ADORA1 that tune phosphatase activity downstream of extracellular signals. Glycogen-associated EPM2A links the same logic to Lafora disease.

STAT5A and STAT5B are closely related transcription factors that convert cytokine and growth factor signals at the cell surface into programmes of survival, proliferation and differentiation, most conspicuously in haematopoietic progenitors and lymphocytes. STAT5 activation depends on receptor-associated tyrosine kinase activity: here the receptor FLT3, engaged by its ligand FLT3LG, autophosphorylates and recruits the adaptors GRB2 and GAB2 together with the phosphatase PTPN11, building a signalling platform from which STAT5 is tyrosine phosphorylated, dimerises and moves to the nucleus to drive genes such as those for cyclins and anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members. Because this output is growth-promoting, it is a frequent target of oncogenic hijacking; internal tandem duplication of FLT3 in acute myeloid leukaemia produces ligand-independent, constitutive STAT5 signalling and is one basis for kinase inhibitor therapy in that disease.

GRB7 recruitment is one branch of growth factor signalling through the ERBB2 receptor, engaged when neuregulin binds ERBB3 and drives formation of a ligand-activated ERBB2-ERBB3 heterodimer. Phosphotyrosines in the ERBB3 C-terminal tail create the docking site for the adaptor GRB7, which carries no catalytic activity of its own but links the receptor complex to proliferative and migratory outputs. Through recruitment of SHC1 it contributes to RAS activation and cell growth, and when GRB7 is itself phosphorylated by integrin-activated focal adhesion kinase it feeds into VAV2-dependent RAC1 activation and cytoskeletal remodelling that supports cell motility. The downstream mechanisms remain incompletely defined. This arm matters clinically because GRB7 lies adjacent to ERBB2 on chromosome 17 and is co-amplified with it in breast cancer, coupling receptor overexpression to invasive behaviour as well as to proliferation.

Transcripts encoding cytokines, growth factors and other short-lived regulators carry AU-rich elements in their 3' untranslated regions, and the proteins that bind those elements set how long the message survives. This is how a cell terminates an inflammatory response on schedule; loss of control produces sustained TNF and other cytokine output and contributes to chronic inflammation and malignancy. Destabilising factors such as ZFP36, KHSRP and HNRNPD recruit deadenylases and hand the body of the message to the cytoplasmic exosome or to decapping and 5'-to-3' decay, while ELAVL1 binding the same elements protects the transcript instead. The balance is set by signalling: the p38 pathway acting through MAPKAPK2 phosphorylates ZFP36, promoting 14-3-3 binding and sequestration, and nucleocytoplasmic transport and ubiquitin-proteasome turnover of the binding proteins add further layers to post-transcriptional gene regulation.

The final step of cell division, in which one cell is physically split into two, depends on a cytoskeleton-dependent cytokinesis programme that positions the division plane, constricts it, and severs the remaining bridge. Getting this wrong produces binucleate cells, tetraploidy and chromosome missegregation, routes toward aneuploidy and tumorigenesis, and in the germ line failed cytokinesis blocks spermatogenesis. RhoA activation through ECT2 and the centralspindlin components KIF23 and RACGAP1 drives assembly of an actomyosin ring with anillin, formins, cofilin and non-muscle myosin, while septins and IQGAP proteins organise the cortex beneath it. The Aurora B–INCENP–survivin complex times the process against chromosome segregation; PLK1 and citron kinase contribute further phosphoregulation. Vesicle delivery by Rab11 and the exocyst feeds the intercellular bridge, and ESCRT-III subunits with CEP55, ALIX and the VPS4 ATPases, plus microtubule severing by spastin, complete abscission.

Cells extend and elaborate projections — axons, dendrites, filopodia, microvilli, cilia — and this pathway covers the signals and machinery that push that process forward rather than restrain it. It matters most in the nervous system, where growth cone advance, axon guidance and dendritic branching wire circuits, and in epithelial and sensory cells that depend on ciliary or brush border structures; loss of these activities underlies neurodevelopmental disability, intellectual disability and failed nerve regeneration. Mechanistically, guidance and growth factor receptors such as the neurotrophin receptors, Eph receptors, plexins and Robo family feed into Rho-family GTPases including CDC42 and RAC1, which in turn drive Arp2/3- and WAVE-dependent actin nucleation, cofilin- and profilin-mediated filament turnover, and microtubule regulators like MAPT and MAP1B. Wnt, BMP and reelin inputs, ciliary transport components, and cytoskeletal kinases such as LIMK1 and PAK1 complete the positive control of projection formation and remodelling.

Late in HIV replication, the virus gathers everything a new particle needs to be infectious: two copies of genomic RNA, a primer tRNA, the envelope glycoprotein, the Gag polyprotein and the Gag-Pro-Pol precursor carrying protease, reverse transcriptase and integrase. Assembly of the HIV virion is essentially a hijacking of host membrane and trafficking machinery at the plasma membrane. Gag is myristoylated by N-myristoyltransferase to anchor it to the inner leaflet, the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase cyclophilin A is recruited through the capsid domain and incorporated into particles, and the envelope precursor is matured by a cellular proprotein convertase of the furin family. Budding depends on the ESCRT-I complex, TSG101 with VPS28, VPS37 subunits, MVB12 and UBAP1, together with ubiquitin, normally used for sorting cargo into multivesicular bodies. Blocking these interactions traps immature particles at the cell surface, a recognised antiviral vulnerability.

Taste buds convert chemicals in food into neural signals, and the sensory perception of taste is what lets an animal seek calories and amino acids while rejecting acids and potential toxins; its loss flattens appetite and food choice. Sweet and umami detection uses TAS1R2:TAS1R3 and TAS1R1:TAS1R3 heterodimers, while a large family of TAS2R receptors covers bitter compounds, TAS2R38 variants explaining common differences in perceived bitterness. These receptors share one cascade: gustducin-containing G protein heterotrimers activate PLCB2, IP3 opens ITPR3 to release stored calcium, and calcium gates TRPM5 to depolarize the cell, with voltage-gated sodium channels amplifying the response and CALHM1:CALHM3 releasing ATP as transmitter to afferent fibres. Sour taste instead depends on proton entry through OTOP1 and inhibition of KCNJ2 in type III cells, and low-salt taste on epithelial sodium channel subunits.

Neutrophils find infection by smelling it: bacterial N-formylated peptides and mitochondrial peptides released by damaged tissue bind formyl peptide receptors, and the resulting chemotactic and antimicrobial response is among the fastest arms of innate immunity. Engagement of FPR1 triggers directed migration, degranulation and assembly of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase, whose cytosolic regulatory subunits NCF1 and NCF2 are needed for the respiratory burst that kills ingested organisms; loss of these subunits causes chronic granulomatous disease with recurrent bacterial and fungal infection. Cytoskeletal reorganisation for chemotaxis runs through PAK1, calcium-dependent signalling through CAMK1, and immunoglobulin-mediated phagocytosis through the low-affinity Fc receptor FCGR2A, while SLC11A1 restricts metal availability to microbes inside the phagosome. Inhibitory and accessory receptors of myeloid cells set thresholds so that this destructive output stays proportionate to the stimulus.

Everything HIV does before it can express its own genes happens here: attachment and entry, uncoating, reverse transcription of the RNA genome into cDNA, nuclear import of the resulting nucleoprotein complex, and integration of viral DNA into a host chromosome. Because integration is irreversible, this phase establishes the latent reservoir that makes infection lifelong and resists therapy. Entry depends on CD4 together with a chemokine receptor coreceptor, either CCR5 or CXCR4, whose usage determines viral tropism and explains why CCR5 loss confers resistance. Host factors are co-opted throughout: cyclophilin A acts on the incoming capsid, an importin supports transport into the nucleus, and chromatin proteins including BANF1, HMGA1 and the tethering factor LEDGF/PSIP1 steer the preintegration complex toward transcribed genes. Nonhomologous end-joining and ligation enzymes then repair the breaks flanking the integrated provirus.

Control over when a ubiquitin ligase is switched on determines when its substrates are destroyed, and here that control is aimed almost entirely at the anaphase-promoting complex, the ligase that drives cells out of mitosis. CDC20 and FZR1 are the substrate-recruiting activators that engage the complex at successive points, CDC20 during metaphase to trigger securin and cyclin B destruction and FZR1 in late mitosis and G1 to keep degradation running until S phase commits. UBE2C and UBE2S are the cooperating ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes that initiate and then elongate the lysine-11-linked chains that mark substrates for the proteasome, so their availability sets the ligase's effective output. Positive regulation of ubiquitin protein ligase activity in this setting therefore enforces the irreversibility of chromosome segregation and mitotic exit; its loss permits premature separation, aneuploidy and unscheduled proliferation.

Skeletal muscle forms when myoblasts exit the cell cycle, switch on contractile genes and fuse into multinucleated myotubes, and this collection governs how strongly and how quickly that conversion proceeds. Its outputs set muscle mass, fibre-type composition and the capacity to regenerate after injury, which is why several members are studied as targets for muscle wasting. Positive regulators include the transcription factors MEF2C, SIX1 and SIX4 and the RNA-binding protein RBM24, which stabilises muscle transcripts and supports splicing alongside the DDX5/DDX17 helicase pair that cooperates with myogenic bHLH factors. Restraint comes chiefly from myostatin, a TGF-beta family ligand that limits myoblast proliferation and differentiation, with retinoic acid catabolism by CYP26B1 and circadian components such as BMAL1 and NR1D2 tuning timing. Chromatin and metabolic modifiers, among them KAT8 and SIRT2, link the programme to acetylation state and mitochondrial capacity.

Inflammation must be actively amplified once a threat is detected, and this collection covers the processes that raise the intensity, speed and duration of the inflammatory response. It underlies effective defence against pathogens and tissue injury, and its overactivity drives fever, septic shock, autoinflammatory syndromes such as familial Mediterranean fever, and chronic conditions from atherosclerosis to arthritis. Pattern-recognition receptors of the Toll-like family sense microbial and endogenous ligands and relieve inhibition of NF- uB, while inflammasome components including NLRP3, NLRC4, AIM2 and the adaptor PYCARD activate caspase-1 to mature IL-1 u and IL-18 and to cleave gasdermin D for pyroptotic release. Downstream amplification runs through TNF, IL-6 and its receptor subunit IL6ST into STAT3 signalling, chemokines that recruit neutrophils and monocytes, prostaglandin synthesis via COX-2, alarmins such as S100A8/A9, and interferon- u-induced guanylate-binding proteins. Several microRNAs and NFKBIA provide counterbalancing restraint.

Lipophilic hormones and metabolites act largely by binding nuclear receptors, ligand-gated transcription factors that convert the presence of a steroid, retinoid, oxysterol or fatty acid into a change in gene expression. This branch of signalling sets reproductive tissue growth, cholesterol and lipid handling, and developmental patterning, and its deregulation underlies hormone-dependent breast cancer, dyslipidaemia and retinoid-related birth defects. Receptors such as the estrogen receptors, progesterone receptor, retinoic acid receptors and the liver X receptors bind DNA as dimers, frequently with RXR partners, and switch between corepressor complexes containing NCOR1/2 and HDACs and coactivators such as the p160 family, CREBBP/EP300 and Mediator, which remodel chromatin and recruit RNA polymerase II. Chaperone complexes with HSP90 and FKBP immunophilins hold unliganded steroid receptors competent for hormone binding and nuclear import. Ligand supply and clearance are themselves encoded here, through retinaldehyde dehydrogenases and CYP26 enzymes, alongside rapid membrane-initiated signalling via SRC, PI3K and MAPK cascades and target genes governing sterol efflux and lipogenesis.

Humans encounter alkaloids as plant-derived drugs and poisons, and this alkaloid catabolic route is how the body dismantles them. It is essentially xenobiotic detoxification carried out by liver and plasma enzymes: butyrylcholinesterase and carboxylesterase 2 hydrolyse ester bonds in compounds such as cocaine and heroin, while cytochrome P450 monooxygenases oxidise, demethylate and hydroxylate substrates including codeine, morphinans and related alkaloids using NADPH and molecular oxygen. The products are more polar and readily conjugated and excreted. Because CYP2D6 and CYP3A4/5 differ widely between individuals in expression and sequence, the rate of this breakdown determines both drug efficacy and toxicity — a poor metaboliser gains no analgesia from codeine, an ultrarapid one risks overdose. The same chemistry is the basis for many drug–drug interactions and for succinylcholine sensitivity when cholinesterase activity is deficient.

Chromosome ends resemble broken DNA, and telomere maintenance in response to DNA damage covers how cells react when a telomere becomes critically short, uncapped or lesion-bearing. The outcome decides whether a cell continues to divide, enters senescence, or suffers end-to-end fusions and genome rearrangement, so this biology sits at the heart of replicative ageing and of the chromosomal instability seen in cancer and in telomere syndromes. Shelterin components such as TRF2, RAP1 and TPP1 suppress inappropriate repair at functional ends, while the SNM1B/Apollo and ERCC1-XPF nucleases and the RTEL1 helicase process telomeric overhangs and resolve replication-blocking structures. When repair is engaged, the shieldin complex with REV7 and RIF1 restricts end resection and biases outcomes toward non-homologous joining, and the INO80 chromatin remodelling complex with base-excision factors including APEX1 and XRCC1 handles damaged telomeric chromatin.

Granulocyte maturation in the bone marrow, and the antimicrobial cargo that neutrophils acquire as they mature, is the theme here. Promyelocytes and myelocytes load their granules with proteins that will later be deployed against bacteria: a lipopolysaccharide-binding bactericidal protein of the BPI family, the adipokine-like secreted factor resistin, prokineticin 2, the soluble pattern-recognition molecule pentraxin 3, and a haematopoietic growth factor of the CLEC11A type that supports progenitor expansion. Alongside them sit regulators that hold inflammatory signalling in check, including the kinase-dead IRAK family member IRAK3, and transport and lipid-remodelling enzymes such as the organic cation/ergothioneine transporter SLC22A4 and a lysophospholipid acyltransferase. A CDK inhibitor of the INK4 family and a linker histone variant point to the exit from proliferation that accompanies terminal differentiation. Together these define innate myeloid effector capacity, whose loss leaves recurrent bacterial infection.

Protein kinases N are Rho effectors: RHOA, RHOB, RHOC and RAC1 bind N-terminal antiparallel-coiled-coil motifs of PKN1, PKN2 and PKN3, relieving autoinhibition and positioning them for activation-loop phosphorylation by PDPK1. Through this route Rho GTPase signalling is converted into control of the actomyosin cytoskeleton, mitotic timing and nuclear transcription. Downstream of PKN activity sit non-muscle myosin heavy and light chains together with the myosin phosphatase holoenzyme and its inhibitor CPI-17, so contractility is set by the balance of kinase and phosphatase acting on myosin light chain. A second branch acts on cell cycle entry into mitosis via CDC25C, whose phosphorylation creates 14-3-3 binding sites that sequester it. In prostate cells PKN1 cooperates with the androgen receptor and histone-modifying enzymes including the demethylases KDM1A and KDM4C to drive expression of target genes such as the kallikreins, linking cytoskeletal signalling to hormone-dependent transcription and prostate cancer.

Dendrites are the receptive surface of a neuron, and how far they grow, how much they branch and where they arborize sets how many synapses a cell can receive. Regulation of dendrite development covers the signals that tune this growth, and its disturbance produces the simplified or over-exuberant dendritic trees seen in intellectual disability, epilepsy and autism. Extracellular cues act through guidance and adhesion receptors such as DCC, EPHA4/EPHB2, PTPRD and the reelin receptors VLDLR and LRP8, converging on Rho- and Rap-family GTPase regulators, actin and microtubule effectors including DBN1, COBL, BAIAP2 and CAMSAP2, and kinases such as GSK3B, CDKL5, MARK1 and CAMK2B. Bone morphogenetic protein ligands and receptors, transcription factors of the CUX and NR2E1 type, ubiquitin ligases including NEDD4 and HECW2, and RNA-binding proteins such as STAU2 add transcriptional and local translational control, linking dendrite shape to activity and to cortical circuit assembly.

Antibody output has to be capped as well as switched on, and this is the braking side of that balance: processes that stop or reduce immunoglobulin production by B cells. Without such restraint, plasma cell differentiation and class switching run unchecked, contributing to hypergammaglobulinaemia, autoantibody formation and allergic IgE responses. The genes here act at several levels. Inhibitory surface receptors such as CD22 and the low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR2B raise the threshold for B cell activation and deliver negative signals from immune complexes, while complement receptor CR1 tunes complement-dependent stimulation. BCL6 holds germinal centre B cells in a proliferative, differentiation-blocked state, opposing terminal plasma cell commitment. FOXP3 marks regulatory T cells that suppress the helper signals B cells require, and NDFIP1 promotes ubiquitin-mediated limitation of lymphocyte responses. Cytokine-side components, including an IL-33 and decoy IL-13 receptor pairing, link tissue signals to restraint of type 2 antibody responses.

Truncating mutations that remove the C-terminal PEST degron of NOTCH1 turn a normally self-limiting developmental signal into a persistent oncogenic one, and they are among the most common lesions in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Normally, ligands such as DLL1, DLL4 and JAG1 on a neighbouring cell trigger sequential cleavage by ADAM proteases and the presenilin-containing gamma-secretase complex, releasing the intracellular domain NICD1, which enters the nucleus, binds RBPJ with a MAML coactivator and displaces NCOR/HDAC corepressors to switch on HES, HEY and MYC transcription. The SCF ubiquitin ligase using the substrate receptor FBXW7 then recognises the phosphorylated PEST region and targets NICD1 for proteasomal destruction. PEST-domain mutants escape this step, so NICD1 accumulates and drives sustained proliferative transcription, explaining why such tumours are sensitive to gamma-secretase inhibition.

Dicarboxylic acids sit at the centre of intermediary metabolism, and the reactions that make and consume them link carbon oxidation, nitrogen disposal and one-carbon chemistry. Much of the set is tricarboxylic acid cycle and anaplerotic enzymology involving succinate, 2-oxoglutarate, malate, fumarate and oxaloacetate: succinate dehydrogenase and fumarase, malate dehydrogenases and malic enzymes, the 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, and the phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinases that commit oxaloacetate to gluconeogenesis. Glutamate and glutamine handling by glutaminases, glutamate dehydrogenase, glutamine synthetase and the aspartate aminotransferases feeds amino groups into these skeletons and into the urea cycle via argininosuccinate synthase and lyase. Folate and polyglutamate metabolism, proline and hydroxyproline oxidation, glyoxylate and 2-hydroxyglutarate turnover complete the picture. Inherited failures here cause organic acidurias, hyperammonaemia, primary hyperoxaluria and 2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria, while IDH and succinate dehydrogenase lesions drive tumour metabolism.

Long-term synaptic potentiation is the persistent strengthening of transmission at a synapse after patterned activity, and it is the cellular basis usually invoked for learning and memory storage in the hippocampus and cortex. Loss or distortion of it accompanies intellectual disability, autism-spectrum disorders and the early cognitive decline of Alzheimer's disease, and several genes here — APP, APOE, MECP2, SHANK2/3, RELN — sit at those disease intersections. Mechanistically, calcium entering through NMDA receptors bearing GRIN2A/2B subunits engages calmodulin and CaMKII, protein kinase C, Ras–ERK and adenylate cyclase–PKA cascades, driving AMPA receptor delivery and anchoring at the postsynaptic density and, through CREB1 and activity-induced products such as Arc, changes in transcription and local translation. Adhesion molecules, scaffolds, sodium–calcium exchangers, neuromodulator receptors and presynaptic release proteins tune the threshold and persistence of the change.

Lymphocyte numbers are set as much by controlled death as by division, and this pathway covers the signals that raise or lower the rate at which T and B cells die by apoptosis. It governs thymic and bone marrow selection, the contraction of clonal expansions after an infection is cleared, and the deletion of autoreactive cells; too little killing permits autoimmunity and lymphoid malignancy, too much produces immunodeficiency and lymphopenia. Pro-apoptotic effectors such as BAX, PUMA and FADD act with TP53, while survival inputs from the IL-7 receptor, IL-2, JAK3 and antigen-receptor kinases including BTK and LYN oppose them. Transcriptional regulators such as BCL6, MYC, FOXP1 and RORC, the glucocorticoid-induced TSC22D3, and immunoregulatory signals including PD-L1, IDO1, IL-10, TGFB2 and galectins tune the threshold, linking lymphocyte lifespan to tolerance and to the resolution of immune responses.

Phagocytes only destroy what they swallow after the phagosome fuses with a lysosome, and phagolysosome assembly is that delivery step: it converts a freshly internalised vesicle into an acidic, hydrolase-filled degradative compartment. Macrophages and neutrophils depend on it to kill bacteria and to clear apoptotic cells and debris, and pathogens such as mycobacteria persist precisely by blocking it. The genes involved carry out sequential maturation: Rab GTPases including RAB7A, RAB20 and RAB34 recruit tethering and motility machinery, ARL8B and a HOPS-related complex with VPS33B and VIPAS39 drive lysosome docking, PIKFYVE supplies the phosphoinositide signal for late endosomal identity, and TMEM175 supports lumenal acidification. Actin- and myosin-based components and a calcium-sensing synaptotagmin time membrane fusion. Loss of these steps impairs antigen processing and microbial killing and, as with CLN3, causes lysosomal storage disease.

Membrane proteins marked for destruction are not simply delivered to the lysosome; they must first be pulled into vesicles that bud into the endosome lumen, so that both their cytoplasmic and extracellular faces are exposed to hydrolases. This sorting route from late endosomes into multivesicular bodies and on to the degradative compartment terminates signalling by activated receptors, and its failure leaves growth factor and cytokine receptors active, contributing to oncogenic signalling and to defects in neuronal protein turnover. Ubiquitinated cargo is captured by HGS and STAM, passed through the ESCRT-I subunits TSG101 and VPS28 with their VPS37 and MVB12 partners, then via the VPS25/SNF8/VPS36 complex to CHMP proteins that polymerise and sever the neck of the inward bud. The same machinery is co-opted for cytokinetic abscission and for enveloped virus budding.

Interleukin-33 signalling is how a tissue reports its own damage. IL33 is an IL-1 family alarmin made constitutively by endothelial and epithelial cells and stored in the nucleus bound to chromatin, and it is not actively secreted; necrosis or mechanical injury releases it, so its appearance outside a cell is itself the danger signal. Extracellular IL33 binds the receptor IL1RL1 (ST2) and recruits the shared accessory co-receptor IL1RAP, forming a complex that drives IL-1-type inflammatory signalling toward NF- fB-dependent gene expression. The main responders are type 2 immune cells, including mast cells, ILC2s and Th2 cells, which makes this axis a driver of allergic airway inflammation, asthma and helminth defence, and a contributor to cardiac and mucosal injury responses. Inflammatory proteases trim the N-terminus and alter potency, and a soluble ST2 variant lacking the transmembrane region acts as a decoy.

Shortening of the poly(A) tail is the first and usually rate-limiting step in cytoplasmic mRNA turnover, and it sets how long a transcript remains translatable. Because the tail bound by poly(A)-binding protein cooperates with the cap-binding initiation machinery to promote translation, trimming it both silences a message and commits it to decay, making deadenylation of mRNA a general lever for controlling gene expression after transcription. Two exonuclease steps are represented: the PAN2-PAN3 complex performs initial trimming, then the multisubunit CCR4-NOT complex, whose catalytic subunits are CNOT6/6L and CNOT7/8 assembled on the CNOT1 scaffold, or the separate PARN enzyme completes it. Terminal uridylyltransferases mark short-tailed transcripts for destruction. This machinery shapes responses to developmental and circadian cues, oocyte maturation, and the clearance of unstable regulatory transcripts.

The liver can regenerate lost mass by driving its parenchymal cells back into the cell cycle, and this pathway covers the signals that set how fast and how far hepatocytes divide. It matters after partial hepatectomy or toxic injury, when restoration of liver mass depends on a burst of proliferation that must then be stopped; persistent stimulation instead favours fibrosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Inflammatory input through TNF initiates the response, with TNFAIP3 and the caspase-8 modulator CFLAR restraining death signalling so that dividing cells survive. Mitogenic and developmental cues arrive via WNT3A, hedgehog signalling through GLI1, and the heparin-binding growth factors midkine and pleiotrophin, while the ubiquitin ligase substrate receptor FBXW7 limits proliferation by degrading cell-cycle drivers. XBP1 links secretory and stress adaptation to growth, and MED1 couples nuclear receptor activity to transcription.

Tissue injury triggers an immediate defensive reaction, and this inflammatory response to wounding is the coordinated recruitment and activation of immune cells that clears damaged material and sets the stage for repair. It matters because too little leads to infection and poor healing, while too much produces chronic inflammation, fibrosis and scarring.
