EPB42 contributes to the deformable membrane skeleton; FLVCR1 exports excess heme and G6PD supplies the reducing power that protects hemoglobin-laden cells from oxidative damage. Cytoskeletal GTPases RAC1 and RAC2 and the actin nucleator DIAPH3 support enucleation and the contractile events of terminal differentiation, linking this process to oxygen transport capacity overall.

The early neural tube is subdivided into territories that will become forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain and spinal cord, and along its circumference into floor plate, motor neuron and dorsal interneuron domains. This patterning fixes where each class of neuron is born, so its failure produces holoprosencephaly, ventralization defects and other structural brain and spinal malformations. Ventral identity is set by SHH acting through PTCH1 and SMO, with signal strength tuned in the primary cilium: intraflagellar transport and transition zone components, the ciliary GTPase ARL13B, and the negative regulators GPR161 and TULP3 determine how much GLI activity a cell sees. Dorsal and boundary cues come from BMP4, WNT1 and WNT3A, while FGF8 with GBX2 and EN1 organizes the midbrain-hindbrain junction. Graded signalling is read out as transcription factor domains such as PAX6 and PAX7, reinforced by Polycomb repression through BMI1 and KDM2B.

Type I interferon signalling must be shut off once a viral threat is cleared, and this braking programme is what limits it. Sustained interferon output damages tissue and drives autoinflammatory disease: loss of the cytosolic exonuclease TREX1 or the dNTP triphosphohydrolase SAMHD1 leaves self nucleic acids to trigger chronic interferon production, as in Aicardi-Goutières syndrome, while ADAR-mediated RNA editing marks endogenous double-stranded RNA as self so it is not read as viral. Downstream, USP18 removes ISG15 conjugates and independently blocks JAK-STAT engagement at the receptor, and the phosphatase PTPN2 dephosphorylates JAK-STAT components. Additional restraint comes from m6A-dependent decay of interferon transcripts through METTL3 and the YTHDF readers, deadenylation by CNOT7, and translational repression via the EIF4E2-GIGYF2 module. Together these set the amplitude and duration of antiviral gene expression and preserve tolerance to self nucleic acids.

Every day each cell loses thousands of bases to spontaneous hydrolysis or to glycosylase excision of damaged ones, leaving abasic sites that stall polymerases and become strand breaks if left alone; resolution of these AP sites is the completion step of base excision repair that restores an intact double helix. The endonuclease APEX1 nicks the backbone 5' to the lesion and displaces the glycosylase, after which one of two routes finishes the job: short-patch repair, in which DNA polymerase beta removes the sugar remnant, inserts a single nucleotide and the XRCC1-ligase III complex seals the nick; or long-patch strand-displacement synthesis by polymerase delta or epsilon with PCNA, RPA and RFC, with FEN1 clipping the flap and ligase I closing it. PARP1/PARP2 mark the break and help recruit repair factors. Loss of this capacity drives mutation accumulation, and defects in MUTYH or NTHL1 predispose to colorectal and other cancers.

This is a broad control layer over where proteins go: the regulated movement of proteins into, out of and within cells, including secretion, nuclear import and export, vesicle budding and the retrieval of misfolded cargo from the secretory pathway. The genes span COPII coat and cargo-selection machinery (SAR1A/B, SEC13, SEC23/24 paralogues, SEC31), ER quality control and retrotranslocation factors (EDEM1/2, OS9, DERL2/3, UBE2J1), nucleocytoplasmic carriers such as RAN, RANGAP1, XPO1 and IPO5, and Rab11-based recycling endosome effectors. A large part of the set concerns regulated exocytosis of hormones, with insulin granule release in pancreatic beta cells prominently represented through glucose sensing, ATP-sensitive potassium channels, SNARE and synaptotagmin-family fusion proteins, and transcription factors that specify islet identity. Kinases, phosphatases and cytokines tune the rate of these steps, linking nutrient state, circadian timing and inflammation to protein delivery, and their dysregulation contributes to diabetes and to disorders of impaired secretory flux.

RHOJ is a small GTPase of the CDC42 subfamily, closely related to RHOQ and CDC42, and its activation cycle shapes the actin cytoskeleton during cell movement. The pathway matters most in endothelium, where RHOJ is highly expressed and controls lamellipodia formation, endothelial motility and tube formation, acting downstream of VEGF signalling to drive retinal and tumour angiogenesis; it also contributes to adipocyte differentiation and to cancer cell migration. Like other RHO proteins it alternates between GDP- and GTP-bound states, switched on by exchange factors such as ARHGEF7 and TRIO and switched off by GAPs of the ARHGAP family, with no GDI partner yet identified. In its active form it engages effectors that remodel actin and membranes, including PAK kinases, CDC42BPA/B, formins, WAS and WASL with WIPF2, and FNBP1 family BAR proteins, linking the switch to protrusion, vesicle traffic and polarity.

Blood and lymphatic vessels grow where endothelial cells receive a vascular endothelial growth factor signal, and that signal begins with ligand binding to a VEGF receptor and the receptor pairing up. The step initiates cascades that drive endothelial proliferation, survival, migration and increased vascular permeability, and it is the point at which tumours recruit their own blood supply and the target of anti-angiogenic drugs. Secreted ligands including VEGFA, VEGFB, placental growth factor and the lymphangiogenic VEGFC and VEGFD engage the receptor tyrosine kinases FLT1, KDR and FLT4 with distinct preferences; receptors mainly form homodimers, though FLT1-KDR heterodimers occur. KDR carries most angiogenic signalling in vivo, FLT1 acts largely as a modulating or decoy receptor, and FLT4 specifies lymphatic endothelium. Loss or dysregulation underlies vascular malformations, lymphoedema and pathological neovascularisation in retinopathy and cancer.

Guanylate binding proteins are interferon-gamma-inducible, dynamin-related GTPases that carry out cell-autonomous defence inside infected cells, attacking pathogens that hide in vacuoles or in the cytosol. Their loss leaves cells unable to restrict organisms such as Salmonella, Shigella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Toxoplasma, and blunts the inflammatory response to cytosolic bacteria. GBP1 binds GTP, dimerizes and hydrolyses it stepwise to GMP, and a prenyl anchor added by farnesyl- or geranylgeranyltransferase subunits lets it insert into pathogen membranes, where it oligomerizes and recruits GBP2, GBP3 and GBP4 into a dense coat. The coat damages bacterial membranes, blocks actin-based bacterial motility, and licenses caspase-mediated non-canonical inflammasome activation with pyroptosis and IL-1 family cytokine release. Regulation runs through PIM1 phosphorylation and 14-3-3 sigma sequestration in the cytosol. GBP2 and GBP5 additionally restrict enveloped viruses by interfering with furin-dependent maturation of viral glycoproteins.

The nephron tubule is the epithelial workhorse of the kidney, reabsorbing filtrate and setting urine composition, and this differentiation programme is how unspecialized metanephric mesenchyme progenitors become the polarized tubular epithelium that performs that job. Its outcome determines nephron number, and failure produces renal hypodysplasia and syndromic kidney malformations. Transcription factors define the sequence: OSR1 marks the early progenitor field, PAX2 and PAX8 drive the mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition, and LHX1 and GATA3 pattern the forming tubule and duct. Wnt signalling through beta-catenin, together with the cytokine LIF, provides inductive cues that trigger epithelialization, while the Hippo pathway effectors YAP1 and WWTR1 couple mechanical and polarity information to progenitor proliferation versus commitment. Surface markers such as CD24 and PROM1 label the resulting cells and their progenitors, linking this biology to nephron progenitor maintenance and regenerative repair.

T cell differentiation traces bone marrow-derived progenitors through the thymus, where double-negative stages assemble a T cell receptor, become double positive for CD4 and CD8, and are selected into naive single-positive CD4+ or CD8+ cells; peripheral antigen and cytokine cues then drive CD4+ cells into helper subsets. This programme supplies the adaptive immune repertoire, and its miswiring underlies immunodeficiency, allergy, autoimmunity and T cell leukaemia. Lineage identity is set by master transcription factors paired with cytokine-driven STAT signalling: TBX21 with STAT4 and IL12 receptor signalling for interferon gamma-producing Th1 cells, GATA3 with STAT6 downstream of IL4 for Th2 cells secreting IL4, IL5 and IL13, and IRF4, MAF, BATF and RUNX factors shaping other fates. Notch signalling through RBPJ and MAML coactivators drives early thymocyte commitment, while histone deacetylase complexes, NuRD, Polycomb rings and MLL/WDR5 methyltransferase modules lock these choices into chromatin.

Lymphocyte differentiation covers the routes by which uncommitted haematopoietic progenitors become T cells, B cells, innate lymphoid and NK cells, and then specialize further into helper, regulatory, cytotoxic and antibody-secreting subsets. It builds adaptive immunity, and its failure produces severe combined immunodeficiency, agammaglobulinaemia, autoimmunity or lymphoid leukaemia. Antigen receptor genes are assembled by RAG1/RAG2 with non-homologous end joining factors such as DCLRE1C, LIG4 and PRKDC, and the resulting receptors signal through LCK, ZAP70, ITK, SYK, BTK and CARD11 to set positive and negative selection thresholds, with AIRE and thymic proteasome subunits shaping self-tolerance. Notch ligands, Wnt and BMP cues from stroma, and cytokines acting through JAK-STAT specify lineage, while transcription factors including BCL11B, PAX5, FOXP3, TBX21, GATA3, RORC and PRDM1, together with chromatin remodelling complexes, lock in identity. Chemokine receptors then direct the mature cells to their niches.

Cells keep large parts of their genome off without changing its sequence, and epigenetic negative regulation of gene expression is that silencing programme: heritable, chromatin-based repression of specific loci. It defines which genes a differentiated cell may use, keeps imprinted alleles monoallelic, inactivates one X chromosome in females, silences transposons and retroviral elements in germ cells and early embryos, and holds developmental regulators in check until needed; its collapse drives derepression of repeats, loss of lineage identity and the promoter hypermethylation and Polycomb misregulation typical of cancer. Mechanistically it converges on histone-modifying and reader complexes — Polycomb PRC1 and PRC2 with EZH2, SUZ12, RNF2 and the chromobox proteins, H3K9 methyltransferases SETDB1 and SUV39H1 with HP1, histone deacetylases and sirtuins — together with DNA methylation by DNMT1, DNMT3A and UHRF1, piRNA-guided targeting, ATP-dependent nucleosome remodelling and anchoring of repressed chromatin at the nuclear lamina.

Formation of the limbic system produces the interconnected structures into which emotion, motivation, reward and the affective coloring of memory are built: the hippocampus and dentate gyrus, amygdala, hypothalamic nuclei and their cortical partners. Building them requires sequential neurogenesis, migration of newborn neurons along radial and tangential routes, and precise axon guidance. Reelin signaling through its receptors and the downstream adaptor DAB1, together with the CDK5 kinase and its neuronal activators and the LIS1/YWHAE motility machinery, positions neurons in their proper layers; WNT/beta-catenin activity with LEF1, hedgehog transduction through SMO and GLI3, and regional transcription factors such as EMX2, LHX5, PROX1, TBR1, DLX1/2 and NEUROD1 specify the fields and their neuron types. Semaphorins, plexins, neuropilins and EPHA5 wire the resulting circuits, while dopamine and serotonin receptors and GABAergic markers mark their mature signaling. Disruption underlies lissencephaly, hippocampal malformation, epilepsy, intellectual disability and autism-spectrum phenotypes.

Phosphate removal is the counterpart to kinase action, and this collection of dephosphorylation activities sets how long a phosphorylation signal lasts on proteins, lipids and small molecules. Serine/threonine phosphatase catalytic subunits and their regulatory partners (PP1, PP2A, calcineurin, PP5, PP6, the metal-dependent PPM family) reverse kinase marks on cytoskeletal, transcriptional and cell cycle substrates, while classical and receptor-type tyrosine phosphatases such as PTPN11, PTPN6, PTEN and CD45 tune growth factor and immune receptor signalling. Dual-specificity phosphatases inactivate MAP kinases, terminating ERK, JNK and p38 output. A large lipid phosphatase contingent — myotubularins, inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatases, synaptojanins, OCRL and phospholipid phosphate phosphatases — remodels phosphoinositides and sphingolipid phosphates to control membrane identity and trafficking. Loss of these activities underlies tumour suppression failure, Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy, myotubular myopathy, Lowe syndrome and Noonan syndrome, and unrestrained inflammatory signalling.

Growing axons are steered as much by repulsion as by attraction, and Sema3A is one of the classic repellents: growth cones that meet it collapse and turn away, which is how sensory and cortical projections are kept out of inappropriate territory and how peripheral nerve and dendrite patterning is set. Signal reception requires neuropilin-1 as the ligand-binding subunit together with a plexin-A family receptor, and the PAK-dependent arm of the response converts that binding into actin disassembly. Rac1 recruited to the receptor complex activates group I PAK kinases, which phosphorylate LIMK1; LIMK1 in turn phosphorylates cofilin, blocking its actin-severing and depolymerising activity and remodelling filaments in the collapsing growth cone. Src-family and Fes kinases and HSP90 chaperones support signal transmission. Loss of this route leaves axons insensitive to a major guidance cue and mistargeted.

Growth factor signals reach the nucleus through the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade, and this route is one of the most frequently corrupted in human cancer: activating mutations in KRAS, NRAS or HRAS occur in roughly a third of tumours, BRAF substitutions in many melanomas and thyroid cancers, and loss of the RAS GAP NF1 achieves the same end by removing a brake. Oncogenic MAPK signalling describes these lesions together with the machinery that normally restrains them – SPRED proteins, DUSP phosphatases that dephosphorylate ERK, and RKIP encoded by PEBP1 – plus scaffolds such as KSR1/2, SHOC2 and CNKSR that set the efficiency of RAF activation. Chromosomal rearrangements producing fusion partners like KIAA1549-BRAF or AGK-BRAF act by the same logic. Persistent ERK output drives proliferation and blocks apoptosis, partly by suppressing BIM, and defines the tumours treated with RAF and MEK inhibitors.

Glycoproteins leaving the Golgi carry branched N-linked sugars whose outer arms are built here, in the medial and trans compartments. This elaboration converts simple oligomannose structures into the hybrid and complex N-glycans that determine protein half-life, receptor clustering, cell adhesion and recognition by lectins of the immune system; loss of branching enzymes causes congenital glycosylation disorders, and altered branching is a hallmark of tumour cell surfaces. Alpha-mannosidase II enzymes trim mannose residues, after which GlcNAc transferases including MGAT2, MGAT4 family members and MGAT5 add antennae, MGAT3 adds a bisecting GlcNAc that blocks further branching, and FUT8 attaches core fucose. Beta-1,4-galactosyltransferases cap the branches, and sialyltransferases such as ST6GAL1 and ST3GAL4 terminate them with sialic acid, with sulfation and fucosylation generating further diversity. Glycoprotein hormone subunits are among the substrates matured this way.

Immunity must be damped as well as triggered, and this collection of brakes covers every process that stops, prevents or reduces immune activation. Without it, lymphocytes are not tolerised, inflammation does not resolve, and autoimmunity, chronic inflammatory disease or immunopathology follows; tumours and chronic infections exploit the same brakes to escape attack. Inhibitory surface receptors such as CTLA4, PDCD1 with its ligand CD274, LAG3, TIGIT, HAVCR2 and the leukocyte immunoglobulin-like and killer-cell receptor families raise the threshold for antigen receptor and Fc receptor signalling, acting through phosphatases including PTPN6, PTPN22 and INPP5D and kinases such as CSK. Intracellular restraint comes from ubiquitin editing by TNFAIP3 and ITCH, SOCS proteins limiting cytokine-driven STAT signalling, negative regulators of innate nucleic acid sensing, regulatory T cell programmes under FOXP3, suppressive cytokines including IL10 and TGFB, complement regulators such as CD55 and CD59, and a large set of microRNAs tuning inflammatory transcripts.

RUNX3 is a Runt-domain transcription factor that partners with CBFB to control cell fate decisions in the immune system and to restrain proliferation in epithelia. It drives CD8+ lineage commitment in thymocytes, shapes innate lymphoid and intestinal T cell programmes, and induces integrin genes such as ITGAL and ITGA4 that support leukocyte adhesion; loss of RUNX3, frequently through promoter hypermethylation, is associated with gastric, colorectal, oesophageal and breast cancers. Its growth-suppressive output runs largely through TGF-beta signalling, where cooperation with SMAD3 and SMAD4 enforces cell cycle arrest via CDKN1A, and through antagonism of proliferative programmes: RUNX3 opposes NOTCH target activation with RBPJ and MAML co-activators, blocks TEAD:YAP1/WWTR1 promoter binding, and intersects with WNT-driven TCF/LEF and MYC transcription. Acetyltransferases and HDAC4 tune its activity, while ubiquitin ligases including SMURF1 and SMURF2 and the proteasome set its abundance.

Host defence against microbes and damaged self must be switched on quickly and amplified, and this collection covers the positive regulators that raise the magnitude, speed and duration of a defence response. It underlies innate immune activation in macrophages, dendritic cells, neutrophils and lymphocytes, and its dysregulation produces autoinflammatory fever syndromes, septic shock and chronic inflammatory disease, while its loss leaves hosts vulnerable to infection. Pattern recognition by Toll-like receptors, cytosolic nucleic acid sensors such as cGAS-STING and RIG-I/MAVS, and NOD- and NLR-family proteins feeds through adaptors MYD88, TICAM1 and the IRAK-TRAF6 axis into NF-kB, MAPK and interferon regulatory factor transcription, yielding interferons, IL-1 family cytokines, TNF and chemokines. Inflammasome components including NLRP3, PYCARD and caspase-1 drive gasdermin-dependent pyroptotic release, and ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases, kinases and microRNAs tune signal output.

Calcium spikes must be terminated as reliably as they are initiated, and this pathway covers the braking mechanisms that damp calcium-mediated signalling once a cell has responded. It sets the duration and amplitude of calcium transients in excitable and immune cells, and its loss leaves signals that run too long, driving pathological hypertrophy, arrhythmia and overactive lymphocyte responses. Several routes converge on the same aim: plasma membrane calcium pumps and sodium-calcium exchange remove cytosolic calcium, an inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatase degrades the messenger that opens the inositol trisphosphate receptor, and Homer and calcineurin-inhibitory proteins such as RCAN1 restrain downstream calcium-dependent transcription. Calsarcin family myozenins act at the sarcomeric Z-disc to hold calcineurin away from its targets in muscle, while CD22 and adaptor proteins dampen calcium flux after antigen receptor engagement in B and T cells.

Cells that have sustained irreparable DNA damage, sustained ER stress, or the loss of survival signals commit suicide through the mitochondrial arm of apoptosis, and this collection of activators is what pushes that decision past the point of no return. Positive regulation of intrinsic apoptotic signaling matters for tumour suppression, developmental sculpting of tissues, and the cytotoxic action of chemotherapy; when it is blunted, damaged cells persist and transform. The core effectors are BH3-only proteins such as BID, BAD, BCL2L11, PMAIP1 and BBC3 that neutralise anti-apoptotic guardians including MCL1, together with the pore-forming BAX and BOK that permeabilise the outer mitochondrial membrane and release cytochrome c. Upstream, TP53 and its cofactors transcriptionally induce several of these effectors, while stress sensors such as DDIT3 link unfolded protein responses to the same mitochondrial endpoint, and microRNAs tune the balance by repressing survival factors.

Ubiquitin ligases must be switched on and off at the right moment, and this control of ubiquitin protein ligase activity is what makes ubiquitin-dependent degradation a timing device rather than a constant drain on the proteome. The genes here point squarely at the anaphase-promoting complex, whose activity dictates when a cell leaves mitosis and whether it can re-enter S phase. Activating subunits CDC20 and FZR1 confer substrate specificity, while the pseudosubstrate inhibitor FBXO5 and the spindle checkpoint proteins MAD2L1 and MAD2L2 restrain the ligase until chromosomes are correctly attached; UBE2C and UBE2S are the cognate E2 enzymes that build and extend the ubiquitin chains. USP44 opposes ubiquitination to stabilise the checkpoint, and CDKN2A links the same circuitry to tumour suppression. Loss of this restraint produces premature sister chromatid separation, aneuploidy and genomic instability.

Sensory perception is the conversion of external physical and chemical stimuli into neural signals, and this collection spans the four modalities for which the molecular steps are best defined: vision, olfaction, taste and hearing. Photoreception depends on opsins coupled through transducin to cGMP phosphodiesterase and cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels, supported by retinoid supply and recycling enzymes such as RPE65, LRAT and the retinol dehydrogenases. Odorants act on the large odorant receptor repertoire signalling via adenylate cyclase 3 and CNGA2, while sweet, umami and bitter tastants act on TAS1R and TAS2R receptors feeding into PLCB2 and TRPM5. Mechanotransduction in hair cells uses tip-link cadherins, TMC channels, unconventional myosins and stereociliary actin regulators. Failure of these components produces retinal dystrophies, anosmia, taste loss and inherited deafness.

Tight junctions seal the space between neighbouring epithelial and endothelial cells, and the interactions described here are the ones that build the sealing strands and anchor the polarity machinery to them. Without them an epithelium cannot hold a solute gradient across itself: leaky junctions underlie renal magnesium wasting, deafness, skin barrier failure and breakdown of the blood-brain barrier. The strands themselves are polymers of claudins, a large family whose members differ in whether they occlude the paracellular route or form selective pores for ions, so the mix expressed by a tissue sets its permeability. Junctional adhesion molecule A contributes adhesion, while PAR-3, PAR-6 isoforms with atypical PKC iota and the CRB3-PALS1-PATJ module are recruited to the apical junction, where they specify the apical membrane domain, maintain the boundary separating it from the basolateral surface, and feed into control of proliferation and morphogenesis.

Innate immune cells detect microbial products and host-derived danger signals and convert that detection into inflammation, and this Toll-like receptor and inflammatory signalling programme is the sensing apparatus that does it. Surface and endosomal receptors for bacterial lipopeptides, lipopolysaccharide, flagellin and nucleic acids (TLR1, TLR2, TLR4, TLR5, TLR6, TLR7, TLR8) act with the LPS co-receptor MD-2 and signal through MyD88 and IRAK-family adaptors toward NF-κB-driven cytokine production; IRAK3 restrains this output to limit tissue damage and endotoxin tolerance. Alongside them sit the effector receptors of myeloid cells: complement and formyl-peptide receptors and the chemokine receptor CXCR2 that guide neutrophil recruitment, Fc gamma receptors and the DAP12 adaptor TYROBP for phagocytosis, inhibitory LILR and Siglec receptors that damp activation, plus leukotriene synthesis and the NADPH oxidase subunit NCF4. The composition reflects granulocyte and monocyte biology, host defence against infection, and the sterile inflammation underlying sepsis and autoimmunity.

Glia outnumber neurons in much of the nervous system, and gliogenesis is the programme by which neural progenitors are diverted away from neuronal fate to produce astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells and microglia, then driven to maturity. Its output supplies myelin, potassium and glutamate buffering, blood-brain barrier support and immune surveillance; its failure or misregulation underlies leukodystrophies, dysmyelinating neuropathies, impaired remyelination and glioma. Lineage identity is set by transcription factors including OLIG1/OLIG2, SOX9, SOX10, NKX2-2, NFIA/NFIB and MYRF, with Notch effectors HES1/HES5 and polycomb components EZH2 and SUZ12 timing the switch from neurogenesis. Extrinsic cues run through Sonic hedgehog, BMP, neuregulin-ERBB2/ERBB3, PDGF-responsive OPC markers such as CSPG4 and PTPRZ1, and cytokine-STAT3 signalling via CNTF, LIF and IL6ST. Microglial specification and maintenance depend on CSF1R, IL34, TREM2 and fractalkine signalling.

Cells that lose contact with their extracellular matrix normally die by anoikis, a detachment-triggered form of apoptosis that keeps epithelia anchored and prevents survival of displaced cells. The processes collected here suppress that death, and their inappropriate activation is a step toward metastasis, allowing tumour cells to survive in circulation and seed distant sites. Suppression works on several fronts: integrin engagement through ITGA5 and ITGB1 with focal adhesion kinase and SRC sustains adhesion-dependent survival signalling; PI3K subunits relay it to downstream kinases; and the anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members BCL2, BCL2L1 and MCL1 hold the mitochondrial permeabilisation step in check. Transcriptional regulators such as SNAI2 and TLE1, together with NOTCH1 signalling and caveolin-1 at membrane microdomains, raise the threshold further, linking anoikis resistance to epithelial-mesenchymal transition and anchorage-independent growth.

The transcription factor RUNX3 acts as a brake on NOTCH signalling, and losing that restraint is one route by which liver cells become tumorigenic. RUNX3 works at two points. It occupies the promoter of JAG1 and represses transcription of this NOTCH ligand, lowering the signal available to neighbouring cells. It also joins the coactivator complex assembled on cleaved NOTCH1 intracellular domain with RBPJ, Mastermind-like proteins and the acetyltransferases CREBBP/EP300 and KAT2A/KAT2B, and blocks activation of the target gene HES1. Because HES1 is a repressor that sustains progenitor states and blocks differentiation, this interference pushes cells toward differentiation and away from proliferation. RUNX3 silencing, common in hepatocellular carcinoma and gastric cancer, releases NOTCH output and links its tumour suppressor function directly to developmental cell-fate signalling.

Integrin signalling couples cells to the extracellular matrix and turns that physical attachment into decisions about adhesion, migration, survival and proliferation, with the platelet receptor alphaIIb-beta3 serving as the best-worked example. Its function is bidirectional: agonists at a site of vascular injury act through Rap1 GTPases and their exchange factors, together with the adaptor RIAM, to recruit talin to the beta3 tail, which breaks the interaction holding the receptor bent and low-affinity. The primed receptor binds fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor, cross-linking platelets into an aggregate; ligand engagement then signals back inward through Src, Syk, FAK and the Cas-Crk module, plus PI3K-dependent AKT activation, driving cytoskeletal contraction and clot retraction. Loss of the receptor or of talin-mediated activation causes bleeding disorders such as Glanzmann thrombasthenia, while the same machinery on adherent cells underlies matrix-dependent anchorage and survival.

Progression through mitosis requires the anaphase-promoting complex to be switched on at the right moment, and that switch is thrown by destroying its inhibitor. Emi1 (FBXO5) binds and restrains APC/C with its activators Cdc20 and Cdh1 (FZR1) through interphase, keeping cyclins and securin stable so that DNA replication is licensed only once; in early mitosis it must be removed. Cdk-mediated phosphorylation of a DSGxxS motif creates a phosphodegron recognised by beta-TrCP (BTRC), the substrate receptor of an SCF ubiquitin ligase built on Cul1 and Skp1. Polyubiquitin chains assembled from ubiquitin precursors then target Emi1 to the 26S proteasome, whose core and regulatory particle subunits make up most of this route. Loss of timely Emi1 destruction leaves APC/C inhibited, blocking mitotic exit, while its stabilisation elsewhere promotes re-replication and genomic instability.

Growth factor signalling through ERBB2 must be switched off as well as on, and downregulation of ERBB2 signaling is the set of brakes that limits how long the receptor and its heterodimers can drive RAS and PI3K-AKT output. Loss of these brakes contributes to breast and gastric cancers in which ERBB2 is amplified or abnormally stabilised. Two mechanisms dominate. Ubiquitin ligases mark the receptor for proteasomal destruction: STUB1 and CUL5 act on non-activated ERBB2, often in concert with the HSP90-CDC37 chaperone system on which the receptor depends, while RNF41 ubiquitinates ERBB3 and thereby clears activated ERBB2-ERBB3 dimers, a step opposed by the deubiquitinase USP8. Separately, the PEST-family phosphatases PTPN12 and PTPN18 strip phosphotyrosines from the ERBB2 tail so adaptors cannot dock. Ligands such as EGF and the neuregulins, and the ERBIN scaffold, set the context in which this attenuation operates.

Long-term potentiation is the lasting strengthening of synapses that underlies learning and memory formation, and this pathway covers the molecules that set how readily it is induced and how long it endures. Tuning matters: too little potentiation impairs hippocampal memory, while unchecked strengthening destabilises circuits, and several members here link the process to Alzheimer disease and intellectual disability. Calcium-stimulated adenylyl cyclases and anchored PKA subunits couple synaptic activity to cAMP signalling and CREB-dependent transcription, while ARC and other activity-induced products remodel receptor content at the postsynaptic density, where scaffolds such as SHANK3 and auxiliary AMPA receptor subunits including SHISA7 organise glutamate receptors. Adenosine and dopamine receptors, reelin, ephrin receptors, APP and prion protein provide extracellular and neuromodulatory constraints, and translational regulators acting locally in dendrites gate the protein synthesis that makes potentiation persistent.

Cells cannot make all the amino acids they need, so carriers must move L-amino acids across the plasma membrane and across organellar membranes, and this transport activity sets the supply for protein synthesis, neurotransmission, nitrogen disposal and nutrient signalling. Distinct families do distinct jobs: excitatory amino acid carriers such as SLC1A2 and SLC1A3 clear glutamate from synapses, vesicular glutamate transporters load it for release, heterodimers built on the SLC3A2 heavy chain with SLC7A5, SLC7A11 or SLC7A8 exchange large neutral or cystine/glutamate pairs, SLC38 members drive sodium-coupled glutamine flux, proton-coupled SLC36 transporters recover amino acids from lysosomes, and mitochondrial SLC25 carriers run the aspartate-glutamate shuttle and ornithine entry into the urea cycle. Loss of individual carriers causes cystinuria, lysinuric protein intolerance, cystinosis, urea cycle failure and excitotoxic injury, and lysosomal arginine sensing by SLC38A9 links amino acid availability to mTORC1-dependent growth control.

Duplication of the genome in S phase is what this pathway accomplishes: origins licensed in late mitosis and G1 are fired once, and once only, to copy every chromosome before division. Origin recognition complex proteins load CDC6 and CDT1, which deposit the MCM2-7 helicase; CDK2 paired with cyclin E and then cyclin A, together with CDC45 and the GINS tetramer, converts these into active replisomes. Primase and DNA polymerase alpha lay down primers, RFC loads the PCNA clamp for processive synthesis by polymerases delta and epsilon, and FEN1 with LIG1 matures Okazaki fragments while RPA coats exposed single strands. Re-replication is prevented by geminin and by ubiquitin-proteasome destruction of licensing factors through SCF-SKP2 and the anaphase-promoting complex. Loss of this control produces endoreduplication, replication stress and the genome instability that underlies tumour development.

Phosphoinositide metabolism converts a minor membrane lipid, phosphatidylinositol, into seven interconvertible phosphorylated species that act as address labels on organelle membranes and as second messengers. Because each compartment carries its own signature lipid, this chemistry tells vesicles, sorting machinery and cytosolic effectors where they are: PI4P marks the Golgi and supports secretory vesicle budding, PI(4,5)P2 dominates the plasma membrane where it organises actin, endocytosis and exocytosis, and PI3P defines early endosomes. Opposing kinases and phosphatases set these levels locally — class I, II and III PI3Ks with their regulatory subunits, PI4 kinases, PIP5 and PIP4 kinases, PIKFYVE with VAC14 and FIG4, against PTEN, the myotubularins, SAC1, OCRL, synaptojanins and INPP4/INPP5 enzymes. Pleckstrin-homology and FYVE-domain proteins read the output. Loss of this control underlies PTEN- and PI3K-driven cancers, myotubular and Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathies, Lowe syndrome and ciliopathies.

Membrane trafficking is the set of routes by which a cell moves proteins, lipids and sugars between its organelles and the cell surface, and it underlies secretion, nutrient uptake, receptor signalling and the maintenance of organelle identity. Newly made cargo leaves the endoplasmic reticulum in COPII-coated carriers, is processed and glycosylated in the Golgi, and is sorted at the trans-Golgi network into carriers that fuse with the plasma membrane; retrieval by COPI and retrograde carriers balances this outward flow. Clathrin and adaptor complexes with dynamin drive endocytosis, Rab GTPases with their activating and inactivating regulators specify compartments, SNAREs and NSF execute fusion, ESCRT components sort ubiquitinated receptors into multivesicular bodies, and kinesin, dynein and myosin motors carry vesicles along cytoskeletal tracks. Defects cause lysosomal and pigmentation disorders, hypercholesterolaemia, bleeding diatheses and neurodegeneration, and impair regulated events such as insulin-stimulated glucose transporter delivery.

Rather than build every nucleotide from scratch, cells recover the bases and nucleosides released by RNA and DNA turnover and phosphorylate them back into monophosphates that re-enter the nucleotide pools. This salvage route is far cheaper in energy than de novo synthesis and is the main supply for cells with limited biosynthetic capacity, such as neurons and lymphocytes, and for mitochondria, which must maintain their own deoxyribonucleotide pools. Phosphoribosyltransferases reattach purine bases to ribose phosphate, while kinases such as thymidine kinase, deoxycytidine kinase and deoxyguanosine kinase act on nucleosides; phosphorylases and deaminases run the catabolic side, degrading or interconverting bases. Loss of HPRT1 causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, adenosine deaminase deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency, and mutations in the mitochondrial kinases produce mtDNA depletion syndromes. The same enzymes activate nucleoside analogue drugs.

These genes mark the differentiated intestinal and colonic epithelium, the absorptive barrier that takes up nutrients, excludes luminal bacteria and renews itself continuously from crypt stem cells. The master transcription factors CDX1 and CDX2, with FOXA3, impose hindgut identity, while EPCAM, CDH17 and the claudins CLDN3, CLDN4 and CLDN7 build adherens and tight junctions that seal the paracellular space. Brush border and apical organisation depend on villin, myosins MYO1A and MYO7B, PLS1 and POF1B; mucins MUC13 and MUC3B, galectin-4 and fucosyltransferases glycosylate the surface; FABP1 and ACSL5 handle absorbed lipid, and GUCY2C transduces guanylin signals controlling fluid secretion. RNF43 restrains Wnt activity in the crypt. Loss of this programme underlies barrier failure in inflammatory bowel disease, congenital diarrhoeas, and the aberrant expression of CEACAM5 and KRT20 seen in colorectal cancer and gastric intestinal metaplasia.

Tissue injury triggers an inflammatory reaction that must be strong enough to clear debris and microbes yet contained enough to allow repair, and this pathway sets that balance by tuning the intensity and duration of the inflammatory response to wounding. Its failure shows up as chronic non-healing wounds, fibrosis, or excessive scarring, and in the gut and skin as persistent barrier inflammation. Alarmins and cytokines released from damaged epithelium, including IL33 and IL17A, recruit and activate leukocytes, while ALOX5 initiates leukotriene synthesis from arachidonate to amplify chemotaxis. Restraint comes from the phosphatase PTPN6, which dampens immunoreceptor signalling, from SIGLEC10 engagement of damage-associated ligands, and from progranulin, whose loss unleashes neuroinflammation. STAT3 couples these cytokine inputs to epithelial survival and proliferation, linking inflammatory control directly to wound closure and regeneration.

The anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome is the ubiquitin ligase that times mitotic exit, and its substrate choice depends entirely on which activator is bound; regulation of APC/C activators between G1/S and early anaphase is how a cell keeps that switch aligned with the cell cycle. Cdc20 accumulates as cells enter mitosis and engages the core complex only in M phase, where it is restrained by the spindle checkpoint proteins Mad2 and BubR1 until chromosomes are correctly attached; Cdh1 (FZR1) takes over in G1 and is excluded at other times by Cdk1- and Cdk2-dependent phosphorylation and by the inhibitor Emi1 (FBXO5), itself destroyed through SCF/beta-TrCP. Plk1 and the cyclins feed into this timing, and the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S build the chains that route substrates to the proteasome. Loss of control produces premature sister chromatid separation and aneuploidy.

Tail-anchored proteins carry their single transmembrane segment so close to the C-terminus that it only emerges from the ribosome after translation ends, so they cannot use the standard cotranslational route and need dedicated post-translational delivery to the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. This insertion pathway builds much of the machinery of vesicle traffic and membrane biology, including SNAREs such as VAMP2, STX1A and STX5, cytochrome b5, emerin and subunits of the translocon itself. A cytosolic chaperone, SGTA, captures the hydrophobic tail on release and passes it via the BAG6-UBL4A-GET4 complex to the ATPase GET3 (ASNA1), which docks at the GET1(WRB)-CAMLG receptor in the ER membrane for ATP-dependent insertion. The same handover is a quality-control decision point: substrates that fail to transfer are held by BAG6 and ubiquitinated for proteasomal destruction, preventing aggregation-prone membrane proteins from accumulating in the cytosol.

Naive CD4 T cells acquire distinct helper identities only when instructive signals push them in one direction, and this pathway collects the events that promote that commitment. It underlies protective immunity to intracellular bacteria and fungi, shapes vaccine responses, and when overactive drives autoimmune and inflammatory disease; the same steps are targets for therapies that block helper subset skewing. Antigen-presenting cells supply the costimulation that licenses differentiation through CD80, CD86 and OX40 ligand, while cytokines of the IL-12 family and their receptors, IL-18 and IL-23 with IL23R, bias the outcome toward Th1 or Th17 programmes. Inflammasome and NF-kB-linked components including NLRP3, RIPK2, MALT1 and the atypical inhibitors NFKBID and NFKBIZ amplify these inputs, transcriptional regulators such as HLX, RARA and the bromodomain proteins BRD2 and BRD4 with EP300 enforce lineage gene expression, and SOCS5 tunes the cytokine response.

Cells that are damaged beyond repair, deprived of growth factors, or stressed in the endoplasmic reticulum kill themselves through the intrinsic, mitochondrial route to apoptosis, the arm of programmed cell death that shapes tissues during development and removes cells with broken genomes. Its failure permits survival of cells that should die and underlies tumour formation and resistance to chemotherapy, while excess activity drives degenerative loss of neurons and other long-lived cells. BH3-only sensors such as BID, BAD, BIM, NOXA and PUMA relay stress signals and neutralise the guardians BCL2 and BCL2L1, allowing BAX and BAK to permeabilise the outer mitochondrial membrane; released cytochrome c nucleates an APAF1 apoptosome that activates caspase-9 and then the executioner caspases 3 and 7, with DIABLO relieving XIAP inhibition. Transcriptional control by p53 and its relatives, and survival input from AKT and 14-3-3 proteins, set the threshold.

Rather than bulk self-digestion, cells can pick out a single damaged organelle or protein aggregate and deliver only that to the lysosome. This targeted quality control keeps mitochondria, peroxisomes, lipid droplets and misfolded protein deposits from accumulating, and its failure is tied to Parkinson's disease and other neurodegeneration. Cargo is first marked: PINK1 accumulates on depolarised mitochondria and activates the ubiquitin ligase PRKN, which decorates outer-membrane proteins such as TOMM20, MFN1/2 and the VDAC channels with ubiquitin, opposed by the deubiquitinase USP30. Receptors including SQSTM1, OPTN, NBR1, FUNDC1 and peroxisomal PEX5 bridge the tagged cargo to LC3 on the forming phagophore, while ATG5-ATG12, ULK1 and AMPK subunits drive autophagosome assembly. Dynein motors and microtubules, with HDAC6 and VCP, concentrate aggregates for aggrephagy and move vesicles toward lysosomal fusion.

Cells and tissues restrain how much fat they esterify into storage triglyceride, and this braking arm of lipid metabolism keeps hepatocytes and adipocytes from accumulating neutral lipid when substrate is plentiful. Loss of such restraint underlies hepatic steatosis, hypertriglyceridaemia and the lipid abnormalities that accompany insulin resistance. The regulators act at several levels: a ubiquitin ligase substrate-recognition subunit targets lipogenic transcription factors and other short-lived proteins for proteasomal degradation, an NAD-dependent deacetylase couples nutrient scarcity to reduced lipogenic gene expression, and a salt-inducible kinase transmits fasting and hormonal cues that suppress transcriptional coactivation of lipid synthesis. Small RNAs contribute post-transcriptional damping of enzymes in the glycerolipid route, while an endoplasmic reticulum thioredoxin-family protein links redox and secretory conditions to lipoprotein and triglyceride handling. Together these constitute negative control over triglyceride biosynthesis rather than the synthetic steps themselves.

Prometaphase is the window of mitosis in which the nuclear envelope breaks down, kinetochores mature on centromeres, and spindle microtubules capture chromosomes and pull them toward the metaphase plate. Getting this right determines whether daughter cells inherit an accurate chromosome complement; errors here produce aneuploidy and chromosomal instability of the kind seen in tumours and in developmental disorders. The machinery assembles in layers: CENP proteins build the inner kinetochore on CENP-A chromatin, the MIS12 and NDC80 complexes form the outer plate that grips dynamic microtubule ends, and tubulin, gamma-tubulin ring components and augmin nucleate and organise the spindle from centrosomes. Aurora B with INCENP and survivin corrects mis-attachments, while MAD1, MAD2, BUB1 and BUBR1 hold the spindle assembly checkpoint to restrain CDC20 until every chromosome is bioriented. Cohesin, condensin and dynein-dynactin contribute chromosome cohesion, compaction and poleward transport.

Ubiquitin marks are reversible, and deubiquitination is the erasing step that decides whether a tagged protein is destroyed, relocated, or simply switched off. It recycles ubiquitin and keeps the pool long-lived, trims inappropriate degradation tags as a quality-control check, processes ubiquitin precursors encoded as fusions and polyproteins, and clears unanchored chains from the proteasome. Cysteine-protease families — USP, UCH, OTU, JOSD and Josephin enzymes — together with JAMM/MPN metalloproteases such as the proteasome subunit PSMD14 and the BRCC36 complex, cleave isopeptide bonds and are themselves tuned by oxidation of the catalytic cysteine and by cofactors like WDR48. The targets define the consequences: chromatin ubiquitylation on histone H2A/H2B, NF-kB and RIG-I-like antiviral signalling, TGF-beta/SMAD output, p53-MDM2, DNA repair, receptor sorting on endosomes and damaged-mitochondrion clearance.

L-serine sits at a junction between glycolysis, one-carbon metabolism and lipid synthesis, and the reactions that make and consume it keep cells supplied with glycine, folate-borne methyl groups, cysteine and the serine headgroups of sphingolipids and phosphatidylserine. The de novo route diverts 3-phosphoglycerate through PHGDH, PSAT1 and PSPH, and proliferating and neural cells depend on it heavily; loss of these three enzymes causes serine deficiency syndromes with microcephaly, seizures and hypomyelination, while their amplification supports tumour growth. Cytosolic and mitochondrial serine hydroxymethyltransferases interconvert serine and glycine while loading tetrahydrofolate for nucleotide synthesis, CBS commits serine to transsulfuration with homocysteine, and serine racemase generates D-serine, the co-agonist at NMDA receptors. Catabolic serine dehydratase and the glyoxylate-handling aminotransferase AGXT link the amino acid to gluconeogenic and hepatic disposal routes.

Glia outnumber neurons in much of the nervous system, and this pathway covers the signals and transcriptional programmes that push progenitors toward glial fates rather than neuronal ones, and that drive immature glia to mature. Its output is the astrocytes that buffer ions and support synapses, the oligodendrocytes that myelinate central axons, and microglia whose survival depends on IL34 signalling. Patterning cues such as SHH act through OLIG2, NKX2-2 and NKX6-2 to specify oligodendrocyte precursors, while MYRF and ZNF488 drive the myelination programme and QKI controls the RNA stability that myelin gene expression requires. Cytokine signalling through LIF, CLCF1 and the shared IL6ST receptor subunit promotes astrocytic differentiation, and Notch, HES1, ID2 and the HDAC1/HDAC2 deacetylases set the timing at which progenitors leave the cycle. Failures impair myelination and repair after demyelinating injury.

Estrogens coordinate development, reproduction, bone and lipid metabolism, and vascular and neuronal function, and estrogen receptor-mediated signaling is how their message is read inside target cells. Ligand-bound ESR1 and ESR2, released from HSP90-based chaperone complexes, act as nuclear receptors that recruit coactivators such as NCOA1-3, p300/CBP and the mediator subunit MED1, along with chromatin-modifying enzymes and cohesin, to assemble RNA polymerase II on target promoters and enhancers; lineage factors FOXA1 and GATA3 direct where the receptor binds, and outputs include CCND1, MYC, PGR, GREB1 and TFF1, driving proliferation and differentiation. A separate membrane-proximal arm, involving palmitoylation, caveolins, SRC, G protein subunits and PI3K-AKT and MAPK cascades, produces rapid responses such as eNOS activation. This circuitry underlies hormone-dependent breast cancer growth and is the target of antiestrogen therapy, while microRNA-loaded argonaute complexes add post-transcriptional control.

Proteins only work where they are put, and this collection covers the many ways cells actively increase the delivery or retention of a protein at a particular site: insertion of transporters and channels into the plasma membrane, recruitment of signalling molecules to receptors and the cytoskeleton, nuclear import and export, and secretory traffic. Such positive regulation of protein localization underlies insulin granule exocytosis, glucose transporter and calcium channel surface delivery, synaptic vesicle release, and receptor turnover; when it fails, hormones are not secreted and aggregation-prone proteins such as tau, alpha-synuclein and amyloid precursor protein are mishandled. Mechanistically the genes span COPII coat components and cargo receptors, importins and exportins, Rab and Arf GTPases with their regulators, chaperonin and HSP90 folding machinery, palmitoyl transferases and thioesterases that switch membrane anchoring, and kinases including PKA, PKC and AKT that trigger translocation downstream of extracellular cues.

The nephron is the filtering unit of the kidney, and its epithelium arises during development when metanephric mesenchyme is induced to convert into polarized tubules and glomerular cells. This programme sets the final nephron number a person is born with, and its disruption underlies congenital kidney and urinary tract malformations, renal hypoplasia, cystic disease and inherited nephrotic syndrome. Nephron progenitors are maintained by SIX2, WT1, EYA1 and SALL1 and are induced by ureteric bud signals, with WNT9B and WNT4 driving mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition and NOTCH and BMP inputs patterning the resulting vesicle into proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule and podocytes. Segment identity is fixed by transcription factors such as HNF1B, PAX2, POU3F3 and LHX1, while podocyte differentiation yields the slit diaphragm proteins nephrin, podocin and CD2AP. Branching morphogenesis, stromal signalling and vascular ingrowth are coordinated with these steps.

Post-embryonic development covers everything that happens between the end of embryogenesis and the mature organism: postnatal growth, organ maturation, tissue remodelling and the acquisition of adult physiology. Failure at this stage shows up as growth retardation, skeletal and craniofacial defects, neurodevelopmental disorders and postnatal lethality rather than as early patterning errors. The genes involved span the machinery that sustains and directs late development: morphogen signalling through bone morphogenetic protein, transforming growth factor beta and fibroblast growth factor receptors; transcription factors such as GATA3, KLF4, FOXP2 and BCL11B that specify or maintain differentiated cell identities; chromatin regulators including MECP2, DNMT3A, ATRX and mixed-lineage leukaemia methyltransferases that keep expression programmes stable; and apoptotic and growth-control components — BAX, BAK1, BCL2 and mTOR signalling — that balance cell survival against tissue expansion, together with metabolic and DNA-repair functions needed for continued growth.

Glial cell differentiation is the route by which neural progenitors and Schwann cell precursors become astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia-supporting partners and peripheral myelinating glia, the cells that insulate axons, buffer extracellular potassium and glutamate, and sustain neuronal metabolism. Its failure or misdirection underlies dysmyelinating leukodystrophies, impaired nerve regeneration, and the reactive gliosis and glioma phenotypes seen in injured or transformed brain. Lineage choice is set by transcription factors including OLIG1/2, SOX10, SOX9, NKX2-2, NFIA and MYRF, acting against the Notch effectors HES1 and HES5 and the inhibitory ID proteins, and instructed by Sonic hedgehog, BMP, FGF and gp130 cytokines such as CNTF, LIF and IL6. Axon-derived neuregulin acting through ERBB2/ERBB3 drives Schwann cell myelination, while downstream PI3K-AKT-mTOR and MAPK cascades, chromatin regulators and RNA-binding factors such as QKI convert these cues into expression of myelin proteins like PLP1, MAG and CNP.

NFE2L2 (NRF2) is the master transcription factor for antioxidant and detoxification genes, and how much of it a cell makes sets the ceiling on its stress defences; tumours that raise it gain resistance to oxidants and chemotherapy, while too little leaves tissues vulnerable to oxidative and electrophilic injury. Beyond the familiar control of NRF2 protein stability, transcription of the gene itself is regulated, and this is where antioxidant capacity is wired into other signalling routes. MYC, the NF- innerB subunit p65 with p50, and the NOTCH1 intracellular domain act at its promoter, and NRF2 with its small MAF partner feeds back on its own gene, while CREBBP and EP300 supply histone acetyltransferase and coactivator function. The result couples proliferative, inflammatory and developmental signals to the size of the cellular antioxidant response.

Amino acids cannot cross lipid bilayers unaided, so cells rely on a large family of carriers to move them into the cytoplasm, across epithelia, and in and out of mitochondria. This transmembrane transport of L-alpha-amino acids supplies substrates for protein synthesis and nitrogen metabolism, loads neurotransmitter pools, and feeds the nutrient sensing that governs growth. Members include the sodium-dependent glutamate and neutral amino acid carriers of the SLC1 family, the SLC38 system A and N transporters, heteromeric exchangers in which SLC3A2 or SLC3A1 chaperones an SLC7 light chain, vesicular glutamate transporters, and mitochondrial carriers for glutamate, aspartate and ornithine. The output is concrete: glutamate clearance at synapses, cystine import for glutathione, urea-cycle flux, renal and intestinal reabsorption. Loss of individual carriers causes cystinuria, lysinuric protein intolerance, hyperornithinaemia and epileptic encephalopathy, and SLC38A9 links lysosomal arginine to mTORC1 activation.

Duplicating the genome once, and only once, per cell cycle is the task of DNA replication, and the fidelity of this process determines whether daughter cells inherit an intact genome or accumulate the mutations and rearrangements that drive cancer. Origin recognition complex subunits mark start sites, CDC6 and CDT1 load the MCM2-7 helicase, and CDC7-DBF4 together with CDK2-cyclin E/A activate it; GINS and CDC45 convert it into the active replisome. Priming by DNA polymerase alpha-primase gives way to processive synthesis by polymerases delta and epsilon on RPA-coated template, with PCNA and the clamp loader RFC coordinating elongation and FEN1, DNA2 and LIG1 finishing lagging-strand joins. Licensing is restricted to one round by geminin inhibition of CDT1 and by ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis through SCF and anaphase-promoting complex activity, while histones supply chromatin for the new strands. Mitochondrial polymerase gamma and TWNK extend the same logic to mitochondrial DNA.

Semaphorins are secreted and membrane-bound guidance cues that tell migrating cells and growing axons where not to go, and their interactions with plexin and neuropilin receptor complexes shape axon pathfinding, cortical wiring, vascular patterning, bone remodelling and immune cell contacts. Binding typically collapses the growth cone: plexins act on small GTPases of the Rho and Ras families, with RhoA-ROCK, Rac1-PAK and LIM kinase feeding onto cofilin and non-muscle myosin II to disassemble actin and retract protrusions, while CDK5 and GSK3B phosphorylate collapsin response mediator proteins to destabilise microtubules and integrin-talin adhesions are weakened. Neuropilin-1 serves as a ligand-binding co-receptor for class 3 semaphorins, and receptor tyrosine kinases such as MET and ERBB2 can be recruited to switch responses toward attraction or invasion. Immune-restricted members signal through CD72 and TREM2-TYROBP, linking this guidance chemistry to myeloid and lymphocyte regulation.

Vitamin A cannot be synthesised by animals, so it must be absorbed from diet as carotenoids or retinyl esters and delivered to tissues that need it for vision, epithelial differentiation and transcriptional control through retinoic acid receptors. This pathway covers that uptake, esterification and distribution. Pancreatic lipase and colipase release retinyl esters from dietary fat, carotenoid cleavage enzymes such as BCO1 and BCO2 generate retinal, and reductases including RDH11 and aldo-keto reductases interconvert retinal and retinol; LRAT re-esterifies retinol for storage. Intracellular and plasma binding proteins RBP1, RBP2 and RBP4, the latter circulating with transthyretin, keep these hydrophobic molecules soluble. Delivery rides on the chylomicron and lipoprotein system, with apolipoproteins, lipoprotein lipase anchored by GPIHBP1 and heparan sulfate proteoglycans, and clearance through LDL receptor family members. Deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia; excess retinoid is teratogenic.

Before a NOTCH receptor can respond to a ligand on a neighbouring cell, it must be transcribed, translated, glycosylated and cleaved into a functional heterodimer, and this maturation route covers all four human receptors. Because NOTCH signalling governs binary cell-fate decisions in development, stem cell maintenance, T cell specification and vascular patterning, the quality of receptor synthesis sets the gain of every downstream decision. Transcription of the NOTCH genes is controlled by factors including RBPJ-associated complexes, RUNX1, E2F/TFDP and p53, with the acetyltransferases EP300, CREBBP and KAT2A/KAT2B acting on chromatin, while a large set of microRNAs loaded into Argonaute-containing silencing complexes damps translation of NOTCH messages. In the endoplasmic reticulum POFUT1 adds O-fucose and POGLUT1 adds O-glucose to EGF repeats; Golgi fringe enzymes elongate the fucose to tune ligand preference, and FURIN cleavage yields the cell-surface heterodimer.

The E2F transcription factor network is the switch that commits a cell to divide, coupling growth signals received in G1 to the burst of gene expression needed for DNA replication. When retinoblastoma protein releases E2F1 and E2F2, they turn on the genes that license and fire replication origins — CDC6 and the origin recognition subunits ORC1 and ORC6 — together with CDC25A and cyclin A2, which drive the kinase activity that carries cells through S phase. The same programme supplies factors for homologous recombination and replication-associated repair, including BRCA1 and RAD54L, and for chromosome segregation and cohesion later in the cycle. Because this network sets the restriction point, its deregulation through loss of retinoblastoma control is a common route to unchecked proliferation in cancer, while excess E2F1 activity can instead trigger apoptosis.

Blood formation requires stem cells to stop renewing themselves and commit to a lineage, and RUNX1, acting with its partner CBFB, is one of the transcription factors that makes that decision. Its best-defined target here is SPI1 (PU.1): RUNX1 brings the histone methyltransferase KMT2A to the SPI1 promoter and upstream regulatory element, depositing activating H3K4 trimethylation, and the resulting PU.1 expression restrains stem cell self-renewal while enabling myeloid and lymphoid commitment. RUNX1 also sits within a TAL1-containing complex with LMO1/LMO2, LDB1, GATA factors and E-proteins that drives MYB transcription, a configuration that in T-ALL promotes proliferation and blocks apoptosis. Proteasome subunits and ubiquitin genes reflect the degradation that limits RUNX1 levels, ITCH and CDK7-containing kinase activity among its regulators. Loss or translocation of RUNX1 underlies familial platelet disorder and acute myeloid leukemia.

Rather than build every pyrimidine nucleotide from scratch, cells recover the bases and nucleosides released when DNA and RNA are degraded and phosphorylate them back to nucleotide monophosphates, which then re-enter the interconversion routes that feed replication and repair. Pyrimidine salvage keeps nucleotide pools balanced at far lower energetic cost than de novo synthesis and is the dominant supply route in tissues with limited biosynthetic capacity, including mitochondria, where thymidine kinase 2 supplies dTMP for mitochondrial DNA; its loss causes mitochondrial DNA depletion and myopathy. Uridine-cytidine kinases act on the ribonucleosides, thymidine and deoxycytidine kinases on the deoxy forms, while phosphorylases and cytidine deaminase recycle or interconvert bases upstream. The same enzymes determine the activation and breakdown of nucleoside-analogue drugs, making this chemistry a determinant of chemotherapy and antiviral response.

Phospholipid metabolism builds, remodels and degrades the lipids that make up cellular membranes, setting membrane fluidity, curvature and leaflet asymmetry while generating the lipid second messengers that organelles use as identity tags. The enzymes here cover glycerophospholipid synthesis from glycerol-3-phosphate through acyltransferases and phosphatidate phosphatases, head-group attachment via CDP-choline and CDP-ethanolamine routes, phosphatidylserine synthesis and its decarboxylation to phosphatidylethanolamine, and cardiolipin production and acyl remodelling in mitochondria. A large phosphoinositide arm couples lipid kinases and phosphatases with PH-domain effectors and transfer proteins to mark endosomes, lysosomes and the plasma membrane for traffic and signalling. Phospholipases release fatty acids and lysophospholipids that feed eicosanoid production and membrane repair. Defects produce myotubular and Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathies, Lowe syndrome, Barth syndrome and lipodystrophy, and this chemistry is a hub for growth-factor signalling and cancer.

Gastrulation converts a uniform epiblast into the three primary germ layers initial ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm from which every tissue of the body is later built, and its failure arrests embryogenesis outright. Nodal and BMP ligands acting through their receptors and SMAD effectors, together with WNT ligands signalling via beta-catenin and LEF1, pattern the primitive streak, while antagonists such as NOG, DKK1 and SFRP2 restrict those gradients in space. Downstream transcription factors including TBXT, EOMES, MIXL1, MESP1 and SOX17 assign mesodermal and endodermal identity, and pluripotency factors POU5F1, NANOG and SOX2 are progressively resolved. Cells ingressing through the streak undergo epithelial-mesenchymal transition driven by SNAI1, remodelling integrin-laminin-collagen contacts and matrix metalloproteinase activity to migrate to their new positions. The same signalling and adhesion logic is reused in later organogenesis and reactivated in tumour invasion.

Heart formation covers the earliest steps that turn mesoderm into a recognisable cardiac rudiment: specification of the cardiac fields, their migration and fusion, and the arrival of cardiac neural crest at the forming organ. Because this is the first organ to function in the embryo, disruption here produces lethal or severe congenital heart defects rather than subtle adult phenotypes. The genes reflect the signalling inputs that pattern the field, with BMP ligands and their receptor, WNT/beta-catenin signalling and its antagonist DKK1, and Notch acting through RBPJ setting where cardiac fate is permitted. MESP1 marks the earliest cardiac mesoderm, while ISL1, MEF2C, GATA5, HAND2 and TBX5 form the transcriptional core that commits and regionalises cardiac progenitors; SMARCD3 links them to chromatin remodelling. Mutations in TBX5 and NOTCH1 cause inherited human heart malformation, placing this programme upstream of chamber and outflow tract morphogenesis.

Porphyrin metabolism covers the making and unmaking of the tetrapyrrole ring that holds iron in heme, the cofactor that lets hemoglobin carry oxygen, cytochromes pass electrons, and catalase and peroxidases dispose of hydrogen peroxide. Synthesis begins with condensation of glycine and succinyl-CoA by an erythroid-specific or housekeeping aminolevulinate synthase, proceeds through ALAD, HMBS, UROS, UROD, CPOX and PPOX, and ends when ferrochelatase inserts ferrous iron; partial blocks at these steps cause the porphyrias, in which accumulated intermediates provoke photosensitivity and neurovisceral attacks. Further tailoring by COX10 and COX15 yields heme A for cytochrome oxidase. On the catabolic side heme oxygenases open the ring to release iron, carbon monoxide and biliverdin, which biliverdin reductases convert to bilirubin for glucuronidation by UGT1A1 and biliary export by ABCC2 and related transporters. The route links iron economy, erythropoiesis and hepatic bile pigment handling; failure of conjugation or export produces jaundice.

Raising cytosolic Ca2+ is the switch that converts agonist binding into a functional response in non-excitable cells, and in platelets it drives shape change, granule secretion, integrin activation and aggregation during haemostasis. Two sources are combined. Phospholipase C-generated IP3 opens the ER channels ITPR1-3 to discharge internal stores; the resulting drop in store content is sensed by STIM1, which gathers at ER-plasma membrane contacts and gates the ORAI1/ORAI2 pore to produce store-operated Ca2+ entry that both sustains signalling and refills the store. Independently, ligand- and receptor-operated routes admit Ca2+ directly: the ATP-gated P2X family, with P2X1 prominent in platelets, and TRPC3/6/7 channels. Loss of STIM1 or ORAI1 function produces immunodeficiency and impaired platelet and lymphocyte activation, while excessive entry favours thrombosis, placing this step at the centre of secretion, adhesion and calcium-dependent enzyme control.

Integrins report the state of the extracellular matrix to the cell interior, and this step is how that report reaches the MAP kinase cascade: GRB2 with its exchange factor SOS1 couples an adhesion complex to Ras, converting matrix attachment into proliferative and survival signalling. The context is the activated platelet or adherent cell, where fibrinogen chains, fibronectin and von Willebrand factor engage the ITGA2B/ITGB3 receptor whose cytoplasmic tail is held by talin, with RAP1A/RAP1B and the adaptor APBB1IP acting upstream to bring the receptor into its high-affinity state. Clustering activates focal adhesion kinase (PTK2) and SRC, which phosphorylate sites that recruit the GRB2:SOS pair; loss of this linkage leaves cells attached but unable to translate adhesion into growth-factor-like ERK output, a requirement for anchorage-dependent growth, migration and platelet aggregation.

The G1/S transition is the commitment step of the cell cycle, the point at which a cell stops responding to growth signals and begins to copy its genome. Cyclin E-CDK2 and cyclin A-CDK2 drive the switch, inhibited by the CDK inhibitors p21 and p27 and by Wee1-mediated phosphorylation that CDC25A reverses. Upstream, cyclin D-CDK4 and CDK7-containing activating kinase relieve repression of E2F-DP transcription factors by RB and the related pocket proteins within the DREAM/LIN complex, switching on genes for replication licensing (ORC, CDC6, CDT1, the MCM helicase), polymerases and primase, and nucleotide supply enzymes such as thymidylate synthase, TK1 and ribonucleotide reductase. Timely destruction of cyclin E, p27 and the licensing inhibitor geminin requires SCF-type ubiquitin ligases and the proteasome. Loss of this control, through RB inactivation or cyclin/MYC overexpression, underlies unchecked proliferation in cancer.

Every transcript made in the nucleus must be processed, checked, moved and eventually destroyed, and this superpathway of RNA metabolism gathers that whole life cycle. It determines how much of each protein a cell makes and which protein isoform, so its failures produce spliceosomopathies, ribosomopathies such as Diamond-Blackfan anemia, and retinitis pigmentosa from defective splicing factors. Nascent messages are capped, spliced by the U1-U6 snRNPs with SF3B and PRPF components, cleaved and polyadenylated by the cleavage/polyadenylation and cleavage stimulation complexes, then exported through the TREX-nuclear pore route. Quality control and turnover follow: nonsense-mediated decay via UPF1 and the SMG proteins, deadenylation by the CCR4-NOT complex, decapping, exosome-mediated degradation, and AU-rich element binding proteins that set message half-life. Parallel arms cover snRNP assembly, ribosomal RNA maturation, tRNA modification and splicing, and mitochondrial RNA processing.

Proteins are synthesized in one place and must work in another, and this broad programme covers the directed delivery of proteins to their correct compartment or cell surface. It underlies secretion, receptor display, organelle biogenesis and regulated release of hormones and neurotransmitters; when it fails the result is mislocalized cargo, ER stress and diseases ranging from lysosomal storage and pigmentation disorders to neurodegeneration. The genes span the main routes: signal-recognition particle and Sec61 translocation into the ER, TOM/TIM import into mitochondria, peroxisomal PEX machinery, karyopherin- and nucleoporin-dependent nuclear transport, COPI/COPII and Golgi tethering steps, clathrin adaptor complexes, Rab GTPases with their GEFs and GAPs, SNAREs and synaptotagmins for membrane fusion, retromer, WASH and sorting nexins for endosomal recycling, and ESCRT components for delivery to lysosomes. Chaperones, ubiquitin ligases and ERAD factors provide the quality control that removes cargo failing to reach its destination.

Glucose metabolism covers everything cells do with their principal fuel: phosphorylating it, breaking it down through glycolysis to pyruvate, oxidising that pyruvate in mitochondria, storing carbon as glycogen or lipid, and running the reverse route of gluconeogenesis when dietary sugar is scarce. Whole-body glucose homeostasis depends on it, and its derangement produces diabetes, hypoglycaemia and the glycogen storage disorders. The core enzymatic steps appear here as families with tissue-specific members — hexokinases and glucokinase, phosphofructokinases, aldolases, enolases, pyruvate kinase, the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex with its inhibitory kinases, and the gluconeogenic enzymes phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, fructose bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase. Layered over them is hormonal and nutrient control: insulin acting through its receptor, IRS adaptors and AKT; glucagon and leptin; AMP-activated protein kinase; and transcriptional regulators including FOXO1, PPARGC1A, PDX1 and sirtuins, some of them tied to circadian timing.

Organophosphate metabolic process gathers the reactions that make, modify and break down phosphate-bearing organic molecules, which is most of the chemistry a cell uses to store energy, signal and build membranes. Its breadth is reflected in the genes: glycolytic and pentose phosphate enzymes plus mitochondrial ATP synthase and respiratory complex subunits handle phosphorylated sugars and ATP turnover; nucleoside and nucleotide kinases, phosphatases and nucleotidases (adenylate kinases, NME family, 5'-nucleotidases, ribonucleotide reductase) supply and balance nucleotide pools; phosphoinositide kinases and phosphatases such as PTEN, OCRL and the myotubularins, together with phospholipases, acyltransferases and choline/ethanolamine pathway enzymes, generate membrane lipids and lipid second messengers; adenylate and guanylate cyclases with cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases set cAMP and cGMP levels. Also included are GPI anchor assembly, coenzyme A and NAD synthesis, and sulfation. Defects across these routes cause mitochondrial disease, myopathy, nucleotide-pool disorders and cancer-associated growth signalling.

Truncating mutations that remove the NOTCH1 PEST domain leave ligand binding and proteolytic activation intact but make the released intracellular fragment abnormally stable, so the receptor signals constitutively. Normally, after Delta- and Jagged-family ligands trigger cleavage by ADAM proteases and the gamma-secretase complex, the liberated NICD1 enters the nucleus, converts RBPJ from a repressor into an activator with Mastermind-like coactivators and acetyltransferases, and induces HES and HEY genes plus MYC before being phosphorylated and marked by the FBXW7-SKP1-CUL1 ubiquitin ligase for proteasomal destruction. Loss of the PEST degron blocks that turnover, prolonging target gene transcription. Because the pathway sets thymocyte fate and proliferative drive, such mutants are recurrent drivers of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, illustrating how signal termination rather than initiation can be the step that fails in cancer.

A promoter-motif-defined grouping rather than a curated process: these genes share an upstream sequence resembling TNCATNTCCYR, the kind of shared cis-element that suggests coordinate transcriptional control by a common factor. The members converge on genome maintenance and basal transcription. RAD50 works within the sensor complex that detects double-strand breaks and initiates end resection, RAD51C supports homologous recombination and is a hereditary breast and ovarian cancer gene, and SMARCAL1 is an annealing helicase that stabilises stalled replication forks, its loss causing Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia. GTF2H1 is a core general transcription factor subunit also used in nucleotide excision repair, ELP4 belongs to the Elongator complex, and MEN1 encodes the menin tumour suppressor that scaffolds chromatin-modifying complexes. Others contribute peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation, nucleotide signalling and vesicle tethering, so the set is best read as a regulatory module inferred from shared promoter architecture.

E-cadherin (CDH1) is the adhesion receptor that holds polarized epithelial sheets together, and the control of its abundance and activity decides whether a cell stays epithelial or converts to a migratory mesenchymal state. Because loss of CDH1 permits invasion, this regulation underlies its behaviour as a tumour suppressor: germline loss-of-function mutations cause hereditary diffuse gastric cancer, and silencing accompanies epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition in many carcinomas. Transcription is repressed by SNAI1/SNAI2, ZEB1/ZEB2 and TWIST factors recruiting histone deacetylases, LSD1 and Polycomb components, while KLF4 and other factors favour expression; microRNAs and Argonaute-containing complexes add post-transcriptional control. The mature protein is made through signal peptide cleavage, N-glycosylation and proprotein convertase processing, then anchored to actin through beta-catenin, alpha-catenin, p120 and vinculin at adherens junctions. Kinases such as SRC and casein kinase 2, HECT-type ubiquitin ligase CBLL1, endocytosis, cathepsins and the proteasome drive its turnover.

Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans are the main space-filling, water-binding components of cartilage and other extracellular matrix, and they also form the inhibitory scars that block axon regrowth in the injured central nervous system. Their metabolism covers the whole life cycle of the chain: xylosyltransferases and galactosyl/glucuronyltransferases build the tetrasaccharide linker on a core protein serine, polymerising glycosyltransferases extend the glucuronic acid-N-acetylgalactosamine repeat, epimerases convert it toward dermatan, and a family of sulfotransferases places sulfate at specific positions to create the binding codes read by growth factors and guidance receptors. Nucleotide-sugar supply and Golgi sulfate transport feed the reactions, while hyaluronidases, sulfatases and exoglycosidases carry out lysosomal turnover. Loss of the linker enzymes causes skeletal dysplasias and connective tissue disorders, and defective degradation underlies mucopolysaccharidoses with progressive storage in bone, cartilage and brain.

Epithelial sheets hold together through three adhesion systems — adherens junctions, tight junctions and desmosomes — and this pathway covers how they are built, remodelled and controlled. Junction organization sets the permeability barrier of skin, gut, kidney tubule and endothelium, establishes apical-basal polarity, and its loss underlies epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, wound healing failure and invasive tumour spread. Classical cadherins and nectins nucleate contacts and link through catenins, vinculin and plakoglobin to actin, while claudins and junctional adhesion molecules create the paracellular seal and select which ions and small solutes pass. Polarity complexes containing PARD3, PARD6 and atypical PKC, together with Rho-family GTPases CDC42 and RAC1 and their exchange factors, position junctions correctly. Cadherin levels are further set by proteasomal turnover, N-glycosylation and signal peptide processing, and by transcriptional repressors such as SNAI1, SNAI2, ZEB1 and TWIST1 acting with histone-modifying and microRNA machinery.

Columnar and cuboidal epithelial cells line the gut, airway, kidney tubules and glandular ducts, and this programme covers their maturation from committed precursors into tall, polarised, secretory or absorptive cells with a free apical surface. It is what gives an epithelial sheet its barrier and transport function; failure produces flattened or poorly differentiated epithelium, mucus depletion, and the loss of polarity that accompanies metaplasia and carcinoma. Transcriptional drivers set identity and differentiation state — KLF5, SPDEF for goblet-type secretory fate, PRDM1, HOXA5, NKX3-2 and the retinoic acid receptors, which make vitamin A status an input into epithelial specification. Growth and mechanical cues arrive through YAP1, SRC, TGFB1 and IL6ST signalling, while C1GALT1-dependent O-glycosylation and YIPF6 support the mucin secretion and Golgi traffic that mature apical surfaces depend on. Hypoxia sensing via HIF1A links differentiation to the oxygen gradients of luminal tissues.

Collagen is the most abundant protein in the body, and its biosynthesis together with the modifying enzymes that mature it determines whether skin, bone, cartilage, blood vessels and basement membranes have tensile strength.
