Procollagen alpha chains from across the family — fibrillar types I, II, III, V and XI, network-forming type IV, anchoring type VII and the FACIT and beaded-filament collagens — enter the endoplasmic reticulum, where prolyl 4-hydroxylases and their P4HB partner, prolyl 3-hydroxylases, lysyl hydroxylases (PLOD1-3), collagen galactosyltransferases, the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase PPIB and the collagen-specific chaperone HSP47 stabilise and fold the triple helix. After secretion, BMP1 and tolloid-like proteases with their PCOLCE enhancers remove C-propeptides while ADAMTS2, 3 and 14 cleave N-propeptides, releasing tropocollagen for fibril assembly. Defects here cause osteogenesis imperfecta, Ehlers-Danlos and dermatosparactic syndromes, epidermolysis bullosa and Alport syndrome.

Formation of the vertebrate camera-type eye turns a patch of anterior neural plate into an optic cup, lens, cornea and retina aligned precisely enough to focus an image on a photoreceptor sheet. When it goes wrong the result is anophthalmia, microphthalmia, coloboma, congenital cataract, or anterior segment dysgenesis with glaucoma. Master transcription factors including PAX6, SIX3, VSX2, PITX2/3 and FOXE3 specify retinal and lens territories, while WNT, BMP, Notch, Hedgehog and ephrin-Eph signals set boundaries, drive invagination and control the timing of progenitor exit. Downstream steps include lens fibre differentiation with crystallin expression, retinal pigment epithelium maturation and retinoid handling for the visual cycle, retinal lamination through adhesion and polarity proteins, ciliary and photoreceptor outer segment assembly, and VEGF-dependent vascularisation of the developing eye. Retinal cell-type identity genes such as NRL and RORB link morphogenesis to the final wiring of vision.

Once HIV-1 has integrated its genome, the late phase of its life cycle turns that provirus into new virions, and it does so almost entirely with borrowed host machinery. Viral gene expression begins with RNA polymerase II and the general initiation factors assembled on the integrated LTR promoter; the viral Tat protein then captures the CDK9/cyclin T kinase to phosphorylate the polymerase C-terminal domain and the negative elongation and DSIF factors, converting stalled short transcripts into full-length message. Capping, elongation through the FACT and elongin complexes, and Rev-directed export of unspliced and partially spliced RNAs through nucleoporins, RAN-cycle components and XPO1 deliver Gag, Pol and Env transcripts to the cytoplasm. Myristoyltransferases, cyclophilin A, furin and the ESCRT machinery with VPS4 ATPases then support particle assembly and membrane scission. These dependencies define the steps targeted by transcriptional silencing and latency-reversal strategies.

Non-coding RNAs make up the bulk of transcriptional output, and their maturation requires dedicated processing and trafficking machinery rather than the route taken by messenger RNAs. The genes here center on one well-defined branch of that biology: biogenesis of the spliceosomal small nuclear RNAs. Newly transcribed snRNAs are capped and bound by the nuclear cap-binding complex with PHAX, exported through the nuclear pore, and assembled in the cytoplasm into Sm-core particles by the SMN complex with its Gemin subunits, aided by the PRMT5-WDR77-CLNS1A methylosome that symmetrically dimethylates Sm proteins. TGS1 then converts the cap to trimethylguanosine, which snurportin recognizes to reimport the particle for splicing. The extensive nucleoporin and RanBP2 content reflects the bidirectional pore transit this cycle demands. Loss of SMN1 function depletes these particles and causes spinal muscular atrophy, linking snRNP assembly to motor neuron survival.

The vertebrate inner ear begins as a thickened patch of head ectoderm that invaginates and pinches off to form the otic vesicle, and the development of this transient structure sets up every later part of the labyrinth: cochlear duct, semicircular canals, vestibular and auditory sensory patches, and the neurons of the cochleovestibular ganglion. Fibroblast growth factor signalling from adjacent tissue, acting through receptors such as FGFR2, induces and patterns the placode, while a transcriptional module including EYA1, SIX1, PAX8, GATA3 and SOX9 specifies otic identity, regionalizes the vesicle along its axes and maintains the progenitors that will become hair cells and supporting cells. Structural and matrix components contribute to the surrounding cartilage capsule. Disruption of these regulators causes congenital deafness and vestibular malformation, as seen in branchio-oto-renal syndrome and related inner ear dysplasias.

Glycogen synthesis begins with glycogenin building a short glucose chain on itself, and that self-glucosylated primer is what glycogen synthase then extends into the branched storage polymer of muscle and other tissues. Glycogen storage disease type XV arises when GYG1 encodes a protein that cannot be autoglucosylated, so no primer is available and muscle glycogen fails to accumulate; patients present with muscle weakness, exercise intolerance and cardiac involvement, with abnormal polyglucosan-like deposits in some fibres. The two participants define the initiation step itself: glycogenin transfers UDP-glucose to its own tyrosine residue and remains attached at the core of the granule, while muscle glycogen synthase encoded by GYS1 elongates the alpha-1,4 chain. The defect illustrates how energy storage in skeletal muscle depends on a single priming reaction rather than on bulk polymer-forming capacity.

Where a protein ends up inside a cell is as regulated as whether it is made at all, and this collection covers the control layer that sets those destinations: targeting proteins to the plasma membrane, sorting them through endosomes, retaining or releasing them from the ER, importing and exporting cargo across the nuclear envelope, and anchoring them at the centrosome, cilium, synapse or cell junction. The machinery is broad but recognisable: COPII coat and ER export components, Rab GTPases and their regulators with retromer and ESCRT sorting factors, clathrin adaptors for endocytosis, SNAREs for fusion, importins, exportins and the Ran system, 14-3-3 proteins, chaperones, and palmitoyltransferases and ubiquitin ligases that add the modifications acting as trafficking signals. Kinases and receptor pathways feed in so that localisation responds to signalling, as when insulin secretion, Wnt or Hedgehog output depends on relocating a key effector.

Conversion of the HIV-1 RNA genome into double-stranded DNA is the step that commits a newly infected cell to harbouring a provirus, and it is the target of the largest class of antiretroviral drugs. In the cytosol of the new host cell, the viral reverse transcriptase heterodimer copies genomic RNA into a minus-strand DNA using a host tRNA primer, degrades the RNA of the resulting RNA:DNA hybrids through its RNase H activity, and completes a plus strand, with two template-switching events that duplicate the long terminal repeats at both ends of the product. The linear duplex is then available for integration into host chromatin. Host factors participate as well: the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase cyclophilin A binds incoming capsid, influencing uncoating and the efficiency of early reverse transcription, and links this stage to innate sensing of the viral core.

Blood coagulation stops bleeding at sites of vascular injury by converting soluble fibrinogen into a cross-linked fibrin clot on a platelet plug, and the same proteolytic network must be restrained so that clots do not spread or persist. Loss of individual components produces haemophilia and related bleeding disorders, while excess activity drives thrombosis and disseminated intravascular coagulation. The programme spans the contact and tissue factor pathways through prothrombin to fibrin, the anticoagulant brake supplied by antithrombin, thrombomodulin, protein C and protein S, and fibrinolysis by plasminogen with its tissue and urokinase activators and their serpin inhibitors. Platelet adhesion and activation machinery contributes von Willebrand factor, glycoprotein Ib, integrin "IIb"3 and released chemokines such as platelet factor 4. Also represented are complement proteins and matrix metalloproteinases with their TIMP inhibitors, reflecting how clotting is coupled to inflammation and wound remodelling.

Cells extend and retract projections — axons, dendrites, dendritic spines, filopodia, lamellipodia, microvilli and cilia — and this pathway covers the control layer that decides when such structures grow, branch, stabilise or disassemble. It underlies neuronal wiring, epithelial brush border and cilium formation, and directed cell migration during development and wound repair; its disruption contributes to intellectual disability, axon guidance defects, ciliopathies and impaired regeneration after nerve injury. Guidance receptors and their ligands (netrins and DCC, slits and ROBOs, semaphorins with plexins, ephrins with Eph kinases) converge on Rho-family GTPases and their many activators and TBC-domain GAPs, which in turn tune actin nucleation through WAVE/WASP and Arp2/3, severing and capping by cofilin and LIM kinases, and microtubule behaviour via MAP2, tau and CRMPs. Neurotrophin, Wnt and Reelin inputs, vesicle traffic through Rab-dependent recycling, and intraflagellar transport set the polarity and membrane supply these projections require.

Neurotrophin signalling ends, in part, at the nucleus, where phosphorylation of CREB on serine 133 converts a resting transcription factor into an activator of genes that keep neurons alive, grow their axons, and consolidate synaptic change into lasting memory. Loss of this step leaves neurotrophin-dependent neurons unable to mount the survival and growth transcription programme that nerve growth factor normally triggers, including in axons signalling retrogradely back to the cell body. The kinases that carry out the modification sit downstream of the MAP kinase cascades: the RSK family members RPS6KA1, RPS6KA2 and RPS6KA3 and the ERK/p38-activated MSK1 (RPS6KA5), together with the p38 effector MAPKAPK2. MSK1 additionally phosphorylates the related factor ATF1, and its activity tracks NGF-induced CREB phosphorylation more closely than that of the RSKs. Serine 133 phosphorylation then permits coactivator recruitment and target gene transcription.

The nephrons of the permanent kidney are built by converting metanephric mesenchyme into epithelium: cap mesenchyme cells acquire apical-basolateral polarity, form adherens and tight junctions, deposit basement membrane and organize into the renal vesicle that elongates into a functioning nephron. This mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition during metanephros morphogenesis sets final nephron number, and its failure produces renal hypoplasia, dysplasia or agenesis. Reciprocal signalling drives it: mesenchyme-derived GDNF induces and guides ureteric bud outgrowth and branching, with GREM1 relieving BMP antagonism, while ureteric WNT9B acting through beta-catenin, together with LIF, induces the surrounding mesenchyme to epithelialize. SIX2 keeps the progenitor pool self-renewing and must be extinguished for conversion to proceed, while PAX2, PAX8 and SALL1 specify nephron identity and hedgehog signalling through SMO patterns the surrounding stroma and collecting system.

Pexophagy is the selective autophagy route that clears surplus or damaged peroxisomes, keeping the organelle population matched to metabolic demand. Because peroxisomes both oxidise branched and very-long-chain fatty acids and generate and detoxify hydrogen peroxide, failure to remove dysfunctional ones allows reactive oxygen species to accumulate, while excessive turnover starves cells of lipid catabolism; the balance shifts with nutrient supply and oxidative stress. Targeting works through ubiquitination of peroxisomal membrane proteins, notably the import receptor PEX5, which recruits the autophagy receptors SQSTM1/p62 and NBR1; these bind LC3 on the forming autophagosome and deliver the organelle to the lysosome. The mitochondrial deubiquitinase USP30 opposes tagging by removing ubiquitin, and ATM signalling links oxidative and stress cues to receptor engagement, placing peroxisome quality control within the broader ubiquitin-dependent organelle turnover system.

Silencing of genes through methylation of cytosines in their promoter CpG islands is one of the stable epigenetic marks that keeps genes off across cell divisions, and it underlies imprinting, X-inactivation, retroelement suppression and the inappropriate silencing of tumour suppressors in cancer. DNMT1 copies the mark onto newly replicated DNA with UHRF1 recognising hemimethylated sites and recruiting it, while DNMT3A, aided by the catalytically inactive cofactor DNMT3L, establishes methylation de novo; USP7 and the chromatin remodeller HELLS support the process at heterochromatin. MECP2 and MPHOSPH8 read methylated DNA and link it to repressive complexes, and EHMT2 couples the mark to histone H3K9 methylation. CTCF and ZNF445 act at imprinted and boundary regions. Loss or misdirection of this machinery causes imprinting disorders, Rett syndrome and widespread promoter hypermethylation in tumours.

Microtubules must be nucleated, elongated, stabilised, severed and reoriented on demand, and the regulation of microtubule cytoskeleton organization is the control layer that sets how much polymer exists and where it points. It governs mitotic spindle assembly and chromosome segregation, centrosome and cilium function, neuronal axon outgrowth and intracellular transport, so its failure produces aneuploidy, microcephaly and neurodegeneration. Plus-end tracking and stabilising factors such as the EB proteins, CLASPs, CKAP5 and TACC3 build and cap growing ends, while CAMSAPs mark minus ends; stathmins sequester tubulin dimers and spastin and katanin subunits sever existing polymer. Post-translational marks written and erased by an acetyltransferase and HDAC6 tune filament mechanics and motor traffic. Mitotic kinases including PLK1 and AURKB, the augmin complex, and GSK3 and Rho-ROCK signalling couple cell cycle and adhesion cues to this remodelling, with MAPT and MAP2 acting in neurons.

RUNX1 is the transcription factor that lets blood form: with its obligate partner CBFB it drives self-renewal of haematopoietic stem cells and the commitment of myeloid, megakaryocytic, T regulatory and B lymphoid progenitors, and its translocation or mutation is among the commonest lesions in acute leukaemia. CBFB does not touch DNA itself; it stabilises the Runt domain on the double helix and relieves RUNX1 autoinhibition. From there RUNX1 recruits coactivators and chromatin machinery — CREBBP/EP300 acetyltransferases, SWI/SNF remodellers, MLL-family and WDR5-containing methyltransferase complexes — or represses targets through Sin3/HDAC1 and Polycomb components, while proteasomal turnover and kinase phosphorylation set its level and activity. Target genes include lineage factors such as GATA1, SPI1, TAL1, PAX5 and FOXP3, platelet genes, and cytokines like IL2 and CSF2; RUNX1 also acts in breast epithelium and nociceptive sensory neurons.

Carboxylic acid transmembrane transport moves amino acids, monocarboxylates, di- and tricarboxylates, fatty acids and folate across plasma and organellar membranes, connecting extracellular nutrient supply to cytosolic and mitochondrial metabolism. It underlies intestinal and renal reabsorption, glutamate clearance at synapses, lactate shuttling between glycolytic and oxidative cells, and delivery of acyl groups and TCA-cycle intermediates into mitochondria. Carriers here span several families: monocarboxylate transporters of the SLC16 group, sodium-dependent and exchange-type amino acid carriers of the SLC1, SLC7 and SLC38 groups, vesicular glutamate transporters, mitochondrial SLC25 carriers for citrate, malate, aspartate/glutamate and carnitine, ABC transporters that import very-long-chain fatty acids into peroxisomes, and the pyruvate carriers MPC1/MPC2. Loss of individual members causes cystinuria, lysinuric protein intolerance, X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, thyroid hormone transport defects and excitotoxic neurological disease, and tumours exploit these routes for glutamine and lactate flux.

NMDA receptor activation and the postsynaptic events that follow are how an excitatory synapse converts coincident presynaptic glutamate release and postsynaptic depolarization into a lasting change in its own strength, the cellular basis of learning and memory. The receptor itself is a heteromer of an obligatory GRIN1 subunit with GRIN2/GRIN3 partners, gated by glutamate plus glycine and unblocked from Mg2+ only when the membrane depolarizes; the resulting Ca2+ entry is the signal. Calcium bound to calmodulin drives CaMKII and CaMKK-dependent kinases, Ca2+-sensitive adenylate cyclases and PKA, Ras exchange factors and ERK, converging on AMPA receptor delivery and on CREB-dependent transcription. Scaffolds of the PSD-95 family, CASK-LIN7 complexes and the kinesin KIF17 position receptors, while tubulins and actin regulators remodel the spine. Dysregulation underlies excitotoxic neuronal death, epilepsy, and cognitive and psychiatric disorders.

Cytosolic DNA is a danger signal, and the cGAS/STING axis is how cells read it, converting detection of mislocalised DNA into type I interferon and inflammatory gene expression against viruses, intracellular bacteria and damaged self. Positive regulation of this pathway sets the gain of that response: too little leaves cells permissive to infection and blunts antitumour immunity, too much drives interferonopathies and sterile inflammation. The regulators here act at several levels. STING is stabilised and activated by post-translational modification, including palmitoylation by a Golgi-resident acyltransferase and ubiquitin transfer by a mitochondrial E3, while a kinase adaptor module feeds into downstream NF-kB-directed inflammatory output. A folate transporter doubles as an importer of extracellular cyclic dinucleotides, allowing cells to respond to second messengers made elsewhere, and a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase contributes signal amplification.

Myeloid progenitors must be held back from becoming monocytes if the marrow is to retain proliferating precursors and generate other lineages, and this restraint on monocyte differentiation is how that balance is kept. It matters because loss of the brake shifts output toward monocytes and macrophages, while its inappropriate persistence blocks maturation, a pattern seen in myeloid leukaemias where differentiation arrest accompanies continued proliferation. The genes involved act at several levels: cell cycle and growth regulators such as CDK6 and MYC keep progenitors cycling rather than maturing, a homeobox factor and the dendritic-cell-restricted factor ZBTB46 impose alternative transcriptional programmes, the inositol phosphatase INPP5D dampens signalling downstream of growth factor and immune receptors, and a microRNA tunes the same decision post-transcriptionally. The result is a checkpoint on lineage commitment within haematopoiesis and innate immune cell supply.

Alpha-beta T cells acquire their identity and effector character through a tightly controlled developmental programme, and this pathway covers the signals and factors that raise or lower the rate and extent of that differentiation. It governs thymic lineage decisions, including the CD4 versus CD8 choice directed by ZBTB7B and RUNX3, and the later commitment of peripheral naive cells to helper and regulatory fates specified by GATA3, TBX21, BCL6 and FOXP3. Cytokines and their receptors, antigen-presenting costimulation, and proximal receptor kinases such as ZAP70, SYK and JAK3 feed into these transcriptional programmes, while SOCS1, SMAD7 and the roquin RNA-binding proteins RC3H1 and RC3H2 restrain them. Loss of control here produces immunodeficiency when differentiation fails, as in adenosine deaminase deficiency, and autoimmunity or unchecked inflammation when effector skewing escapes regulation.

Cells continually encounter foreign chemicals a drugs, plant toxins, pollutants, carcinogens a and this response programme detects them and converts them into products that can be excreted. It sets the pharmacokinetics of most medicines, determines individual susceptibility to chemical carcinogenesis and hepatotoxicity, and explains much clinically important drug-drug interaction. Ligand-activated transcription factors such as the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and the pregnane X receptor, together with the oxidative-stress sensor NFE2L2, induce the enzymes that do the work: cytochrome P450 and flavin monooxygenases, epoxide hydrolase and carbonyl reductases oxidise or hydrolyse the compound, then glutathione S-transferases, UDP-glucuronosyltransferases, sulfotransferases and N-acetyltransferases conjugate it. Solute carrier uptake transporters and ATP-binding cassette efflux pumps move substrates and conjugates across membranes, chiefly in liver, intestine and kidney. Common variants in these enzymes and transporters underlie pharmacogenetic differences in drug response and toxicity.

Cells change shape, adhere, and migrate by continually rebuilding their actin scaffolding, and this cytoskeletal remodeling programme couples adhesion receptors and growth-factor signals to that rebuilding. It underlies wound healing, immune cell motility, platelet spreading and tissue stiffness sensing, and its deregulation contributes to fibrosis and to tumour invasion. Focal adhesion components link integrins to actin and transmit mechanical force: talin bridges integrin tails to filaments, zyxin concentrates at stress fibres and adhesion sites where tension is sensed, and filamin A cross-links actin while binding numerous membrane partners. A spectrin-family scaffold supports cortical membrane organisation, clathrin adaptor machinery couples remodeling to endocytic turnover of surface receptors, and AKT1 and TGFB1 supply the signalling input that drives cytoskeletal reorganisation, survival and contractile gene expression during migration and matrix remodeling.

Platelets stop bleeding by sticking to damaged vessel walls and then amplifying that contact into a clot, and the genes here cover both the adhesion step and its coupling to the coagulation cascade. The glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex, encoded by GP1BA, GP1BB, GP9 and GP5, is the receptor for von Willebrand factor and captures platelets from flowing blood under high shear; GP6 binds exposed collagen and triggers the signalling that drives granule release and integrin activation. Loss of these receptors or of von Willebrand factor causes inherited bleeding disorders, while excessive engagement underlies arterial thrombosis, which is why this axis is a drug target. Other members temper or support the response: PROS1 acts as a cofactor for activated protein C in restraining thrombin generation, PCSK6 processes secreted precursors, and SEPT5 contributes to regulated granule exocytosis.

The permanent kidney forms its filtering units when mesenchymal progenitors of the metanephros convert into polarized epithelium and elaborate the nephron tubule; this differentiation step sets nephron number at birth, and its failure produces renal hypoplasia, dysplasia and reduced lifelong filtration reserve. Induction begins with signals from the ureteric bud, including the LIF cytokine acting through STAT signalling, which drive mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition in the cap mesenchyme. The paired-box transcription factors PAX2 and PAX8 are the identity determinants here, marking induced renal vesicles and sustaining the tubular epithelial programme through comma- and S-shaped body stages into proximal tubule, loop and distal segments. The Hippo pathway effectors YAP1 and WWTR1 couple cell shape, adhesion and mechanical cues to progenitor proliferation and epithelial maturation, balancing expansion against differentiation. The same regulators are reactivated during tubular injury repair and are recurrently deranged in Wilms tumour.

Bone acquires its stiffness when osteoblasts deposit hydroxyapatite into collagenous matrix, and this pathway covers the signals that set how fast and how much mineral is laid down. Getting the balance right distinguishes normal skeletal growth from rickets and osteomalacia on one side and pathological calcification of cartilage, vessels and soft tissue on the other. Much of the control is hormonal and phosphate-centred: parathyroid hormone, vitamin D activation by CYP27B1 acting through the vitamin D receptor, and FGF23 with its co-receptor klotho tuning phosphate availability, while ENPP1, ANKH and PHOSPHO1 govern the local pyrophosphate-to-phosphate ratio that permits or blocks crystal growth. Bone morphogenetic proteins and their receptors, WNT ligands and SMAD3 drive the osteogenic transcriptional programme, and matrix proteins such as osteocalcin, MGP and matrilin act as mineralization inhibitors or nucleators within the extracellular matrix itself.

Cells read the extracellular matrix through adhesion receptors and convert that contact into decisions about shape, movement, survival and differentiation. Cell-extracellular matrix interactions are built on integrins, represented here by the beta-1 subunit, whose short cytoplasmic tails recruit cytoplasmic adaptors that physically couple the membrane to actin filaments and to signalling. A central module pairs the pseudokinase ILK with PINCH proteins and parvins, working alongside kindlin-2, filamins, actinin, paxillin and migfilin at focal adhesions; downstream effectors such as a Rac/Cdc42 exchange factor, TESK1 and VASP tune actin dynamics, lamellipodial protrusion and adhesion turnover, allowing cells to spread and migrate. Signals travel in both directions, so matrix composition and stiffness are reported inward while integrin activation state is projected outward. This biology underlies tissue assembly and wound repair, and its subversion contributes to tumour invasion and to muscle and skin fragility disorders.

Heme oxygenase 1 breaks down heme into biliverdin, carbon monoxide and free iron, and because heme is both a cofactor and a pro-oxidant, how much of this enzyme a cell makes is tightly controlled. Its induction is one of the standard cytoprotective responses to oxidative stress, hypoxia, heavy metals, inflammation and hemolysis, limiting tissue injury; loss of the enzyme in humans causes a rare syndrome of hemolysis, endothelial damage and inflammation. Control runs mainly through antioxidant response elements in the promoter, where small MAF partners such as MAFK dimerize either with NFE2L2 to drive transcription or with the heme-sensing repressor BACH1 to silence it, so that rising heme itself relieves repression. Beyond transcription, the enzyme works as a dimer anchored in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane until the intramembrane protease HM13 releases a soluble form that reaches cytosol, mitochondria and nucleus.

Chromosome segregation is stochastic at the level of individual kinetochore-microtubule attachments, and the mitotic spindle checkpoint is what keeps a cell from dividing before every chromosome is properly attached, preventing aneuploidy. An unattached kinetochore generates a diffusible inhibitory signal built around MAD1, MAD2, BUB1, BUBR1 and BUB3, which sequesters CDC20 and blocks the anaphase-promoting complex from ubiquitinating securin and cyclin B, so sister chromatids stay together and mitotic exit is delayed. The genes here cover the platforms on which this happens: the constitutive centromere-associated network, the MIS12 and NDC80 complexes that bind microtubules, the RZZ complex and dynein that strip checkpoint proteins once attachment forms, Aurora B and the chromosomal passenger complex that correct erroneous attachments, and phosphatase and kinesin activities that tune tension. Chronic failure produces chromosomal instability characteristic of tumours.

Cells respond to TGF-beta family ligands by halting proliferation, remodelling their adhesion and matrix, and switching on a defined transcriptional programme; the genes induced by TGFB1 trace that response. It governs epithelial growth arrest, wound healing and fibrosis, immune tolerance, and its loss is a common route to tumour progression, while germline defects in receptor components cause vascular and skeletal syndromes. Ligand engages type I and type II serine/threonine kinase receptors with co-receptors such as endoglin, activating SMAD3 and, on the BMP arm, SMAD1; nuclear partners including TGIF1, SKI, SKIL and TRIM33 with histone deacetylase complexes set the output. Much of the induced set is feedback machinery: inhibitory SMAD6 and SMAD7, the ubiquitin ligases SMURF1 and SMURF2, the phosphatase PPM1A and PMEPA1 all damp signalling, alongside effectors like SERPINE1, THBS1, JUNB and the ID proteins.

Organs acquire their shape through iterative signalling between epithelium and mesenchyme, and this pathway covers the inputs that promote and amplify that shaping rather than restrain it. It matters because the same signals set kidney branching, limb and craniofacial outgrowth, gonad and mammary development, and heart field patterning; their loss produces renal agenesis, skeletal and palatal defects, and disorders of sex development. Secreted ligands of the FGF, BMP, WNT and GDNF families act through receptors such as FGFR1 and the adaptor FRS2, with CTNNB1 transducing canonical WNT input, while SPRY1 and DKK1 tune the amplitude of these cues. Transcription factors including SIX1, SOX9, GATA3, MSX1 and posterior HOX genes translate the signals into regional identity and cell fate, and guidance receptors ROBO1 and ROBO2 position the responding progenitors. Hormonal and cytokine inputs such as AR, TGFB1 and CSF1 modulate the process.

Heme is the iron-containing tetrapyrrole that lets hemoglobin carry oxygen and lets cytochromes, catalase and P450 enzymes do redox chemistry, and its biosynthesis is concentrated in erythroid precursors and hepatocytes. The route begins in mitochondria with condensation of succinyl-CoA and glycine by ALA synthase, whose erythroid-specific form ALAS2 sets the pace of red cell heme supply while ALAS1 serves other tissues. Four cytosolic steps build and decarboxylate the tetrapyrrole ring through porphobilinogen, uroporphyrinogen III and coproporphyrinogen III, after which the intermediates return to mitochondria for side-chain oxidation and insertion of ferrous iron by ferrochelatase. Enzyme deficiencies cause the porphyrias, in which accumulated photoreactive porphyrins damage skin or neurotoxic precursors provoke acute attacks; ALAS2 loss instead gives sideroblastic anemia. Transport proteins handle porphyrin and heme efflux, and downstream heme a synthesis feeds cytochrome c oxidase assembly.

Bone, teeth and cartilage acquire their hardness through controlled deposition of calcium phosphate mineral, and this pathway covers the signals that set how fast and how far that mineralization proceeds. Its balance determines skeletal strength and enamel integrity, and its failure produces rickets and osteomalacia, osteopetrosis or osteoporosis, ectopic calcification of vessels and soft tissue, and enamel and dentin defects. BMP and TGF-beta ligands acting through their type I and II receptors and SMAD3, together with Wnt ligands, Notch effectors and transcription factors such as ATF4, SOX9 and TWIST1, drive osteoblast and chondrocyte differentiation. Superimposed on this is mineral chemistry: PTH, FGF23 with its coreceptor klotho, and vitamin D activation via CYP27B1 and the vitamin D receptor set systemic phosphate and calcium, while pyrophosphate handling by ENPP1 and ANKH, matrix Gla protein and osteopontin-like phosphoproteins, and enamel matrix proteins including amelogenin and enamelin act locally as promoters or inhibitors of crystal growth.

Cargo that has finished transiting the Golgi must be sorted and packaged for onward delivery, and vesicle budding at the trans-Golgi network is where that decision is made. It sends lysosomal hydrolases to the endolysosomal system, recycles receptors, and dispatches secretory and plasma membrane proteins along microtubules to the cell surface. Heterotetrameric adaptor complexes, chiefly AP-1 and its relatives AP-3 and AP-4, recognise sorting signals in transmembrane cargo such as the mannose-6-phosphate receptors and sortilin, recruit clathrin triskelia to curve the membrane, and hand off to dynamin and accessory factors for scission and uncoating, with ARF1 and GBF1 licensing coat assembly. Related machinery builds lysosome-related organelles including melanosomes and platelet granules, so defects here cause Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome, mislocalised hydrolases and lysosomal storage disease, and spastic paraplegia.

This grouping captures the secreted output of activated myeloid cells: inflammatory and counter-regulatory cytokines alongside basement membrane components and matrix-degrading enzymes. Macrophages and dendritic cells shape an inflammatory response not only by releasing IL6 and the Th17-promoting IL23A subunit but by restraining it, through IL10 and the receptor antagonist IL1RN that blocks IL-1 signalling without triggering it. At the same time they remodel the tissue they infiltrate, with MMP9 and MMP19 cleaving collagen and other matrix substrates to open routes for migration and to liberate matrix-bound signals, while laminin beta-3 and gamma-2 chains contribute the epithelial anchoring laminin-332 of the basement membrane being crossed. Vasoactive endothelin-1, the actin-severing protein gelsolin and stratifin place this activity at the interface of inflammation, wound healing and epithelial repair, biology that is co-opted in tumour invasion and chronic fibrosis.

Cardioblast proliferation is the expansion phase of heart development, in which cells already committed to a cardiac fate keep dividing rather than differentiating, so that the heart field contains enough precursors to build chambers, outflow tract and conduction tissue. Getting the size of this pool wrong leads to hypoplastic chambers and septal and outflow defects, and the same genes reappear in congenital heart syndromes. The programme couples cardiac transcription factors such as ISL1, TBX5 and HAND2, which specify and maintain precursor identity, to proliferative inputs from Wnt signalling through beta-catenin, from Notch and its target HES1, and from the EYA1-SIX1 pair, with the kinase PIM1 and a microRNA of the miR-17~92 family acting on survival and cell cycle output. Timing matters as much as amount: proliferation must be sustained and then relinquished for terminal cardiomyocyte differentiation to proceed.

When DNA damage is too extensive to repair, cells commit to death from within, and this regulatory arm pushes that decision forward by amplifying mitochondrial apoptotic signalling downstream of genotoxic stress. It matters because the threshold it sets decides whether a damaged cell is eliminated or survives with mutations, making it part of tumour suppression and a determinant of how tissues respond to radiation and chemotherapy. Several of the components act through p53: ribosomal proteins can enhance p53 translation and stability, a SUMO E3 ligase modifies p53 and other damage-response factors, and a checkpoint clamp subunit links lesion sensing to downstream effectors. Others act at the mitochondrion itself, where an outer-membrane protein promotes permeabilisation and cytochrome c release, or by relieving transcriptional repression that would otherwise blunt death signalling. Loss of such positive regulation favours survival of genomically unstable cells.

Naive CD4 T cells choose among effector fates after antigen encounter, and the control of T-helper cell differentiation sets how strongly and in which direction that choice is made. The balance determines whether an immune response clears intracellular pathogens, recruits antibody help, or restrains itself; skewing it produces autoimmunity, allergy, or failure to control infection. Cytokines and their receptors provide the instructive signals, with IL-12 and IL-23 family subunits and IL-27 acting through JAK3 and STAT5A, while co-stimulatory ligands on antigen-presenting cells and MHC class II molecules supply the context. Lineage-defining transcription factors read these inputs out: TBX21 for Th1, BCL6 for follicular helper, ZBTB7B for CD4 commitment, FOXP3 for regulatory cells, with IRF4, BATF and JUNB as shared partners. RNA-binding repressors such as ZC3H12A and the roquin proteins, together with SOCS5 and SMAD7, damp the programme once engaged.

Innate immune activation must be damped as well as triggered, and the negative regulation of innate immune response covers the brakes that keep antiviral and inflammatory signalling proportionate and self-limited. Without them, interferon and inflammasome output persists after a threat is cleared, producing interferonopathies, autoinflammation and tissue damage; excessive braking instead permits infection or tumour escape. The mechanisms are varied: deubiquitinases and ubiquitin-editing enzymes such as TNFAIP3, USP18 and TRIM21 dismantle activating signalling complexes; nucleic acid-handling enzymes including TREX1, ADAR and SAMHD1 limit the endogenous ligands that would otherwise engage cytosolic sensors; NLRC3, NLRX1 and NLRP4 restrain pattern-recognition and inflammasome pathways from within the cell. Inhibitory surface receptors and their ligands — TIGIT, HAVCR2, LILRB1, CEACAM1 and the HLA class I molecules read by NK cells — enforce self-tolerance, while phosphatases, complement regulators, TGFB1 and RNA-binding and microRNA factors tune the magnitude and duration of the response.

Mesangial cells sit between the capillary loops of the kidney glomerulus, providing structural support and controlling filtration surface area; their proliferation expands that population during glomerular development and, pathologically, in mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis and diabetic nephropathy, where it precedes matrix accumulation and sclerosis. The dominant mitogenic input here is platelet-derived growth factor: several PDGF ligands acting through PDGFRB drive mesangial cell expansion, a requirement evident in the failure of mesangial recruitment to the glomerulus when this axis is lost. Bone morphogenetic proteins and the nephron transcription factor WT1 supply developmental and restraining context, while IL6R signalling links inflammation to proliferative drive, EGR1 couples growth factor stimulation to immediate-early transcription, and CFLAR biases cells away from death receptor apoptosis. The balance of these signals determines whether glomerular injury resolves or progresses to chronic kidney disease.

Purine nucleoside phosphorylase normally strips the sugar from inosine, deoxyinosine, guanosine and deoxyguanosine, releasing hypoxanthine or guanine for salvage back into nucleotides and clearing the products of nucleic acid turnover. When the enzyme is defective, this phosphorolysis step fails and its substrates build up; deoxyguanosine is rephosphorylated to dGTP, which poisons ribonucleotide reductase and blocks DNA synthesis in dividing cells. T lymphocytes, with their high deoxynucleoside kinase activity and demanding proliferative programme, are the most vulnerable, so loss of activity produces a profound T cell deficiency with variable B cell involvement, recurrent infection, and in many patients neurological impairment and autoimmunity. The disorder sits alongside adenosine deaminase deficiency as an inborn error of purine catabolism causing combined immunodeficiency, and illustrates how a single salvage reaction supports lymphoid development.

Type I classical cadherins — E-, N-, P-, R- and M-cadherin — are calcium-dependent adhesion receptors whose homotypic trans-dimers hold epithelia and other tissues together, and their levels are controlled at nearly every step from transcription to degradation. This regulation matters because loss of E-cadherin releases cells from adherens junctions, licenses epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and invasion, and underlies hereditary diffuse gastric cancer. Transcriptional repressors including SNAI1/SNAI2, ZEB1/ZEB2 and TWIST recruit histone deacetylases, the LSD1 demethylase and Polycomb components to silence the CDH1 promoter, while microRNAs and the RNA-induced silencing machinery restrain the transcript. Newly made cadherin passes through signal peptidase, N-glycosylation and proprotein convertase processing before reaching the surface, where catenins (CTNNB1, CTNNA1, CTNND1, JUP) link it to actin and vinculin; Src- and CK2-dependent phosphorylation, ubiquitination and proteasomal or cathepsin-mediated turnover set junction stability.

Cells are bounded by lipid bilayers that solutes cannot cross unaided, and transmembrane transport is the collective machinery that moves ions, sugars, amino acids, nucleotides, metals, lipids, drugs and water across those barriers. It sets membrane potential and excitability, drives nutrient uptake and metabolite exchange between cytosol and organelles, maintains cellular pH, osmotic balance and ion gradients, and underlies epithelial secretion and reabsorption in kidney, gut and airway. The transporters here span the major families: ATP-driven pumps such as the Na+/K+-ATPase, sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pumps, V-type proton ATPases and ABC efflux carriers; secondary-active and facilitative carriers of the SLC groups, including mitochondrial carriers; aquaporin water channels; and gated channels for sodium, potassium, calcium and chloride, together with mitochondrial protein import and calcium uniporter components. Because so much physiology rests on these gradients, mutations in individual members cause cystic fibrosis, channelopathies of heart, muscle and brain, and renal tubulopathies.

Interferon gamma, released mainly by T cells and NK cells, converts responding cells into an antimicrobial and antigen-presenting state, and the genes it induces define that state. The response underlies clearance of intracellular bacteria, protozoa and viruses, drives tumour immune recognition, and when chronic contributes to autoimmunity, macrophage activation syndromes and immune checkpoint-mediated escape. Receptor engagement signals through JAK2 and STAT1 with IRF1 and IRF9 amplifying transcription, raising class I and class II MHC together with the peptide-loading machinery TAP1, TAPBP and the immunoproteasome subunits PSMB8 and PSMB9, and CIITA and NLRC5 as the transactivators that coordinate them. Downstream products include chemokines CXCL9, CXCL10 and CXCL11 that recruit lymphocytes, adhesion molecules, complement components, guanylate-binding proteins, IDO1-mediated tryptophan depletion, nucleic acid sensors, apoptotic effectors, and PD-L1 plus SOCS1 as brakes limiting the response.

ERK1 and ERK2, encoded by MAPK3 and MAPK1, are the terminal kinases of the classical mitogen-activated cascade, and MAPK1/MAPK3 signaling is how growth factors, cytokines and adhesion cues are converted into decisions to proliferate, differentiate, migrate or survive. Receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR, FGFRs, KIT, MET, PDGFRs and RET recruit GRB2/SHC adaptors and SOS or RASGRP exchange factors to load RAS with GTP; RAF kinases then activate MAP2K1/2, which phosphorylate ERK, with scaffolds (KSR1/2, SHOC2, CNKSR), prenylation and palmitoylation enzymes controlling membrane localisation. Output is restrained by RASA1 and neurofibromin as RAS GTPase-activating proteins, SPRED proteins, DUSP phosphatases, PP2A and proteasomal turnover. Cytokine receptor chains and JAK kinases feed in as parallel inputs, and synaptic scaffolds and NMDA receptor subunits couple the cascade to neuronal plasticity. Activating mutations in this route underlie many cancers and the developmental RASopathies.

Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans are the space-filling, water-binding components of cartilage and other extracellular matrices, and they also form the inhibitory scars that block axon regrowth after central nervous system injury. Their biosynthesis begins with xylose transfer to serine residues of a core protein by xylosyltransferases, extension of the tetrasaccharide linker by galactosyl- and glucuronyltransferases, and polymerisation of alternating glucuronic acid and N-acetylgalactosamine by the chondroitin synthase and polymerising-factor complexes. Sulfotransferases acting at the 4-O, 6-O and uronyl positions then generate the charge patterns that dictate growth-factor binding, while nucleotide-sugar supply and Golgi transporters for UDP-sugars and the sulfate donor PAPS set the ceiling on output. A phosphatase removes a transient xylose phosphate to license chain elongation. Loss of linker-region enzymes causes skeletal dysplasias and connective tissue fragility, including forms of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Once a cell has committed to die, the execution phase carries out the demolition that makes apoptosis recognisable: chromatin condenses, DNA is cut into fragments, the nucleus and other organelles break down, and the cell shrinks, blebs and detaches from its neighbours. Effector caspases 3, 6 and 7, activated downstream of initiator caspase 8, cleave a defined set of structural and regulatory substrates rather than degrading the proteome wholesale. Targets include the nuclear lamins and lamin-associated factors, cytoskeletal and membrane-anchoring proteins such as vimentin, plectin, spectrin, gelsolin and adducin, junctional components including desmosomal cadherins, plakophilin, occludin and tight-junction scaffolds, and the inhibitor of the DNA fragmentation nuclease, whose cleavage releases nuclease activity. ROCK1 and PAK2 cleavage drives membrane blebbing, while DNM1L participates in mitochondrial fragmentation. Orderly execution keeps dying cells packaged for phagocytosis, limiting inflammation during tissue turnover.

FLT3 is a receptor tyrosine kinase on haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells that, on binding its ligand FLT3LG, drives survival and expansion of early myeloid and lymphoid precursors and dendritic cell development; activating FLT3 mutations are among the most common lesions in acute myeloid leukaemia and a target of kinase inhibitor therapy. One arm of its output runs through SRC family kinases, with FYN, HCK and LCK, together with the related kinase SYK, recruited to the activated receptor. Their contribution is mixed rather than uniformly stimulatory: some promote downstream signalling read out as increased STAT5 activation and proliferation, while others feed into ubiquitin ligase recruitment that attenuates the receptor by degradation. The pathway therefore sets both the strength and the duration of FLT3 signalling in normal progenitors and in leukaemic blasts.

Cells facing amino acid deprivation, heme limitation, viral RNA, or protein misfolding in the ER converge on a single adaptive circuit: the integrated stress response. Its purpose is to buy time — global translation is throttled so that folding capacity and nutrient demand fall, while a small set of stress mRNAs is selectively translated to rebuild homeostasis. The core event is phosphorylation of the eIF2 alpha subunit by one of the eIF2 alpha kinases, here represented by HRI, PERK and GCN2, with GCN1 and IMPACT tuning the amino acid-sensing arm and the mitochondrial OMA1–DELE1 axis relaying organelle damage. Output is transcriptional: ATF4 and CHOP, together with CEBP, AP-1 and NFE2L family partners, drive recovery genes, and PPP1R15A/B feed back by promoting eIF2 alpha dephosphorylation. If stress persists, the same wiring commits the cell to death, linking this response to neurodegeneration, ER stress disease and tumour cell survival.

Membrane traffic and organelle remodelling form the common thread here: newly folded cargo leaves the endoplasmic reticulum in COPII-coated vesicles built from SEC23A and SEC24B, is delivered through early endosomes marked by the tethering factor EEA1, and reaches the plasma membrane by SNARE-directed fusion, with STXBP3 acting among the Sec1/Munc18-family regulators of that step. Lipid composition and cytoskeletal geometry are managed alongside cargo flow: the inositol phosphatase SYNJ1 dephosphorylates PI(4,5)P2 to uncoat vesicles after endocytosis, TMEM30A serves as the accessory subunit that allows P4-ATPase flippases to translocate aminophospholipids across bilayers, and the microtubule-severing ATPase SPAST shapes tubules and axonal microtubule arrays. Additional members touch nuclear pore transport, transcriptional control by RB1, and ADAM9-mediated ectodomain shedding, linking secretory and endocytic capacity to cell surface signalling, neuronal maintenance and proliferation control.

Lateral mesoderm development traces the fate of the most lateral band of mesoderm emerging from the gastrulating embryo, the tissue that gives rise to the heart and blood vessels, the body wall and limb bud connective tissue, and the splanchnic layer that surrounds the gut. Its progression depends on Nodal signalling through SMAD2 and the FOXH1 transcriptional partner, BMP reception via BMPR1A, FGF input, and Hedgehog signalling through SMO, with DAND5 acting as an antagonist that biases left-right asymmetry. MESP1 marks the earliest cardiovascular progenitors leaving the primitive streak, while FOXF1, TBX20, TEAD2 and the YAP1 coactivator sustain splanchnic and cardiac identity downstream. Disruption of these steps produces congenital heart malformations, laterality defects, and diaphragmatic or body wall closure anomalies, linking early patterning decisions to the structural integrity of the trunk.

ATP biosynthesis is how cells convert nutrient-derived reducing equivalents and glycolytic intermediates into the nucleotide that powers essentially all energy-requiring work, from ion pumping to biosynthesis to motility. Most of the genes here build the mitochondrial machinery: the many NDUFA/NDUFB/NDUFS subunits and mitochondrially encoded ND proteins of complex I, the four succinate dehydrogenase subunits, and the full F1Fo ATP synthase with its catalytic ATP5F1 head, c-ring and peripheral stalk, which uses the proton-motive force to phosphorylate ADP. Glycolytic contributors such as aldolase A, enolase 1 and lactate dehydrogenase provide substrate-level phosphorylation. Regulation and quality control are represented too, including the ATP synthase inhibitory factor, assembly factors, cardiolipin remodelling by tafazzin, and PINK1/parkin-dependent removal of damaged mitochondria. Loss of these components causes mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, Leigh syndrome, paraganglioma and parkinsonism, and limits the energy supply of neurons and muscle first.

Hedgehog signalling converts a secreted morphogen gradient into patterned gene expression, and it is what tells cells in the limb bud, neural tube and developing skeleton which position they occupy; in adults it maintains stem and progenitor compartments. Loss of output causes birth defects such as holoprosencephaly and polydactyly, while inappropriate reactivation drives basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma. Ligands SHH, IHH and DHH are lipid-modified and released, then bind the receptor PTCH1, relieving its inhibition of Smoothened. Signalling is organised at the primary cilium, so intraflagellar transport components, the anterograde kinesin motor, retrograde dynein and tubulins are integral rather than incidental. In the off state, GPR161 raises cAMP and protein kinase A, GSK3 and casein kinase 1 prime GLI proteins for processing by the ubiquitin-proteasome system into repressors; SUFU sequesters them. Activation preserves full-length GLI activators, with SPOP, ITCH and SMURF ligases tuning the response.

Gut endocrine cells sense a meal and release hormones that amplify insulin secretion before blood glucose has fully risen, and incretin synthesis, secretion and inactivation covers that whole life cycle. Proglucagon in intestinal L cells and GIP in K cells are made as precursors, cleaved by the signal peptidase complex and by the prohormone convertase PCSK1 to yield active GLP-1 and GIP; transcription factors including CDX2, PAX6, ISL1, GATA4 and TCF7L2, with beta-catenin, specify these cells and drive hormone gene expression. Secretion is triggered by nutrients acting through long- and medium-chain fatty acid receptors FFAR1 and FFAR4, the lipid sensor GPR119, taste-type G protein subunits, and by gastrin-releasing peptide and leptin. Circulating incretins are then truncated within minutes by dipeptidyl peptidase IV, the reason DPP4 inhibitors lower glucose in type 2 diabetes.

Connective tissue owes its tensile strength and elasticity to a collagen-rich extracellular matrix, and these genes cover its construction, decoration and controlled turnover. Fibrillar and network collagens of several classes are represented, including basement membrane COL4A1, the fibril-associated COL12A1 and COL14A1, and cartilage COL10A1 and COL11A1, alongside the crosslinking peroxidase PXDN and elastic-fibre and microfibril components such as EMILIN1, MFAP2/4/5 and fibulin-family EFEMP1 and EFEMP2. Small leucine-rich proteoglycans including decorin, osteomodulin and podocan bind collagen fibrils and set their diameter and spacing, while TIMP1 and TIMP3 restrain metalloproteinases and ADAMTS enzymes process procollagen and proteoglycans. CTGF and TGFB1I1 tie the programme to TGF-beta-driven fibrogenesis, and tenascin C marks remodelling matrix. Sustained activation of this output underlies fibrosis, scarring and tumour stroma; loss-of-function affects skeletal, vascular and corneal integrity.

Columnar and cuboidal epithelia line the gut, airway, kidney tubules and glands, and a newly specified cell of this shape must still acquire the transporters, junctions and secretory apparatus that make the sheet functional. This maturation step is distinct from the morphogenetic change that gives the cell its column or cube shape; it is the final differentiation that confers barrier and absorptive competence, and when it fails the epithelium remains immature, leaky or poorly polarised. The genes here act at several levels: a homeobox transcription factor patterns regional epithelial identity, a hypoxia-responsive transcription factor couples differentiation to local oxygen tension, TGFB1 supplies the paracrine cue that drives epithelial maturation and restrains proliferation, and TMIGD1 is an adhesion molecule of the intestinal and renal brush border. Lipid acyltransferase activity contributes membrane and lipid-droplet remodelling to the mature phenotype.

Commitment to DNA replication is decided in late G1, when E2F transcription factors switch on the genes a cell needs to copy its genome. G1/S-specific transcription is what makes that switch: E2F1 with its DP partners activates origin licensing factors such as ORC1, CDC6, CDT1 and CDC45, the replisome components PCNA and the DNA polymerase alpha catalytic subunit, nucleotide-supply enzymes including RRM2, TYMS, DHFR and thymidine kinase, and the cyclins and CDC25A that drive the transition forward. Restraint comes from retinoblastoma-family proteins RBL1 and RBL2, repressive E2Fs, and the DREAM complex with its LIN components, histone deacetylase and RBBP4, which silence these promoters in quiescence. Loss of this restraint gives unscheduled proliferation and is a common route into cancer.

Newly made lysosomal enzymes are not secreted; they are diverted at the trans-Golgi network into clathrin-coated carriers that deliver them to the endosomal-lysosomal system, and lysosome vesicle biogenesis is that diversion step. Without it, acid hydrolases escape into the extracellular space and the lysosome cannot degrade the macromolecules it receives, a failure mode shared with lysosomal storage disease. Cargo bearing mannose 6-phosphate is captured by its receptor, which recruits the AP-1 adaptor complex and clathrin triskelia; ARF1 licenses coat assembly on the membrane, dynamin and endophilin contribute to scission, and uncoating chaperones recycle the machinery. SNAREs including VAMP7 and VAMP8 then fuse the carriers with their target compartment. An AP-4 adaptor arm handles a distinct set of trans-Golgi cargoes, and mutations in its subunits cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, linking this sorting route to neuronal maintenance.

Chromosome organization covers everything cells do to build, shape, arrange and take apart chromosomes, from covalent histone marks to the large-scale geometry of centromeres, telomeres and chromosome arms. It is what allows a genome to be replicated once, segregated accurately, recombined in meiosis and repaired without loss of sequence; its failure produces aneuploidy, chromosome fusions, telomere attrition and the genome instability typical of cancer and progeroid syndromes. The members span core histones and chromatin remodellers such as the SWI/SNF and INO80 complexes, cohesin and condensin rings with their loaders and releasing factors, kinetochore and spindle-checkpoint machinery, topoisomerases, the telomerase holoenzyme with shelterin and CST, double-strand break repair and crossover factors, and the synaptonemal complex proteins that pair homologues during gametogenesis. Together these define chromatin state, sister chromatid cohesion, chromosome end protection and faithful inheritance.

Transmission across chemical synapses is how one neuron passes information to another neuron, a muscle fibre or a gland cell, and it is the basis of all fast neural computation, movement and memory. An arriving action potential opens presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, and the calcium rise drives SNARE-mediated fusion of neurotransmitter-filled vesicles with the terminal membrane, using SNAP25, VAMP2, syntaxin, synaptotagmin and their priming partners. Vesicular and plasma-membrane transporters load and then reclaim glutamate, GABA, glycine, acetylcholine, dopamine and serotonin, while acetylcholinesterase and monoamine oxidase terminate signalling enzymatically. On the postsynaptic side, ionotropic AMPA, NMDA, kainate, GABA-A, glycine and nicotinic receptors change membrane potential directly, whereas metabotropic receptors act through G proteins, adenylate cyclases, phospholipase C and inwardly rectifying potassium channels; scaffolds such as DLG4 and kinases including CAMK2A tune receptor number and underlie synaptic plasticity. Disruption produces epilepsy, myasthenia and neuropsychiatric disease.

Alpha-dystroglycan links muscle and nerve cells to their basement membrane, but only if it carries matriglycan, a long linear glucuronic acid-xylose polysaccharide built on threonines in its mucin-like domain. This sugar is the actual laminin-binding element of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex, so its loss uncouples the cytoskeleton from the extracellular matrix and produces the alpha-dystroglycanopathies " congenital and limb-girdle muscular dystrophies that in severe forms add brain malformations, seizures and eye defects. It is also the entry receptor exploited by Lassa and other arenaviruses. Construction proceeds stepwise through a Core M3 trisaccharide, addition of two ribitol-phosphate units by CRPPA, FKTN and FKRP, a xylose-glucuronate primer laid down by RXYLT1 and B4GAT1, and finally chain elongation by the bifunctional glycosyltransferases LARGE1 and LARGE2, with nucleotide-sugar transporters supplying the Golgi lumen.

Fatty acids are both a fuel and a building block, and this programme covers the enzymes that activate, break down, and synthesise them together with the mitochondrial machinery that finishes the job. Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases and the CD36 transporter feed fatty acids into carnitine-dependent mitochondrial import via CPT1A and CPT2, after which acyl-CoA dehydrogenases of differing chain-length specificity and the hydratase-dehydrogenase-thiolase steps of beta-oxidation yield acetyl-CoA for the citric acid cycle and, in liver, ketone bodies through HMGCS2 and HMGCL. Counterbalancing routes include FASN-driven lipogenesis, peroxisomal oxidation of very long and branched chains, and lipolysis by monoacylglycerol lipase, with PPARA coordinating the transcriptional response to fasting. The set matters for energy supply to heart and muscle during fasting, and defects in the dehydrogenases or carnitine transport cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and metabolic crisis.

Natural killer cells kill virally infected and transformed cells without prior sensitization, and this is the biology that raises the threshold-crossing signals that license them to do so. Enhancing NK-mediated immunity matters for tumour surveillance, control of herpesvirus infection, and the maternal-fetal interface, where NK recognition of HLA-C, HLA-E and HLA-G shapes trophoblast tolerance. Activating receptors such as NKG2D (KLRK1) paired with CD94/KLRD1, the nectin-binding receptors CD226 and CRTAM, and the SLAM-family adaptors SH2D1A and SH2D1B feed into VAV1 and RASGRP-dependent signalling that triggers cytotoxic granule release, with LAMP1 marking the degranulating lytic compartment. Cytokines add a second tier: IL-12 subunits, IL-18 receptor accessory signalling and IL-21 drive STAT5-dependent proliferation and interferon-gamma output. Stress-induced ULBP/RAET1 ligands on damaged cells supply the target-side cues that make this activation tumour-selective.

Protein secretion is the route by which newly made proteins move from the endoplasmic reticulum through the Golgi to the cell surface or to lysosomes, and by which cells release hormones, enzymes, matrix components and signalling molecules. Without it, cells cannot present receptors, remodel their environment, or deliver hydrolases to degradative compartments, and secretory capacity limits specialised cells such as pancreatic and immune secretory cells. The machinery here spans each step: COPI and COPII coat subunits and cargo receptors for ER exit and retrieval, ARF GTPases and their activators for Golgi traffic, clathrin and adaptor complexes for budding, Rab GTPases for compartment identity, and SNARE proteins with their SNAP fusion factors for membrane fusion. Mannose-6-phosphate receptors sort lysosomal enzymes, while ESCRT components link the pathway to endosomal sorting and extracellular vesicle release. Defects produce lysosomal storage and congenital trafficking disorders.

Tissue repair has to be limited as well as initiated, and this collection covers the braking processes that damp the rate and extent of wound healing after injury. Restraint matters because unchecked repair gives fibrosis, hypertrophic scarring and excessive clot, while too much braking leaves bleeding and chronic non-healing ulcers. Much of the content is haemostatic counter-regulation: anticoagulant and fibrinolytic control through protein C, thrombomodulin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor and plasminogen with its activators, opposed by serpin inhibitors such as SERPINE1 and SERPINF2, alongside contact-system and fibrinogen chain components that set clot formation and dissolution. Other members restrain the cellular phase — platelet activation via GP1BA and PF4, endothelial nitric oxide and endothelin tone, PDGF and FGF2 signalling to migrating fibroblasts, TGF-beta/SMAD3 output, PTEN, and microRNAs including MIR34A and MIR200B that limit proliferative and matrix responses.

Triglyceride catabolism releases fatty acids from stored or circulating triesters of glycerol, supplying fuel for oxidation and substrate for membrane and signalling lipids. It operates in two arenas. In the gut and bloodstream, pancreatic lipases digest dietary fat while lipoprotein lipase, anchored to capillary endothelium by GPIHBP1 and modulated by apolipoproteins such as APOC2 (an activator) and APOC3 (an inhibitor), hydrolyses triglyceride carried in chylomicrons and VLDL; hepatic and endothelial lipases act on remnant particles. Inside adipocytes, sequential action of ATGL (PNPLA2) with its coactivator ABHD5, hormone-sensitive lipase, and monoacylglycerol lipase strips the glycerol backbone, controlled by PKA phosphorylation of perilipin at the lipid droplet surface. Loss of function produces severe hypertriglyceridaemia and pancreatitis, while impaired droplet lipolysis causes neutral lipid storage disease; the same reactions set fatty acid supply during fasting and exercise.

Wnt signalling instructs cell fate, stem cell maintenance and axis patterning during development and renews epithelia such as the intestinal crypt in adults, so its output must be held within narrow limits; the regulators collected here set how strongly and how long the pathway fires. They act at every tier: secretion and diffusion of Wnt ligands, extracellular decoys and antagonists such as the SFRPs, DKKs, WIF1 and sclerostin, receptor availability controlled by RSPO ligands acting through LGR4/5/6 against the ubiquitin ligases RNF43 and ZNRF3, and the destruction complex of APC, AXIN1/2, CK1 and GSK3 that phosphorylates beta-catenin for degradation. Tankyrases, deubiquitinases, phosphatases and TLE/Groucho corepressors tune signal strength and TCF/LEF-dependent transcription further, while PRICKLE1, VANGL2 and PTK7 feed the planar cell polarity arm. Loss of this restraint drives colorectal and other cancers; excess inhibition impairs bone mass and limb and kidney development.

Connective tissue fibroblasts build and maintain the collagen-rich scaffold that gives organs their mechanical form, and this group of extracellular matrix and matrix-associated proteins marks that stromal programme. Secreted structural and regulatory components dominate: lumican and fibulin-1 bind collagen and elastic fibre networks, procollagen C-endopeptidase enhancer promotes collagen maturation, and SFRP4 tunes Wnt signalling in the surrounding tissue. Alongside them sit mesenchymal identity factors such as TWIST1 and PRRX1, the PDGF receptor alpha that drives fibroblast proliferation and migration, and caldesmon, linking matrix output to actomyosin contractility. Together these activities govern wound healing, tissue stiffness and organ morphogenesis; sustained activation underlies fibrosis and the desmoplastic stroma of tumours, where such signatures mark cancer-associated fibroblasts and predict invasive behaviour.

When unfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, the kinase PERK is released from the chaperone BiP, dimerizes and phosphorylates the translation initiation factor eIF2alpha on Ser52, shutting down most cap-dependent translation while permitting selective expression of stress-response genes. This arm of the unfolded protein response lowers the load of newly synthesized protein entering the ER, depletes short-lived proteins such as Cyclin D1 to stall the cell cycle in G1, and drives a transcriptional programme through ATF4 together with CHOP (DDIT3), ATF3 and C/EBP and NF-Y factors, inducing chaperones, amino acid supply enzymes such as asparagine synthetase, and inflammatory mediators. Prolonged signalling tips the outcome from adaptation toward apoptosis. mRNA decay machinery, including deadenylases and the exosome complex, shapes the resulting transcript levels. Loss of PERK function in humans causes Wolcott-Rallison syndrome with infantile diabetes, reflecting the demands of secretory cells.

This is the step that lets a death receptor signal reach the mitochondrion. When Fas or TNF-family receptors engage, caspase-8 in the receptor complex cleaves the BH3-only protein BID, and the resulting truncated fragment is N-myristoylated by N-myristoyltransferase and targeted to the outer mitochondrial membrane. There it promotes BAX and BAK oligomerization and neutralizes anti-apoptotic BCL-2 relatives, so cytochrome c release and apoptosome-driven caspase activation amplify a signal that began at the cell surface. Granzyme B delivered by cytotoxic lymphocytes cleaves BID at a distinct site, giving killer cells the same route into the mitochondrial death machinery. The pathway therefore couples the extrinsic and intrinsic arms of apoptosis, and matters most in cells whose receptor-initiated caspase activity is too weak to kill without mitochondrial amplification, such as hepatocytes during immune-mediated liver injury.

Cells spend and remake their ATP continuously, and this pathway covers the reactions that generate and consume it, together with the regulators that match supply to demand. Two routes dominate: glycolysis, from hexokinases and phosphofructokinases through aldolase, GAPDH, enolase and pyruvate kinase, and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, represented here by the complex I subunits, succinate dehydrogenase, and the F1Fo ATP synthase with its inhibitory factor. Adenylate kinases interconvert adenine nucleotides to buffer the energy charge, while AMP-activated protein kinase and mTOR complex components sense it and reset anabolic and catabolic programmes, and HIF1A shifts flux toward glycolysis in hypoxia. Also included are ATP-consuming ion pumps, insulin and insulin-receptor signalling that drives glucose uptake, and mitochondrial quality control through PINK1 and parkin. Defects here cause mitochondrial myopathies, glycolytic enzymopathies with haemolysis, and the metabolic rewiring typical of tumours.

Touch, hearing, balance and mechanical pain all begin with a cell converting force into an electrical signal, and this is the transduction step of that sensory perception. Hair cells of the inner ear and mechanoreceptive and nociceptive neurons of the dorsal root ganglia depend on it; when it fails the result is deafness, vestibular dysfunction, loss of discriminative touch, or altered pain thresholds. Force-gated channels sit at the centre: PIEZO2 in light-touch and proprioceptive endings, TMC1 and TMC2 with the accessory subunits LHFPL5 and the tip-link and stereocilia proteins whorlin, stereocilin, PTPRQ and the very large adhesion GPCR ADGRV1 in cochlear hair bundles, alongside acid-sensing channels and TRPA1 in irritant and mechanical nociception. Voltage-gated sodium channels including SCN9A and SCN11A and potassium channels such as KCNQ1 and KCNK2 then shape the resulting receptor potential into propagated firing, with neurotrophin and transcriptional regulators supporting the sensory cells themselves.

Cells change shape, crawl, divide and hold their junctions by continuously rebuilding actin filaments and microtubules, and this pathway covers the control layer that decides when and where those polymers are assembled, bundled or taken apart. It underpins cell migration, neurite and dendritic spine growth, spindle assembly and cytokinesis, epithelial and endothelial barrier integrity, and muscle sarcomere organization; its failure contributes to tumour invasion, immunodeficiency and neurodevelopmental disease. Rho-family GTPases with their many exchange factors and GAPs relay signals from growth factor receptors, integrins and chemokine receptors to effectors such as ROCK, PAK and LIMK, which in turn control cofilin severing, profilin- and formin-driven elongation, Arp2/3 branching via WAVE and WASP complexes, and capping by CapZ and tropomodulins. In parallel, plus-end tracking proteins, stathmins, katanin, CAMSAPs and augmin-dependent nucleation tune microtubule dynamics and centrosome behaviour.

Mesenchymal to epithelial transition is the reverse of the better-known epithelial exit: a loose, migratory mesenchymal cell acquires apical-basolateral polarity, builds adherens and desmosomal junctions, deposits basement membrane and becomes a stable epithelium. It is how tubules and organ parenchyma are built during development, and how some injured tissues re-epithelialize; its inappropriate reactivation contributes to metastatic colonization at distant sites. The genes here point strongly at nephron formation, where Wnt9b and Wnt4 signalling from the ureteric bud and stroma, transduced through Frizzled receptors and beta-catenin, converts Six2/Cited1-positive cap mesenchyme into renal vesicles. Transcriptional regulators including WT1, PAX2, PAX8, SALL1 and GATA3 impose epithelial identity, while GDNF, LIF and the BMP antagonist GREM1 tune the inductive dialogue. Loss of these inputs truncates branching and nephron endowment, producing renal hypodysplasia.

Vitamins A, D, E and K cannot be absorbed or moved through the blood without lipid carriers, and the metabolism of fat-soluble vitamins covers both their uptake from the diet and their conversion into usable forms. Dietary carotenoids are cleaved by BCO1 and BCO2 to retinal, which is reduced and esterified by LRAT for storage, while retinol-binding proteins and transthyretin carry retinol to target tissues. Vitamin K quinone is prenylated by UBIAD1 and recycled by the VKORC1 reductases that regenerate the cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors, the step blocked by warfarin. Absorption depends on pancreatic lipase and colipase, chylomicron apolipoproteins, lipoprotein lipase tethered by GPIHBP1, and LDL-receptor-family and proteoglycan receptors for particle clearance. TTPA selects alpha-tocopherol for export; its loss causes vitamin E deficiency with ataxia, and retinoid failure impairs vision and epithelial maintenance.

Vitamins are dietary organic compounds that human cells cannot make in sufficient amounts, and this branch of metabolism converts them into the active cofactors that intermediary metabolism depends on, then regenerates those cofactors as they are consumed. It underlies energy production, one-carbon and amino acid metabolism, vision, bone formation and blood coagulation, and its failure produces deficiency diseases from megaloblastic anaemia to methylmalonic acidaemia and bleeding disorders. Uptake and delivery come first: dedicated transporters and carriers move folate, thiamine, riboflavin, biotin, pantothenate and ascorbate across membranes, while intrinsic factor, cubilin-amnionless and transcobalamins route cobalamin to intracellular processing. Kinases and synthetases then build the working forms tgeneratethiamine pyrophosphate, FAD, NAD, coenzyme A, pyridoxal phosphate, tetrahydrofolate and its one-carbon derivatives, adenosyl- and methylcobalamin, molybdopterin, and reduced vitamin K for gamma-carboxylation. Retinoid and lipoprotein-associated handling covers the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.

Inflammation must be bounded, and this is the braking side of leukocyte trafficking: processes that stop or damp the recruitment, chemotaxis and tissue entry of neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes. Without such restraint, inflammatory infiltrates persist and drive tissue damage in arthritis, atherosclerosis, colitis and sepsis; the same brakes are exploited to keep tumour-infiltrating cells in check. Mechanisms are varied. Inhibitory surface receptors such as CD200R1 and CD300A raise the threshold for myeloid activation, SLIT2 acts as a repellent that counters chemokine-driven movement, and RIPOR2 restrains integrin-dependent adhesion and polarity. Anti-inflammatory mediators including HMOX1, DUSP1, TNFAIP6 and adenosine signalling through ADA and ADORA1 suppress the chemotactic response, while microRNAs such as MIR146A and MIR223 lower the output of inflammatory signalling. Several chemokines appear because receptor desensitisation and competing gradients can retain or divert cells rather than attract them.

Cells cannot synthesise all of the amino acids they need, so they rely on carrier proteins that bring them in across the plasma membrane into the cytosol. This import supplies substrates for protein synthesis, neurotransmitter and glutathione production, nitrogen handling and mTOR-dependent growth signalling, and it sets how much dietary protein the intestine and kidney actually recover. Most of the work is done by solute carrier families with distinct selectivities and driving forces: sodium-dependent glutamate and aspartate transporters such as SLC1A2 and SLC1A3 clear synaptic glutamate in astrocytes, neutral amino acid and glutamine carriers of the SLC38 group feed metabolism, heterodimeric exchangers pair a light chain with the SLC3A2 heavy chain, and SLC7A11 imports cystine to support antioxidant defence. Accessory and regulatory proteins, including ACE2 and its homologue CLTRN, control surface delivery of intestinal and renal transporters; loss of individual carriers causes aminoacidurias, Hartnup disorder and neurological disease.

When a naive CD4+ T cell meets antigen on a dendritic cell in the presence of the right cytokines, it can commit to the T helper 2 fate, the arm of adaptive immunity that defends against helminths and drives allergic inflammation, asthma and IgE class switching. IL2-driven STAT5 dimers open the IL4 locus and induce IL4R, and IL4 signalling then generates STAT6 dimers that switch on GATA3, the master regulator whose expression is reinforced by NFATC2 downstream of the T cell receptor and by Notch receptors acting through RBPJ and Mastermind-like coactivators. Commitment is largely a chromatin problem: GATA3 and STAT6 act at a locus control region within the RAD50 gene beside the clustered IL4, IL5 and IL13 genes, recruiting histone acetyltransferases such as CREBBP/EP300 and MLL-type methyltransferase complexes while HDAC, NuRD, NCoR and Polycomb complexes restrain the alternative programmes.

Ghrelin is the hunger hormone: released mainly by gastric X/A-like cells, it rises with fasting, peaks before a meal, and acts on the growth hormone secretagogue receptor in hypothalamus and pituitary to stimulate appetite and growth hormone release, linking gut nutrient status to energy balance and somatic growth. Its maturation is unusual among peptide hormones. Preproghrelin enters the secretory pathway through signal peptidase cleavage, and the acyltransferase MBOAT4 attaches an octanoyl or decanoyl group to serine-3, a modification without which the peptide cannot activate its receptor. Prohormone convertase 1/3 then releases mature acyl ghrelin and C-ghrelin. Secretion is restrained by insulin, leptin, glucagon and glucose and promoted by IGF1, while circulating butyrylcholinesterase and platelet-activating factor acetylhydrolase strip the acyl chain to give des-acyl ghrelin, terminating receptor signalling. This axis is of interest in obesity, cachexia and metabolic disease.

Excitable cells encode information in how quickly and how far their membrane potential swings positive, and this pathway covers the processes that tune that depolarization rather than simply carrying it. Control of the rate, frequency and extent of depolarization sets heart rate, conduction velocity and neuronal firing patterns, and its derangement produces arrhythmia and seizure susceptibility. Much of the gene content converges on the cardiac sodium channel and its auxiliary beta subunits, together with trafficking and scaffolding partners such as ankyrin-G, NEDD4L, SLMAP and RANGRF that determine how much channel reaches the sarcolemma. Hyperpolarization-activated HCN channels supply the pacemaker current that drives spontaneous depolarization in sinoatrial and neuronal cells, while a T-type calcium channel, TRPM4, a chloride channel, gap junction connexin and P2RX7 shape the threshold and shift the membrane in the depolarizing direction. Transcriptional and kinase inputs, including TBX5, CREB1, CAMK2D and SRC, adjust this machinery over longer timescales.
