Immune responses have to be dialled down as well as switched on, and this pathway collects the brakes that limit how much antibody, cytokine and other soluble mediator gets made. It keeps humoral and inflammatory output proportionate to the threat, and its failure underlies autoantibody production, allergy and chronic inflammatory disease. Inhibitory surface receptors carrying ITIM motifs, including the B cell coreceptor CD22, the low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR2B and several leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptors, raise the threshold for lymphocyte activation and curb immunoglobulin secretion. Suppressive cytokines of the TGF-beta family and IL10 act on responding cells, with SMAD7 feeding back on TGF-beta signalling, while FOXP3 specifies the regulatory T cells that deliver much of this restraint. Intracellular negative regulators such as IRAK3 damp Toll-like receptor-driven cytokine production, and BCL6 and TBX21 shape which mediators a differentiating lymphocyte will make.

Cell-cell adhesion covers the molecular attachments by which one cell binds another, holding tissues together and letting cells recognise their neighbours. It underlies epithelial sheet integrity, endothelial barrier function, synapse formation, and the transient contacts immune cells make when a lymphocyte scans an antigen-presenting cell. The machinery falls into recognisable families: classical and non-classical cadherins with their catenin and plakophilin adaptors at adherens junctions and desmosomes, claudins and junctional adhesion molecules with ZO scaffolds at tight junctions, clustered protocadherins and neurexin-neuroligin pairs giving neurons individual identity, and immunoglobulin-superfamily receptors, selectins, integrins and their ligands such as ICAM1, VCAM1 and nectins mediating leukocyte arrest and costimulation. Adhesive engagement is coupled through actin, talin, vinculin and Src-family kinases to signalling that tunes proliferation, polarity and migration. Loss of these contacts drives epithelial dedifferentiation, invasion, blistering skin disease and barrier failure.

Platelet homeostasis is the resting state that keeps circulating platelets quiescent until vessel injury demands otherwise, and its loss tips the balance toward thrombosis or, in the other direction, bleeding. Healthy endothelium releases prostacyclin and nitric oxide, which act on platelets through the prostacyclin receptor and soluble guanylate cyclase to raise cyclic nucleotides; protein kinase G and its substrate IRAG then suppress inositol trisphosphate receptor-mediated calcium release, while phosphodiesterases set the duration of the signal. Much of the remaining machinery governs cytosolic calcium itself: SERCA and plasma membrane calcium pumps and sodium-calcium exchangers remove it, STIM1 with ORAI channels and TRPC and P2X purinergic channels admit it. Calcium-activated potassium channels, PECAM1, and phosphatases including SHP-1 and PP2A add inhibitory tone, linking endothelial vasodilator signalling to platelet activation thresholds and vascular smooth muscle relaxation.

Chromosome ends resemble double-strand breaks, and the cell must stop its repair machinery from ligating them together. Protection from non-homologous end joining at telomeres is what keeps this from happening: without it, telomere fusions generate dicentric chromosomes, which break during mitosis and drive the translocations, aneuploidy and genome rearrangements characteristic of crisis and early tumorigenesis. Shelterin components TERF2 and its partner TERF2IP bind duplex telomeric repeats and suppress ligase-mediated end joining while also repressing an ATM-dependent damage response at the end; ACD (TPP1) contributes through the single-strand binding arm of the same complex. Associated nucleases handle the G-overhang and any intermediates generated during replication of the end, with DCLRE1B (Apollo) and the ERCC1-ERCC4 structure-specific endonuclease processing telomeric ends so they remain capped rather than repaired. The pathway therefore sits at the interface of telomere maintenance and double-strand break repair choice.

Kidney epithelium development covers the formation and maturation of the tubular and glomerular epithelia that ultimately filter blood and reabsorb solutes. It begins with reciprocal signalling between the ureteric bud and metanephric mesenchyme: GDNF acting through RET drives branching, while WNT9B and WNT4 induce mesenchymal cells held in the progenitor state by SIX2 and CITED1 to undergo mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition and form nephrons. BMP, Hedgehog, Notch and FGF inputs pattern proximal-distal segment identity, with transcription factors such as PAX2, PAX8, WT1, HNF1B, LHX1 and SALL1 specifying podocyte, proximal tubule and loop-of-Henle fates. Maturation brings in the terminal machinery of function — slit-diaphragm proteins NPHS1 and NPHS2 with CD2AP, aquaporin water channels, organic anion transporters and uromodulin. Disruption produces renal agenesis, hypodysplasia, cystic disease and congenital nephrotic syndrome, and limits nephron endowment for life.

Thymocytes bearing an alpha-beta T cell receptor must be pushed through lineage commitment and, once mature, directed toward particular helper or regulatory fates; this set collects the signals and factors that promote that differentiation. It underwrites adaptive cellular immunity, and its loss produces immunodeficiency — mutations in ADA or the shared cytokine receptor chain IL2RG block T cell development outright, while defective FOXP3 removes the regulatory subset and causes systemic autoimmunity. Antigen receptor signalling through ZAP70 and SYK is coupled to NF-kB activation via MALT1, and lineage decisions are enforced by transcriptional regulators including RUNX1, RUNX3, CBFB, ZBTB7B and ZBTB16 together with the acetyltransferase EP300. Antigen-presenting surfaces (MHC class II, CD80, CD86, CD83) and polarising cytokines such as IL-12, IL-18 and IL-23 supply the extrinsic instruction, with SOCS1 and TGF-beta receptor signalling setting limits on the response.

KIT is a receptor tyrosine kinase whose activating mutations, typically in the juxtamembrane region, drive gastrointestinal stromal tumours and contribute to melanoma and acute myeloid leukaemia by locking the receptor into ligand-independent growth signalling. Such tumours initially respond well to imatinib, the first tyrosine kinase inhibitor approved for cancer, and this dependence on a single oncogenic kinase is what makes targeted therapy work. Resistance is the recurring clinical problem described here: most patients relapse as secondary mutations arise in the ATP-binding pocket or the kinase activation loop, sterically or energetically blocking drug binding or favouring the active kinase conformation that the inhibitor cannot engage. The result is restored downstream proliferative and survival signalling despite continued treatment, motivating second- and third-line inhibitors chosen according to which resistance mutation a tumour has acquired.

Neutrophils are the first leukocytes to arrive at infected or damaged tissue, and their recruitment depends on a panel of chemoattractant receptors that read the chemical signature of injury and convert it into directed migration. Most of the members are G protein-coupled receptors tuned to distinct cues: complement C5a, bacterial and mitochondrial formylated peptides, short-chain fatty acids from microbial fermentation, platelet-activating factor, IL-8, thrombin-derived protease signals, and the chemokine PROK2, with a G protein gamma subunit representing the shared heterotrimeric transduction step. Receptor engagement drives actin remodelling and chemotaxis up the gradient, together with adhesion, degranulation and the oxidative burst once the cell arrives. Insufficient recruitment leaves bacterial and fungal infection unchecked; excessive or poorly resolved recruitment underlies tissue damage in sepsis, acute lung injury, gout and chronic inflammatory disease, making these receptors long-standing anti-inflammatory drug targets.

Immune effector processes are the business end of immunity — cytokine secretion, antibody production, complement-mediated lysis, cytotoxic killing, degranulation and phagocytosis — and this pathway covers the machinery that sets how strongly and how long they run. Tuning matters in both directions: too little permits infection and tumour escape, too much drives autoimmunity, allergy and cytokine-driven tissue damage. The genes span activating and inhibitory receptor pairs on lymphocytes and myeloid cells, including checkpoint receptors such as PDCD1, HAVCR2, LAG3 and TIGIT with their ligands, NK receptors of the KLR family and their stress-induced MHC-like ligands, and Fc and complement receptors. Soluble regulators include interleukins, interferons and TGF-beta family members, plus complement components and the factors that restrain their activation. Lineage transcription factors such as FOXP3, TBX21, GATA3 and BCL6 fix the effector programme a cell adopts, while kinases, adaptors and phosphatases like SYK, BTK, PTPN6 and INPP5D set signalling thresholds, and vesicle-trafficking components govern granule release.

Apoptosis is the orderly self-destruction of cells that lets tissues remove damaged, infected or surplus cells without inflammation, and its regulation sets the balance between degeneration and cancer. The core machinery here is the caspase cascade: initiators such as CASP8 and CASP9 activate the executioners CASP3, CASP6 and CASP7, which dismantle structural and nuclear substrates including lamin A/C, spectrin and keratin 18 and unleash DNA fragmentation. Two entry routes converge on this cascade — death receptor signalling through FAS and its ligand or TRAIL, and the mitochondrial route where BAX, BID, BIM and NOXA oppose BCL2L1 and MCL1 to release cytochrome c and SMAC/DIABLO, relieving XIAP inhibition. Stress and damage inputs enter through p21, GADD45, CHOP and JUN, while CFLAR, BIRC3 and antioxidant enzymes restrain commitment. Inflammatory caspases and cytokines link the programme to immune killing.

Newly transcribed pre-mRNA must be capped, spliced, cleaved and polyadenylated before it can be exported and translated, and this grouping covers factors that increase the rate or extent of those maturation steps. Enhancing mRNA processing sets how much functional message a gene produces and which isoform predominates, so it feeds directly into tissue-specific splicing programmes, transcription-coupled RNA handling, and quality control of aberrant transcripts. The cap-binding complex subunits NCBP1 and NCBP2 mark the 5' end for splicing and export; SNRNP70 is a core U1 snRNP protein and PRPF19 and SNW1 act within the spliceosome; PRMT5 with its partner WDR77 methylates Sm proteins to license snRNP assembly. Tissue-biased RNA-binding proteins such as CELF3, CELF4, TRA2B and DAZAP1 promote particular splice choices, while UPF1 and UPF3B couple processing to nonsense-mediated decay of transcripts carrying premature stop codons.

In unstressed cells the tumour suppressor p53 is kept scarce, continuously ubiquitinated by MDM2 (with MDM4 and COP1 as further negative regulators) and destroyed by the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core and regulatory subunits is represented here along with ubiquitin itself. DNA damage reverses this: ATM, activated by double-strand breaks, phosphorylates p53 on Ser-15 and, through CHEK2, on Ser-20, while also modifying MDM2, so that the p53-MDM2 interaction is disrupted and p53 escapes turnover. ARF, encoded at the CDKN2A locus, sequesters MDM2 in response to oncogenic signalling, and PHF20 binding contributes to accumulation. The resulting rise in p53 levels licenses transcription of cell cycle arrest, repair and apoptotic targets. Loss of this stabilization step, common in cancers with amplified MDM2 or silenced ARF, leaves cells with wild-type p53 that never accumulates.

This signature marks the B lymphocyte lineage and its terminally differentiated antibody-secreting progeny, the plasma cells that sustain humoral immunity and long-lived serological memory. Much of it is immunoglobulin itself: heavy chain constant regions for IgM/IgD and IgG, kappa and lambda variable and constant segments, and the joining chain that links secretory IgA and IgM into polymers, so the set effectively reads out how much antibody a tissue is making. Around these sit surface and signalling components of B cells — the inhibitory co-receptor CD22, the Src-family kinase BLK, the adaptor STAP1, Fc receptor-like proteins, and the transcription factor SPIB — together with markers of plasma cell identity such as the BAFF/APRIL receptor TNFRSF17 and ER proteins supporting heavy secretory output. Expression of this kind dominates germinal centres and marrow plasma cell niches, tracks tumour-infiltrating B cells, and is the hallmark of myeloma.

Selenium reaches the body as selenite, selenate, selenomethionine or selenocysteine, and selenoamino acid metabolism is the route by which all of these converge on selenide, the common donor used to build selenocysteine and, through it, the selenoproteins that support antioxidant defence and thyroid hormone metabolism. Selenocysteine lyase and cystathionine gamma-lyase release selenium from dietary and recycled forms, methyltransferases and methionine-cycle enzymes handle methylselenol, and excess selenium leaves as methylated or sugar-conjugated species, so the same chemistry sets both nutritional sufficiency and the narrow margin before selenium toxicity. Selenocysteine itself is made on its own tRNA: a kinase phosphorylates the seryl intermediate and SEPSECS converts it to selenocysteinyl-tRNA, which a dedicated elongation factor and a SECIS-binding protein deliver to ribosomes that recode a UGA codon. The large ribosomal and aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase complement reflects this translational step.

Activated CD4 helper T cells that have committed to the Th1 fate display a distinctive set of plasma membrane and membrane-associated proteins, and this surface signature of stimulated Th1 cells is useful both as a marker panel for identifying the subset and as a source of targets for modulating it. Th1 responses drive macrophage activation and clearance of intracellular pathogens, and when unrestrained they contribute to autoimmune tissue damage. The genes here include the inhibitory checkpoint receptor LAG3, which is induced on activated T cells and dampens further responses, the thrombin receptor F2R, orphan G protein-coupled receptors, a tetraspanin, a synaptic vesicle protein and an adaptor of the NEDD4-family ubiquitin ligase network that tunes receptor turnover. Together they mark the shift in surface composition that accompanies antigen-driven activation and effector differentiation rather than a single signalling cascade.

Interferon-inducible guanylate-binding protein 1 coats intracellular bacteria and parasite vacuoles, recruiting caspase-4 and driving pyroptotic death of the infected cell; because that response is destructive, its intensity has to be restrained, and this pathway describes the brakes on GBP-mediated host defense. Caspase-1 cleaves GBP1 at Asp192, generating fragments that can no longer decorate cytosolic Salmonella, recruit caspase-4, or trigger pyroptosis, a negative feedback loop that limits inflammatory cell death during bacterial infection but is not engaged against Toxoplasma, so regulation is pathogen-specific. In parallel, the kinase PIM1 phosphorylates GBP1 at Ser156, creating a binding site for the 14-3-3 protein sigma encoded by SFN, which holds GBP1 in the cytosol away from pathogen membranes. GTP binding allosterically breaks the PIM1 complex, coupling nucleotide state to release. Loss of this tuning shifts the balance toward excessive inflammation and tissue damage.

Rho family GTPases are the switches that let cells rebuild their actin cytoskeleton on demand, and their nucleotide cycle is what sets the timing. Cell migration, adhesion, polarity establishment, cytokinesis and vesicle traffic all depend on it, which is why the same machinery shapes neuronal morphogenesis, leukocyte function and vascular tone, and why its deregulation contributes to invasion and metastasis, immunodeficiency and neurological disease. Classical members such as RHOA, RAC1 and CDC42 alternate between GTP-bound active and GDP-bound inactive states: numerous exchange factors of the DBL and DOCK families load GTP, a large family of GAPs accelerates hydrolysis, and GDIs such as ARHGDIA sequester the inactive protein in cytosol. Activated forms then engage effectors including ROCK kinases, PAKs, formins and WASP/WAVE complexes. Atypical relatives, among them the RND proteins, RHOH and RHOBTB members, lack appreciable hydrolysis and are regulated instead through expression and degradation.

Cells continuously encounter insults — DNA damage, heat, oxidants, nutrient shortage, hypoxia, misfolded protein burden — and this broad response programme is how they detect the damage, pause growth, repair what can be repaired, and die when it cannot. Its coverage here spans the DNA damage checkpoints and repair routes (ATM/ATR, p53, mismatch, nucleotide- and base-excision, homologous recombination and end joining), the heat shock chaperones and HSF1, endoplasmic reticulum stress sensors with ERAD and the integrated stress response through eIF2α kinases and ATF4, antioxidant defence via NRF2, KEAP1, superoxide dismutases and peroxiredoxins, hypoxia sensing by HIF prolyl hydroxylases, nutrient sensing through mTORC1 and AMPK, autophagy and mitophagy, and apoptotic execution. Outcomes include cell cycle arrest, senescence, or death. Deficits give genome instability and cancer predisposition, neurodegeneration, and premature ageing syndromes.

The nucleolus concentrates ribosome biogenesis and a set of stress- and telomere-related activities, and proteins reach it only through targeting signals and chaperone-like escorts; increasing that traffic is what this regulatory process does. Promoting nucleolar accumulation of a partner protein determines where it can act: nucleophosmin shuttles between nucleolus and nucleoplasm and helps retain client proteins there, NMD3 works in the export of the large ribosomal subunit, and PINX1 together with telomerase reverse transcriptase links nucleolar sequestration to control of telomere elongation, since holding telomerase in the nucleolus keeps it away from chromosome ends. Other members, including MCRS1 and the chaperone SIGMAR1, act as binding partners that drive or stabilise this relocalisation. Regulated nucleolar residence of this kind couples ribosome production, cell growth signalling and stress responses to the availability of specific proteins in the right compartment.

Integrin-mediated cell-cell adhesion is how one cell grips another directly, most visibly when leukocytes bind endothelium and each other during immune surveillance. It underlies firm arrest and transmigration of white blood cells at inflamed vessels, immune synapse formation between T cells and antigen-presenting cells, and platelet aggregation in clot formation; loss of it produces leukocyte adhesion deficiency, with recurrent infection and impaired wound healing. Heterodimers pair a beta chain such as ITGB1, ITGB2 or ITGB3 with alpha partners including ITGAL, ITGAM and ITGA4, and engage counter-receptors of the immunoglobulin superfamily, notably ICAM1 and VCAM1. Adhesion is not passive: the intracellular activator FERMT3 (kindlin-3) shifts integrins to a high-affinity state, while SKAP1, WNK1 and the kinase PTK2 couple receptor occupancy to cytoskeletal tension and chemokine-driven signals, linking adhesion to migration and mechanosensing.

Stem and progenitor pools have to be restrained as well as replenished, and this pathway covers the braking signals that slow or halt stem cell proliferation so that cells exit cycle and differentiate. In epithelia this restraint sets the boundary between a dividing basal compartment and the differentiating layers above it: KDF1 limits keratinocyte progenitor divisions and its loss causes ectodermal dysplasia, while the OVOL1 and OVOL2 transcriptional repressors curb progenitor self-renewal and suppress the epithelial-to-mesenchymal shift that SNAI2 promotes. Several microRNAs, including the miR-29, miR-221/222, miR-181 and miR-16 families, act post-transcriptionally on cell cycle and self-renewal transcripts to reinforce the same outcome, with FERMT1 and FBLN1 contributing adhesive and matrix context. Failure of this control permits progenitor expansion, hyperplasia and tumour initiation; excessive restraint depletes regenerative capacity in skin and other renewing tissues.

The interleukin-1 family drives the acute inflammatory response: fever, neutrophil recruitment, acute-phase protein production, and the alarm signalling that follows infection or tissue damage. Eleven related cytokines, including IL1A, IL1B, IL18, IL33 and the IL36 proteins, pair with heterodimeric receptors such as IL1R1, IL18R1 and IL1RL1 that share the IL1RAP co-receptor, while IL1RN, IL1R2, IL18BP and SIGIRR act as decoys or antagonists that keep the response bounded. IL1B and IL18 are made as inactive precursors and require inflammasome caspase-1 cleavage before release, linking this signalling to pyroptotic cell death through gasdermin D. Activated receptors recruit MYD88, IRAK kinases and TRAF6, and through TAK1 and the IKK complex trigger ubiquitin- and proteasome-dependent degradation of IkB, freeing NF-kB, alongside p38, JNK and ERK activation. Excessive output underlies autoinflammatory syndromes, gout and psoriasis, and is blocked therapeutically by receptor antagonism.

When a presynaptic terminal releases neurotransmitter, the receiving cell must convert that chemical signal back into an electrical and biochemical one, and this postsynaptic arm of synaptic transmission is where that conversion happens. It sets the speed and strength of every synapse, and its plasticity underlies learning and memory, while mutations in its receptor subunits cause epilepsies, myasthenic syndromes, hyperekplexia and intellectual disability. Ligand-gated channels "" AMPA, NMDA and kainate glutamate receptors, GABA-A and glycine receptors, nicotinic and serotonin type 3 receptors "" mediate fast excitation and inhibition, while metabotropic GABA-B receptors act through G protein subunits, adenylate cyclases, phospholipase C and inwardly rectifying potassium channels. Downstream, calmodulin, CaMKII, PKA, PKC and ERK relay calcium entry to CREB-dependent transcription. Scaffolds such as PSD-95 family proteins, GRIP and PICK1, together with AP-2 adaptors, motors and tubulin, control receptor trafficking, anchoring and turnover at the postsynaptic density.

When a vessel wall is breached, platelets must stick to the damaged surface and then to each other to seal it; platelet aggregation is that plug-forming step, and without it bleeding continues, while inappropriate activation produces the occlusive thrombi of heart attack and stroke. Tethering begins with the GPIb-IX-V complex capturing von Willebrand factor on exposed collagen, and firm adhesion follows when integrin alphaIIb-beta3 switches to a high-affinity state and cross-links neighbouring platelets through fibrinogen chains and fibronectin. Inside the platelet, RAP1B loading by CalDAG-GEFI and cAMP-responsive exchange factors, together with talin binding to the beta3 tail, drives that conformational change, while Src-family and SYK kinases, FAK and adaptor scaffolds transmit force and receptor occupancy back into the cytoskeleton. Thrombin and adrenergic receptors amplify the response, linking coagulation and sympathetic tone to plug stability.

A mixed group of broadly expressed regulators that keep housekeeping functions of the cell running: chromatin-associated and transcriptional components, RNA-binding proteins, and machinery for endosomal membrane traffic and cytoskeletal contractility. Several members act on gene expression — a chromatin-interacting subunit of a histone deacetylase-containing repressor complex, a cyclin partner of the CDK8 kinase module of Mediator, and the zinc-finger transcription factor SP3. Others control the fate of mRNAs after they are made: MBNL1 governs alternative splicing of muscle and neuronal transcripts, FMR1 represses translation at synapses and its loss causes fragile X syndrome, and G3BP2 nucleates stress granules when translation stalls. A third arm handles membranes and organelles, including the ESCRT-associated ATPase VPS4B in multivesicular body formation, a phosphoinositide phosphatase acting at the Golgi and ER, and a myosin phosphatase targeting subunit that tunes actomyosin tension.

Cells acquire iron from their surroundings either by pumping it across the plasma membrane or by internalising iron-loaded carriers, and this import step sets how much iron is available for haem synthesis, iron-sulfur cluster assembly and oxidative metabolism. It matters most in the duodenal enterocyte, where dietary iron enters the body, and in hepatocytes and macrophages that buffer systemic iron; too little causes anaemia, too much drives tissue iron overload. Because only ferrous iron is transported, surface ferrireductases such as CYBRD1 and the STEAP proteins reduce Fe(III) before the divalent metal transporter SLC11A2 carries it into the cytoplasm, with SLC39A8 and SLC39A14 providing additional routes shared with manganese and zinc. A transferrin receptor family member reports iron status to hepatic signalling, secreted lipocalin-2 scavenges siderophore-bound iron, and inflammatory and hypoxic inputs adjust the whole process to demand.

Cells that lose contact with the extracellular matrix normally die, and the tuning of that death programme — the regulation of anoikis — determines whether a detached epithelial cell survives or is eliminated. This surveillance keeps epithelia anchored and confines them to their proper tissue compartment; when it is dampened, detached cells persist, which is a prerequisite for invasion, circulation in the bloodstream and metastatic colonisation. Integrin engagement through fibronectin-binding subunits such as ITGA5 and ITGB1 sustains adhesion-dependent signalling via focal adhesion kinase, SRC and PI3K subunits, feeding into anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members BCL2, BCL2L1 and MCL1 that hold back mitochondrial permeabilisation. Set against these are suppressors of metastasis and transcriptional regulators including BRMS1, SNAI2, NOTCH1 and Groucho-family corepressors, which shift the threshold in either direction. The balance links cell adhesion and matrix sensing to apoptotic commitment.

Moving proteins, membranes and cargo between compartments is the logistical backbone of a eukaryotic cell, and intracellular transport covers the steps by which newly made proteins enter the secretory pathway, vesicles bud and fuse, endosomes mature, and macromolecules cross the nuclear envelope. Without it, secretion and receptor turnover fail and misfolded protein accumulates. Distinct arms are represented here: a signal recognition particle subunit and the SEC63 translocon component direct cotranslational entry into the endoplasmic reticulum, where TMX1 assists oxidative folding; nucleoporins of the NUP107-133 scaffold form part of the nuclear pore for nucleocytoplasmic exchange; an exocyst subunit targets vesicles to the plasma membrane; clathrin-associated CLINT1 supports endocytic uptake. Phosphoinositide kinases PIK3C2A and PIKFYVE generate the lipid marks that specify endosomal identity, read by FYVE-domain proteins, while the AAA-ATPase VPS4B recycles ESCRT machinery during multivesicular body formation.

Cap-dependent translation begins when the 5' cap of an mRNA is recognised and the message is prepared for loading onto a small ribosomal subunit. This step sets the rate of protein synthesis for most cellular mRNAs and is the point at which growth factor and nutrient signalling control how much protein a cell makes. eIF4E must first be freed from the inhibitory 4E-BP, after which it joins the scaffold eIF4G and the helicase eIF4A to form the cap-binding complex; eIF4B and eIF4H stimulate unwinding of secondary structure near the 5' end, while poly(A)-binding protein links the two ends of the message. The activated mRNA is then bound by the 43S pre-initiation complex their small subunit proteins, eIF3 subunits, the ternary eIF2-GTP-Met-tRNA complex and eIF1A committing the transcript to scanning and start codon selection.

Meiosis must not proceed until chromosomes have been replicated, paired, recombined and correctly attached to the spindle, and meiotic cell cycle checkpoint signaling is the surveillance that enforces that order. Its outputs are the delays that give cells time to repair double-strand breaks and to correct faulty kinetochore attachments; when the surveillance fails, gametes carry unrepaired breaks or the wrong chromosome number, a route to infertility, oocyte loss and aneuploid conceptions. Two arms are represented here. HORMAD1 and HORMAD2, with the AAA+ ATPase TRIP13 that removes them from synapsed axes, monitor synapsis and unrepaired recombination intermediates along meiotic chromosomes, while HUS1 and RAD1 contribute to the clamp that senses damaged or stalled DNA. Kinetochore components including KNL1, ZWINT and the MPS1-family kinase encoded by TTK support attachment error correction and spindle checkpoint signaling before anaphase.
